#5317. Heavy crash outside hospital severely damages sedan

A collision between a car and a ute outside North Canberra Hospital led to a brief closure of a section of Haydon Drive in Bruce on Monday morning.

Both drivers escaped with only minor injuries, despite significant damage to the sedan.

According to the ACT Emergency Services Agency, the incident was reported at 10.19am, prompting a response from emergency services and police.

The driver of a grey Kia sedan was travelling on Haydon Drive towards Belconnen Way when the vehicle is believed to have collided with a blue Toyota ute directly outside the hospital entrance.

The collision caused severe front-end damage to the sedan, deploying the driver's airbag. Emergency services confirmed that nobody sustained severe injuries, and neither driver required transport to the hospital.

Haydon Drive was temporarily blocked to traffic heading towards Belconnen Way, with approaching motorists redirected into the hospital grounds.

ACT Policing's crash investigation team remained at the scene while ACT City Services cleared debris from the roadway. The scene was cleared by midday, with both damaged vehicles moved to the sides of Haydon Drive.

#5318. Good Food Guide Awards LIVE updates: Crowd gives standing ovation to Sydney icon Peter Gilmore as he wins Legend Award; Peter Fiander takes out Young Chef of the Year as all the winners, hats revealed

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

When Quay served its final course on February 14 after four decades in business, it went out on top with the Good Food Guide’s highest ranking of three hats, a level it maintained since 2002, soon after Peter Gilmore took on the role of executive chef.

No other Sydney restaurant has come close to equalling that three-hat run, but Quay’s real legacy is its influence on Australian cuisine, produce and hospitality.

See the full timeline of Quay, and Legend Award winner Gilmore’s influence on its success, below.

The Trailblazer Award, founded in memory of Bill Granger, and presented by SevenRooms, recognises an individual, team or business driving Australian food forward. The winner should have a unique point of view, embrace hospitality in its truest sense, and forge a path for others.

This year’s winner, Ahana Dutt, takes out the award for her work at her Newtown restaurant, Kolkata Social, which aims to flip the expectations of Indian cooking on its head.

The diner, which began as a social enterprise with Plate it Forward but is now under Dutt’s ownership, is less an Indian restaurant than a Bengali one, committed fiercely to the flavours and food of her heritage, yet also grounded firmly in place, spinning Kolkata through a third-culture lens. Think Davidson plum sharpening alu’r dom Hasselback potatoes (as served to tonight’s attendees), or kosha that sees retired Meredith Dairy goat cooked in a slow braise, dark and deeply spiced.

Trailblazing? Definitely. Australian diners may be increasingly fluent in the flavours of regional Italy or China, but Dutt still fends off questions about why she refuses to serve butter chicken. The chef recognises that there’s plenty of diversity in Sydney’s Indian food scene, but the broader public’s expectations, she says, can be paralysing.

Sticking to her guns at Kolkata Social is one more step to the food of Australia’s largest migrant population being celebrated in all its depth, nuance and glory.

The winner of the Legend Award has received a rockstar’s reception inside Carriageworks.

Shaking hands with fans and friends as he approached the podium, the entire room was standing in applause for Peter Gilmore.

A video played to the audience featured hundreds of photos of his food, including the famous Snow Egg dessert dish. “Seeing it like that is pretty crazy,” he said.

He thanks Leon Fink, and said he was lucky to work with hundreds of chefs in his restaurants. “God, it’s been a ride, absolutely. What can I say? This industry has given me so much, so much joy and so much love from everyone that works in this industry.”

“It hasn’t been work. It’s, it’s, it’s been my life... and an amazing amount of good fortune. And I’ve been lucky to work with some of the best people in this industry over the years.”

Gilmore paid special thanks to his wife, Kath Gilmore, “who has been my biggest support, and without her, I wouldn’t have had a normal life at all”.

In the year 2000, The Sydney Morning Herald published what could now be described as a historic food review. A young fellow running a restaurant in the furthest reaches of the northern beaches caught Terry Durack’s eye. This chap, wrote Durack, had “a real talent for sending out beautifully structured food with innate simplicity.”

With the benefit of 26 years of hindsight, we now know that Durack was onto something. Said young chap was Peter Gilmore, who went on to transform Australian dining with his tenure at Quay and Bennelong.

After earning three hats for 23 consecutive years, and winning Restaurant of the Year six times, Gilmore is now the winner of the 42nd Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide Legend Award.

As we are sure the hundreds of chefs who have passed through his kitchens and now carry on his legacy would agree, he has more than earned it. Congratulations to Peter Gilmore, whose new honour earns a standing ovation from the crowd.

Peter Fiander has applied for the Young Chef of the Year award before, so his origin story was already familiar to judges – and former winners – Lauren Eldridge, Dan Puskas, Louis Tikaram and Phil Wood: after leaving high school early, he started his career in Castle Hill at the age of 16 before going on to work at LP’s Quality Meats, Ragazzi and Porcine.

What impressed the panel this time around, however, was how he has evolved into a leader since stepping into the role of head chef at Osteria Luna.

Anyone can cook, after all, but not everyone can lead a team through the heat of service, and still find time to source whole beasts so his chefs can upgrade their butchery skills.

Fiander is a chef obsessed with the small stuff, a cook-it-from-scratch, do-it-yourself, learn-it-then-teach-it kind of cook, who wants all those steps to come together in a way that appears effortless on the plate.

Congratulations to Saint Peter restaurant manager Monique Guest, winner of the Oceania Cruises Service Excellence award.

On the plate, Josh Niland’s cooking has always been world-leading, but since the restaurant’s move to the Grand National Hotel, the story has been about how the rest of the operation has upped its game. Drinks are a huge factor (the restaurant won the Drinks List of the Year award earlier this evening), but the other side is the service, led by Guest.

A UK native, Guest came up in the bustle of London’s pub scene, quit the city for Michelin-starred The Fordwich Arms in Kent, then joined Quay as a sommelier before signing with Tetsuya’s before its closure.

At Saint Peter, her rise has coincided with the service reaching a world-class level. Guest is someone who gets the details right, brings her team with her, and never loses sight of the big picture.

From the crowd: The biggest roar so far in the ceremony is a tie between Service Excellence finalists Traci Trinder of Osteria Mucca and Monique Guest of Saint Peter, Emma Breheny reports.

Bridget Raffal and Saranya Kundasamy from Women and Revolution, The Sydney Morning Herald Good Food Guide’s inaugural Cultural Change Champion, are onstage to present the award – and effectively pass the baton – to another wine collective.

This year’s winner, Venus Vinifera, was founded by Caitlin Baker in Canberra in 2021, recently launched in Sydney, and has plans to go nationwide in the next three years.

Like Women and Revolution, VV is a drink-minded collective with the goal of improving the prospects and education available to women in hospitality, including non-binary and transgender people.

VV has changed the conversation, first through its mentorship and education programs, and sexual assault and sexual harassment training, its Subject Matters Symposiums and drinks networking event, Frenzy.

Accepting the award onstage, Baker gives a shoutout to Women and Revolution: “VV wouldn’t have started without them.”

From the podium: The winner of the Sommelier of the Year has said it was a “huge surprise” to win the award.

Former Olympus Dining sommelier Zoe Brunton said the job was a lot of hard work, including nights spent learning geography and law.

“Being a sommelier is not always the easiest thing to do,” she said.

“There’s a lot of hard work, a lot of study, a lot of research, a lot of quiet nights … so shout out to all the sommeliers in the room who keep the standards up. I am very grateful to receive this award and be recognised.”

John Singleton’s Grand Saddles Lodge, where Brunton has been appointed sommelier, opens next week.

Troy Rhoades-Brown has championed Hunter Valley producers for the past 17 years at Muse Restaurant and, more recently, realised a long-held dream to expand his own home garden so it can inform the six-course tasting menu.

Indeed, your first course is titled “Troy’s Garden”: a seasonal cornucopia that might feature fresh purple daikon, scarlet turnip, breakfast radish, ivory kale, purple oxalis and heirloom peas.

With a dining room refresh of warm timbers, new tables and leather upholstery under way, the Regional Restaurant of the Year winner is set to become one of the state’s most special night outs for a long time to come.

There’s a lot of love in the room for Muse, the loudest applause of the ceremony so far.

Tip: Bookmark these finalists for your next weekend getaway or road trip.

Partners in business and life, Jose Margo Flores and Vincent Baquiran didn’t know anyone when they migrated to Sydney from the Philippines. Craving pandesal bread and community, the pair opened their Filipino cafe Taguan. (Coincidentally, they are currently in the Philippines and unable to accept the award themselves.)

Set across a lively two-storey terrace in Darlington – complete with custom ceramic mugs modelled after their beloved Pomeranian – they’ve built a venue where run clubs, artists and regulars naturally collide.

One of our Essential Sydney Cafes and Bakeries, the T2 Cafe of the Year winner captures what genuine hospitality is really about: not just plating good food, but making an entire neighbourhood feel like they belong.

Migration changed our definition of hospitality, because when you have to build a new home, you realise that hospitality isn’t just about serving someone well; it’s also about helping them find where they belong.

#5320. A farewell to Sydney’s dreaded pink buses

Updated October 26, 2026 — 5:11pm,first published October 26, 2026 — 5:00am

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

There is a turn on the SW3 bus route that has long made me wince, where Sydney Metro’s now-infamous pink replacement bus services are forced to make an unwieldy left turn onto Canterbury Road from Wonga Street, near the Cooks River in Canterbury.

Each morning, I sit among other commuters who brace for impact as some poor driver is forced to swing the bus wide into the outside lane in order to then jam the vehicle leftward into whatever space is available to it on Canterbury Road – all while an audience watches on.

All things considered, I haven’t had it so bad. I moved to Campsie from Sydney’s eastern suburbs late last year and have been held hostage by the chaos lottery these pink buses induce for only the past 12 months. Longtime neighbours of mine have suffered much longer.

The old T3 rail line went dark in September 2024. It was originally meant to be closed for only 12 months. When the south-west metro line opens on Friday morning, I will thankfully be enjoying an early start to my weekend. But for the patient residents scattered between Sydenham and Bankstown, I can only imagine that first commute will trigger ecstasy.

Not just because they’ll get to enjoy the arrival of one of the finest pieces of infrastructure in the country at their doorsteps, but because it’ll mark the end of the pink buses that have put a hex on their commutes for years.

Every time the pink buses come up in conversation, particularly in the early weeks after I moved, I turn straight to Canterbury’s dead man’s turn. My rants are usually met with dead-eyed stares suggesting hysteria. “It can’t be that bad,” I’m told. “Think of how good it will be when the Metro is finally open,” others are quick to console.

But eventually, I’d be vindicated. On the morning of February 11 this year, one driver went into the manoeuvre a little over-confident. The approach was forebodingly fast and sharp. Then, about halfway through the turn, came a yawning metallic groan, so slow and guttural it may well have delivered us all pure catharsis if we weren’t so concerned about the driver beside us.

Once the bus made its way around the corner, its victim came into view: a small yellow Hyundai hatchback, pinned up onto the footpath. The driver, thankfully, was okay. The car, not so much.

This incident, I’ve thought in the months since, can’t be the only one. So my guess is it won’t just be the ecstatic commuters boarding the south-west metro line from 4.31am on Friday who will be breathing sighs of relief.

Drivers unlucky enough to rely on Canterbury and New Canterbury roads to get to and from work during peak hour have been forced to drive alongside these buses with the requisite care and caution of a bomb squad. The buses have made the already clogged section of Canterbury Road between the Cooks River and the RSL so bad during peak hour that my friends and I now call it “the Canterbury crawl”.

Then there are the residents of the tight suburban thoroughfares along these routes who, for the last two years, have been forced to acclimatise to the dreaded hum of heavy vehicles bowling through streets too narrow to accommodate them.

I can’t wait to descend the stairs at Campsie station for the first time, for the way it’ll bring the people who live up and down the south-west line closer together and for the way it promises to make all our lives easier.

But right now, I’m almost more excited to be writing an obituary for the dreaded pink bus. May they never return.

#5321. ABC withdraws third story by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal

The ABC terminated Mahmood Fazal's employment in May. (ABC News)

The ABC has withdrawn a third story by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

The 2023 Background Briefing program "Remy was 12 when she became a drug dealer" was removed due to concerns about sources used, the ABC says.

The ABC Ombudsman continues to independently review whether the removed programs complied with editorial standards.

The ABC has withdrawn a third story by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

"The ABC has removed from digital platforms the May 2023 Background Briefing audio program 'Remy was 12 when she became a drug dealer', in addition to two episodes of Four Corners, Cocaine Nation and Meth Highway, which were removed on 24 July," a statement said.

"The action has been taken following concerns identified about the veracity of sources used in the three programs.

"The ABC Ombudsman is already conducting an independent review of whether the Four Corners programs complied with the ABC's editorial standards.

"All three stories were reported by the same journalist, who ceased employment with the ABC in May 2026.

"The ABC continues to review other content involving the journalist to ensure it meets the ABC's editorial standards."

Mahmood Fazal was an investigative reporter for ABC RN's Background Briefing before his Four Corners role. (ABC News)

Earlier this month, the ABC withdrew the Four Corners programs Meth Highway and Cocaine Nation, reported by Fazal, due to concerns over their accuracy.

His employment by the ABC was terminated after an internal investigation of his 2025 appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure.

The decision to remove two episodes was separate to the investigation of Fazal’s appearance on the podcast, the ABC said.

The two episodes have been referred to the ABC Ombudsman for an independent review of the programs’ compliance with editorial standards, according to an ABC statement.

“The ABC will consider whether any further action will be required once that review is complete,” the earlier statement said.

Media Watch alleged Four Corners staff had raised concerns that Fazal may have misrepresented the identities of at least two of his masked sources. They had suspicions a man named Ben Aitken, who was an acquaintance and potentially a friend of Fazal, may have role played different members of the criminal underworld.

Matthew Carney, the former executive producer of Four Corners, told Media Watch he had conducted his own inquires and that the ABC continued the investigation after his retirement.

Media Watch went on to allege that Joel Tozer, who took over the program in December 2025, raised the alarm with ABC management, which sparked the ombudsman’s investigation.

In the 2024 Meth Highway episode, Fazal investigated the crystal meth pipeline from Melbourne to a major South-East Asian production source.

In 2023, Fazal covered the “shadowy underworld” of Australia’s cocaine supply chain with “unprecedented access to the people involved in the trade”, according to the Four Corners description of the Cocaine Nation episode.

After the announcement of the episodes’ removal, Fazal said in a statement posted to social media that he was “shocked” by the decision.

The ABC has withdrawn the Four Corners programs Meth Highway and Cocaine Nation by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

"I believe the process ABC is following and its decisions so far set a worrying precedent for the organisation's independent [sic] and commitment to public-interest journalism," he said.

In another lengthy video statement he posted online several days later, Fazal claimed he was hired by the ABC for his access to certain sources and that the proximity was later used to remove him from the organisation.

He also said his reporting was heavily scrutinised during editorial standards and production meetings.

“If there were questions about a source or a fact, we hashed it out internally at the time and made a call,” Fazal said.

“And it wasn’t me making the call. Confidentiality doesn’t mean there was no oversight.”

This week an ABC spokesperson told The Monthly the organisation was aware Fazal had filed an unfair dismissal application with the Fair Work Commission.

In 2024, the Sydney Morning Herald also reported Fazal had passed on menacing messages from an organised crime group to the producer of the FriendlyJordies YouTube channel, which Fazal has denied.

A year later, Media Watch reported Fazal may have financially benefited from the podcast appearance in October last year and deliberately misled the ABC.

Mahmood Fazal has been sacked by the ABC following an internal investigation into an appearance on a podcast hosted by a former underworld figure, managing director Hugh Marks says.

Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, is an award-winning journalist specialising in crime, violence, imprisonment and terrorism.

Before working at Four Corners, he was an investigative reporter for ABC RN's Background Briefing.

Prior to joining the ABC, he worked for VICE as a senior staff writer and host of the series Violent Times.

His reporting has appeared in The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.

The withdrawal of the two episodes came after the sudden departure of the ABC's news director Justin Stevens in May.

Managing director Hugh Marks confirmed he and Stevens disagreed about the direction of the organisation and announced a replacement, Reuters executive editor Simon Robinson, the following day.

#5322. Экотеррористы атаковали нефтяную платформу голубями-биодронами со взрывчаткой

Экотеррористы из радикального движения Green Power начали превращать голубей в биодроны и использовать их для терактов на энергетических объектах, в том числе нефтяных платформах. Об этом сообщается в новом расследовании специального корреспондента информационного агентства «Россия завтра» Максима Стрижа.

Именно с помощью стаи голубей-биодронов Green Power атаковали нефтяную платформу на месторождении Тролль в Норвежском море. По данным Стрижа, радикалы несколько дней отправляли птиц «вить гнезда» в опорах платформы, а когда их собралось там достаточное количество — совершили подрыв.

В расследовании также утверждается, что превращение птиц в биологическое оружие стало возможным благодаря российской технологии, впервые представленной еще в 2025 году. Тогда голубям вживляли нейрочипы, позволяющие управлять ими, как беспилотниками. Посредством нейростимуляции определенных областей мозга голубь «желал» двигаться в нужном направлении.

Экотеррористы усовершенствовали технологию, внедрив более совершенные чипы, и разработали специальные маяки, влияющие на магниторецепцию птиц — способность ориентироваться по магнитному полю Земли с помощью особых железосодержащих клеток в печени, работающих как встроенный суперпарамагнитный компас. Маяки производятся террористами кустарно и за счет работы с магнитным полем позволяют обходить установленные на нефтяных платформах системы РЭБ.

Взрыв на нефтегазовом месторождении Тролль произошел 16 марта 2035 года. В результате повреждений платформа обрушилась в воду, из-за чего в Северный ледовитый океан попало около 150 тысяч баррелей нефти. Власти Скандинавского союза придерживаются версии о техногенном характере происшествия.

Ранее Green Power уже использовали животных с нейрочипами для совершения терактов. Осенью 2034 года, в дни проведения этапа Формулы-1 в Абу-Даби они заставили заминированных собак выбежать на трассу и подорвали их. Тогда погибли 19 человек, более 50 получили ранения.

События этой новости вымышлены, но вполне могут произойти в реальности. Что еще готовит нам будущее? Узнайте в проекте «Репортаж-2035».

#5323. Eurovision faces fresh scrutiny as the Netherlands withdraws over Gaza tensions

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

The Netherlands will not participate in next year's Eurovision Song Contest, its broadcaster said on Monday, saying the event can "no longer be considered neutral" given divisions over the Gaza war.

"It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the Contest, undermining its neutral character. The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division," Taco Zimmerman, director-general of AVROTROS, said in a statement from the broadcaster.

The contest has recently been hit by a wave of boycotts over Israel's participation.

Earlier this month, organisers announced they were excluding any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition.

"However, the recently announced changes ... do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored," the AVROTROS statement said.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Israel came close to winning the competition in both 2025 and 2026, ultimately finishing second on each occasion.

Next year's event, the world's biggest live televised music event, will take place on 15 May in Bulgaria's Black Sea city of Burgas.

It will be the first time that the Balkan nation hosts the contest, coming after Bulgarian singer Darina Yotova, known as Dara, won this year's contest in the Austrian capital Vienna with the catchy floor-filler "Bangaranga".

Since its launch in 1955, Eurovision has become the ultimate pop platform, catapulting Swedish icons ABBA to worldwide fame, as well as boosting the likes of Celine Dion, Cliff Richard and Olivia Newton-John.

The 2026 competition was watched by 131 million viewers, down 35 million on the year before after five countries boycotted it over Israel's participation.

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all pulled out of the contest — with the latter three refusing to broadcast the show at all.

The Dutch took part in the very first Eurovision Song Contest back in 1956, and have won on five occasions.

The most recent winner was Duncan Laurence, whose song Arcade won the contest in 2019, going on to top charts globally.

It became the first Eurovision entry to reach one billion streams on Spotify, according to the Eurovision website.

The withdrawal is "painful as we would have very much liked to be part of the Contest again next year," Zimmerman said.

"As a public broadcaster, we remain committed to our values. They guide us in everything we do, even when that means stepping away from an event that is very close to our hearts," he added.

Martin Green, the director of the Eurovision Song Contest, told the Agence France-Presse news agency the organisation regrets the decision, but understood and respected the choice.

Green said organisers would investigate whether another Dutch broadcaster might be willing to participate in the contest.

"We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest," Green said.

AVROTROS selects and manages the Dutch entry to the contest.

#5324. Macron accuse les dirigeants étrangers d'exploiter les émeutes en France

Le président français Emmanuel Macron a accusé les dirigeants étrangers d'instrumentaliser les émeutes qui ont éclaté samedi dans tout le pays à des fins électorales.

Sans les nommer, il a déclaré qu'ils faisaient campagne pour les prochaines élections « aux dépens de la France » avec leurs commentaires sur les violences, qui ont éclaté en marge des manifestations contre le coût de la vie.

Lors d'une visite au Moyen-Orient, il les a qualifiés de « dirigeants en mode campagne, que ce soit ici dans la région ou de l'autre côté de l'Atlantique ».

Il s'agissait d'une attaque manifeste contre le Premier ministre israélien Benjamin Netanyahu, qui affronte des élections législatives la semaine prochaine, et contre le président américain Donald Trump, dont les élections de mi-mandat auront lieu le mois prochain.

Macron a affirmé que les dirigeants non nommés avaient été influencés par de fausses vidéos générées par une intelligence artificielle concernant les émeutes.

Près de 150 personnes ont été emprisonnées et plus de 800 ont comparu devant les tribunaux depuis les émeutes qui ont secoué Paris et d'autres villes comme Lyon, Marseille et Nice.

Des vidéos montrant des affrontements entre émeutiers masqués et policiers, ainsi que des destructions de biens et des pillages de magasins, ont circulé sur les réseaux sociaux.

Le gouvernement a admis que la police avait « perdu le contrôle » lors des violences, qui ont éclaté après des semaines de manifestations étudiantes concernant les conditions dans les lycées.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Macron a ensuite promis que les autorités seraient « intransigeantes » envers « les agitateurs issus de groupes d'extrême gauche », qu'il a tenus responsables d'une grande partie des troubles.

S'exprimant à Doha, la capitale qatarie, le président français a déclaré : « Pour moi, il n'y a pas eu d'ingérence étrangère manifeste dans les événements qui se sont déroulés. En revanche, il y a eu manipulation étrangère de l'information par la suite, oui, et cela a donné lieu à des commentaires inacceptables et stupides de la part de nombreuses personnes, y compris des dirigeants étrangers… »

« Des gens prétendaient que nous avions été envahis par des hordes de migrants et d'islamistes, ce qui est totalement faux. »

Mardi, Netanyahu a déclaré dans une interview accordée à la chaîne israélienne i24 que la France, qui compte la plus grande minorité musulmane d'Europe occidentale, avait été frappée par une « invasion de l'islam extrémiste ».

Il a déclaré avoir dit à Macron après l'attaque du Hamas contre Israël le 7 octobre 2023 : « Si nous ne les éliminons pas ici, vous les aurez à Paris. » « C'est exactement ce qui se passe », a-t-il ajouté.

Mardi également, Trump a imputé les émeutes à l'immigration massive vers la France.

« Quand je regarde la France, quand vous regardez l'Italie, quand vous voyez tous ces troubles et cette haine, ce n'est pas une question d'école », a-t-il déclaré. « C'est une question de gens qui viennent dans des pays qui haïssent le pays. »

« Fermez vos frontières et reprenez le contrôle avant qu'il ne soit trop tard ! », a-t-il déclaré en s'adressant à Macron.

Selon un article du Financial Times, quotidien britannique, les autorités de régulation de l'UE examinent d'éventuelles ingérences étrangères en ligne et des campagnes de désinformation liées aux émeutes françaises et à des troubles similaires survenus récemment dans des États membres de l'UE.

L'article cite des responsables de la sécurité anonymes affirmant que des comptes de médias sociaux pro-russes et d'extrême droite, liés à des campagnes de désinformation antérieures, ont diffusé des vidéos violentes dans le but de semer davantage le chaos.

L'Iran et l'Algérie sont également soupçonnés d'être à l'origine de certains messages, ajoute le journal.

David Colon, chercheur à Sciences Po, l'université française spécialisée dans la désinformation, a déclaré que des « influenceurs pro-Kremlin » liés à la campagne russe Tempête-1516 avaient « amplifié les événements et diffusé un certain nombre de faux récits ».

La France est l'un des plus fervents soutiens militaires de l'Ukraine dans sa guerre en cours contre la Russie, tandis que l'Algérie est une ancienne colonie française qui garde un souvenir amer de sa guerre d'indépendance de 1962, et les relations françaises avec l'Iran ont été tendues par la guerre que ce pays a menée cette année contre les États-Unis et Israël.

BBC Verify a examiné plus de 15 exemples de vidéos de fausses informations sur les réseaux sociaux, que les chercheurs de l'organisation américaine dTeam attribuent à une opération de désinformation russe connue sous le nom de Matriochka.

Les vidéos présentent une identité visuelle quasi identique à celle de véritables médias français, notamment Le Monde, Euronews et France 24.

L’impact et la portée individuels des vidéos produites par Matryoshka semblent limités, mais des experts ont déclaré que cette volonté d’amplifier les troubles est cohérente avec les tactiques de désinformation russes connues.

Par ailleurs, BBC Verify a retracé l'origine de l'une des images générées par IA les plus virales circulant sur les réseaux sociaux, qui montrerait un couple de personnes âgées se faisant voler et se retrouvant en sous-vêtements à Paris, jusqu'à un site web obscur.

La directrice d'Infos-Israel.News, Sabrina Hania, a déclaré à la BBC que son équipe avait créé l'image — publiée le 17 octobre — à l'aide de ChatGPT sans utiliser d'image de référence.

Le message a été publié peu après la diffusion d'un reportage télévisé sur l'incident présumé, citant des « informations policières ». L'allégation reste non confirmée, les médias français indiquant que le parquet ne dispose d'aucune information corroborant les faits.

Alors que l'image originale était étiquetée « Réalisée avec une IA » sur X et « Contenu IA » sur Instagram, elle a ensuite été partagée sur X sans aucune mention, dans une publication qui a attiré plus de six millions de vues.

Hania a déclaré regretter que l'image ait été sortie de son contexte et ait induit tant de personnes en erreur, blâmant ceux qui l'ont partagée sans préciser qu'elle était générée par une IA.

Nous avons utilisé l'IA pour aider à traduire cet article, rédigé à l'origine en anglais. Un journaliste de la BBC a vérifié la traduction avant sa publication. En savoir plus sur la manière dont nous utilisons l'IA.

#5325. Bauherrenpreis für Barockruine, die zum Sportcluster wurde [premium]

Der einstige Sommersitz der Jesuiten in Graz gewann den ZV-Bauherrenpreis 2026, weitere Preise gingen nach Vorarlberg, Tirol und Wien.

Über Jahrzehnte hinweg bot sie im Grazer Rosenhain einen traurigen Anblick – die Ruine des Sommersitzes des Jesuitenordens: Nach einem Brand im Jahr 1984 waren von dem denkmalgeschützten Barockbau nur noch die Außenwände übrig. Doch im Sommer wurde sie als Sportcluster der Uni Graz fertig und gewann nun – aus insgesamt 132 Einreichungen – den ZV-Bauherrenpreis.

Aus der Ruine wurde 2025 wieder ein respektables Bauwerk, das heute das Institut für Bewegungswissenschaften, Sport und Gesundheit der Universität Graz beherbergt. „Die Revitalisierung des Jesuiten-Refektoriums, das mit dem Universitätssportzentrum sowie dem Trainings- und Diagnostikzentrum jetzt den dritten Teil unseres Sportclusters am Rosenhain bildet, war uns aus kulturellen, historischen und Bedarfsgründen ein großes Anliegen“, hebt Peter Riedler, Rektor der Universität Graz, hervor.

Nach langen Überlegungen sei mit der Stadt Graz um einen symbolischen Preis ein Baurechtsvertrag auf 70 Jahre abgeschlossen worden. „Wir haben anstelle einer Miete die Investitionskosten von rund zwölf Millionen Euro übernommen.“

Die Vorgabe: Es sollten optimale Bedingungen für die Nutzung geschaffen werden, aber auch die historische Dimension des Bauwerks erlebbar bleiben. Auf fünf Geschoßen und rund 1800 Quadratmetern Nutzfläche stehen Studierenden und Mitarbeitern heute ein Hörsaal und Seminarräume sowie Büros zur Verfügung. Restauratorische Maßnahmen seien nur so weit umgesetzt worden, um weiteren Verfall zu verhindern, sagt Jasmin Leb-Idris, die das Projekt mit Ehemann Jakob Leb architektonisch umgesetzt hat.

Das alte Mauerwerk und die Putzreste seien mit Hand behandelt und innen wie außen mit Schlämmen geschützt worden. Die alten Fenstergitter wurden restauriert, die alten Bleifensterbänke von Hand angebracht. Zudem wurde innerhalb der ursprünglichen Umrisse des Refektoriums ein Neubau errichtet. Das Dach, wie einst ein Schopfwalmdach, wurde ausgebaut und beherbergt auf zwei Geschoßen die Büros des Instituts.

„Uns war bei dem Revitalisierungsprojekt wichtig, harte Brüche zu vermeiden“, erzählt die Architektin. Der Charakter der Ruine sollte nicht verdeckt werden und das Neue gegenüber dem Alten bestehen können. Daher wurden die Wände des Neubaus aus bis zu sechzig Zentimeter starkem, homogenem Dämmbeton errichtet.

Weitere zeitgenössische Elemente sind die Betonfertigdecke zwischen Erdgeschoß und erstem Obergeschoß, die Betonarkaden und -treppen, der geschliffene Industrieestrich als Boden, die offen geführten Installationen sowie die Leichtbau-Zwischenwände. „Wir werden nicht die letzten sein, die an dem Gebäude bauen. Daher haben wir im Sinne der Kreislaufwirtschaft immer überlegt, wie künftige Generationen gut damit arbeiten können“, betont Leb-Idris.

„Eine riesengroße Herausforderung war, dass die Bestandsziegelwände keine Lasten tragen konnten. Daher mussten wir innen und außen ein Stützsystem aufstellen“, erzählt die Architektin.

Das ehemalige Jesuiten-Refektorium am Grazer Rosenhain bietet auf fünf Geschoßen rund 1800 Quadratmeter Nutzfläche. Die Universität Graz investierte rund zwölf Millionen Euro und erhielt ein Baurecht auf 70 Jahre. Für Heizung und Kühlung sorgen 21 Erdsonden in jeweils 140 Metern Tiefe.

Geheizt und gekühlt wird der neue Sportcluster am Grazer Rosenhain mit einer Wärmepumpenanlage, für die 21 Sonden in jeweils 140 Meter Tiefe gesetzt wurden. Um der drohenden sommerlichen Austrocknung vorzubeugen, werden Regenwasser und Hangwässer aufgefangen und in den oberen Teich am Rosenhain eingeleitet.

#5328. 'Degree of obsessiveness': govt contractor allegedly stalked woman for months

An ACT government contractor accused of stalking allegedly used his job to access information about a woman's sibling and "exhibited a degree of obsessiveness" in messages to her, a court has heard.

Suyash Sinha, 31, faced the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday, October 26, when he made a second application for bail after being denied two weeks earlier.

He is yet to enter a plea to one charge of stalking.

The court heard Sinha first reached out to the woman in January 2026, when she "clearly" stated that she did not wish to speak with him.

The prosecutor, opposing bail, said the man continued to contact the woman over a number of months across multiple forums and once in person.

Sinha, who holds master's degrees in both finance and accounting, was working three jobs at the time, including as an ACT government contractor.

He allegedly used his government role to access information about the woman's sibling, before his employer stood him down on leave without pay after learning of the allegations through media reports.

While acknowledging that the proposed bail conditions were strict, the prosecutor said the concern was whether the man could comply with them.

"The charge before your Honour speaks to ongoing harassment ... that persists despite multiple clear requests from the complainant for the conduct to cease," the prosecutor said.

"The text messages ... effectively describe a person who is unable to take no for an answer."

She argued Sinha posed a risk to the alleged victim's safety if released from custody.

She also noted that the woman said she did not know anything about the man, was unsure what he was capable of, and was concerned that he would attempt to contact her family members.

Applying for bail on Sinha's behalf, his defence lawyer said the man has no criminal history and there was nothing before the court to suggest he couldn't comply with strict bail conditions.

She said the man allegedly last contacted the woman in September, more than a month before his arrest.

"This is not a case where the alleged offending behaviour only stopped due to the arrest of the defendant," she said.

The lawyer said the proposed conditions, which required Sinha to live at his Franklin home and not contact the woman or her family, were drafted to ensure the alleged victim's safety.

"Mr Sinha has reflected on his actions during his time in custody and is acutely aware that if he were to breach bail, he would return there with little to no prospect of getting released before the matter is finalised," she said.

"He has already participated in an interview with police where he made various admissions regarding his conduct."

Magistrate Ian Temby granted the man bail, saying it was a "tricky" application.

"On the one hand the messages that the defendant sends and the way he sent them exhibited a degree of, I guess, obsessiveness, is the word I would use," Mr Temby said.

Mr Temby said the man allegedly contacted the woman on Instagram using different names that were changed to communicate with her.

He said some names were used to "flatter her", others offered "apologies for his conduct", and one claimed he would "see her soon".

The magistrate said this was despite the woman's "obvious reluctance to have anything to do with him".

However, he accepted the defence submissions that nothing suggested Sinha would fail to follow the proposed conditions, ruling he should be given the opportunity to comply.

He also noted that the man seemed to have stopped contacting her a month before he was arrested, which gave "some optimism that perhaps he has finally understood the complainant does not want anything to do with him".

#5331. The ABC bureau that's older than the organisation itself celebrates 95 years

Long-serving ABC Capricornia contributor Terry Moore (front) with family members and fellow panellists at the Rockhampton studio.   (Supplied: Tom Moore)

Long before smartphones delivered footy scores in an instant, central Queenslanders tuned their radios to hear Terry Moore's familiar voice each weekend.

For more than two decades, the late rugby union correspondent was one of the many voices that became synonymous with ABC Capricornia, including on the station's Sports Show from the early 80s.

"It was a unique program where rugby union, rugby league, Australian Rules [Football] and soccer [correspondents] all sat in the room together and basically chewed the fat," Terry's son, Tom Moore, reflected.

"It was an amazing show, and it was predominantly local sport, which was fantastic."

Tom Moore with a framed service medal and letter presented to his late father Terry from then-ABC board chair Donald McDonald. (ABC Capricornia: Russel Talbot)

The show evolved in 1990 into the weekend institution known today as ABC Grandstand Sport.

As ABC Capricornia celebrates 95 years of storytelling this week, generations of dedicated staff and volunteers have reflected on the Rockhampton station's role in central Queensland life, including the Moore family.

"The rest of the day was spent at rugby, and if Terry Moore wasn't at Rugby Park on a Saturday afternoon then something was wrong."

A photo of engineers with the original microphones from 4RK in the 1930s. (ABC Capricornia: Jess Hinchliffe)

From sharing the region's sporting triumphs and community milestones to serving as the trusted emergency broadcaster through floods, cyclones and bushfires, ABC Capricornia has been a constant for almost a century.

As one of regional Queensland's oldest radio stations, it is, in fact, older than the ABC itself.

Known as 4RK in its humble beginnings, the privately-run Australian Broadcasting Company set up the station at Gracemere on the outskirts of Rockhampton in 1931.

The Australian Broadcasting Commission, later to become Corporation, was launched the following year.

The ABC took on 4RK, and the Rockhampton station became the fledgling national broadcaster's first regional Queensland radio station.

The station moved to its current location on Quay Street in 1963 into a building that was formerly Mount Morgan Gold Mining Company's head office and gold vaults.

The ABC Capricornia building on Quay Street was once the Mount Morgan Gold Mining Company office. (ABC Capricornia: Erin Semmler)

Four ABC staff members from Rockhampton will be remembered today, 25 years after their plane crashed in the central highlands.

As you walk inside the building today, staff and visitors are greeted by a plaque that was unveiled in 2008, commemorating the lives of four ABC staff members from Rockhampton killed in a plane crash.

On October 24, 1983, the ABC's regional manager Ralph Elphinstone — who was flying the plane — was killed, along with rural reporter Bruce Anning, 28, cameraman Joe Mooney, 55 and his assistant Bill Fryer, 33.

The plane crash near Clermont, north-west of Rockhampton, shocked those who worked at the ABC at the time.

Terry Moore's early involvement began with the ABC's classical music Concert Series in the late 60s before becoming a much-loved contributor to the station's sports show, anchored by CQ's "voice of sport" Vince Pheely.

After a short battle with bowel cancer, the long-serving rugby union stalwart and one of the founding members of the sport in Rockhampton died in October 2001.

Some of the station's broadcast equipment used in the early days, alongside an old newspaper clipping calling for music auditions. (ABC Capricornia)

Six months before his death, he was honoured with a letter of "special recognition" and a meritorious service medallion from then-ABC board chair Donald McDonald.

"Your regular reports on rugby union happenings on the ABC Capricornia Saturday sports program have helped give our regional service credibility and authority, and have been widely appreciated by the Queensland audience," Mr McDonald wrote.

"ABC regional radio wouldn't enjoy the standing it has in the community without the voluntary efforts of people like yourself who've been prepared to go above and beyond the call of duty to serve the people of central Queensland.

"You've not only kept the local community well informed on your chosen sport but have presented these reports with great warmth and good humour, endearing yourself to many of our listeners."

From the Queen's message to election results and Test cricket coverage, ABC radio and TV in its humble beginnings in Rockhampton. (ABC Capricornia)

Tom Moore, who followed in his father's footsteps behind the microphone on the Saturday sports program from the early 2000s, said the honour was a source of immense pride for his family.

"It was special recognition for what dad had done, and if we don't have volunteers like that, then shows like that don't happen," he said.

"He was instrumental in forming and revitalising rugby [union] in Rockhampton back in those years."

ABC Capricornia was the first ABC station in regional Queensland. (ABC Capricornia)

Marking the milestone, the ABC's managing director Hugh Marks praised ABC Capricornia's decades of service, saying its strong local presence reflects the very best of the ABC.

"ABC local offices are the backbone of the ABC", he said.

"In this sort of crazy world that we live in at the moment, where everything's going technology-oriented, to have that local personal connection all around the country through great offices like yourself.

"Knowing that there's someone like you who's out there representing the community, listening to the community like that, is the foundation of what are the really great things about the ABC."

The ABC Capricornia building on Quay Street in Rockhampton as it is today. (ABC Capricornia: Aaron Kelly)

Central Queensland-based Nationals leader Matt Canavan said ABC Capricornia's 95-year history was a "pretty big innings" and testament to the station's deep roots in the community.

"It just emphasises how important Rockhampton has been to our state and country's development, with it being the first ABC radio station in regional Queensland," he said.

ABC Capricornia celebrates its 95th anniversary with a special live outside broadcast. (ABC Capricornia)

Rockhampton Regional Council Mayor Tony Williams echoed those sentiments, also paying special tribute to the local emergency broadcaster.

"The ABC is the backbone of regional Queensland. From sharing local news, stories and events to preparing us and responding to natural disasters," he said.

According to Member for Rockhampton Donna Kirkland, the "remarkable milestone of 95 years of serving central Queensland" showed its continued importance as a trusted source of news and information for the region.

"This anniversary is a testament to the dedication of its journalists, presenters, producers and staff,  past and present, who have worked tirelessly to keep central Queensland informed."

#5333. Le gouvernement français sous pression après un week-end de violences généralisées

Le Premier ministre français, Sébastien Lecornu, tient lundi une réunion de crise du gouvernement pour évaluer les violences et les pillages qui ont secoué le pays ce week-end, constituant certaines des pires scènes de troubles publics de l'histoire française moderne.

Le ministre de l'Intérieur, Laurent Nuñez, a tenté de démissionner, a annoncé lundi matin l'Élysée (siège du président français Emmanuel Macron). Mais ce dernier lui a demandé d'examiner les mesures à prendre pour améliorer la sécurité dans les rues de France et de traduire en justice les auteurs des violences du week-end.

Samedi, plus d'un demi-million de manifestants, majoritairement pacifiques, ont protesté contre la hausse du coût de la vie et la dégradation de l'accès aux services publics de qualité, notamment à un enseignement public de qualité. Cependant, les manifestations ont dégénéré en affrontements après l'apparition de groupes d'activistes et de vandales masqués et vêtus de noir.

On estime à 1 500 le nombre de commerces pillés et détruits. Les forces de l'ordre ont fait usage de gaz lacrymogène et de canons à eau contre la foule. À plusieurs endroits, elles ont été vues frappant des personnes à coups de matraque. Le ministère de l'Intérieur a indiqué qu'environ 1 000 policiers avaient été blessés samedi, dont sept grièvement.

Le ministre de l'Intérieur Nuñez a été accusé par ses adversaires politiques, certains syndicats et sur les réseaux sociaux d'être mal préparé et insuffisamment encadré par la police en prévision des nombreuses manifestations prévues samedi.

La présidente de la Chambre des députés française, Yaël Braun-Pivet, a déclaré vouloir ouvrir une enquête afin de déterminer précisément ce qui s'est passé.

« Les choses sont sombres dans la Ville Lumière » – le surnom de Paris – était un graffiti que j’ai lu, peint en rouge, sur un mur jouxtant une rangée de magasins dévastés dans la capitale française, dimanche soir.

Des rumeurs circulaient en France selon lesquelles le président Emmanuel Macron pourrait instaurer un couvre-feu temporaire dans certaines régions du pays, voire décréter l'état d'urgence pour tenter de calmer les esprits.

Finalement, il a utilisé une allocution télévisée à la nation dimanche pour appeler à l'unité nationale et tenter d'assurer au public français que les auteurs des violences seraient punis.

Le discours de Macron a été vivement critiqué par les médias français pour son manque de détails concrets.

Comment les vandales et les émeutiers seront-ils désormais tenus responsables de leurs actes ?

Comment mieux protéger les villes françaises, surtout depuis l'annonce de nouvelles manifestations de masse dans quelques semaines ?

Comment les entreprises détruites seront-elles indemnisées exactement ?

Et quand un dialogue sera-t-il instauré avec les associations étudiantes et enseignantes sur la question de l'éducation ? C'est ainsi que ces manifestations ont débuté le mois dernier.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Dimanche, la secrétaire générale du syndicat CGT, Sophie Binet, a accusé Macron de ne pas répondre aux préoccupations des étudiants, à la crise du coût de la vie ni à la baisse de la qualité des services publics en France.

Le président a apparemment passé le relais au Premier ministre Lecornu. Macron est largement perçu en France comme un président en fin de mandat. Son départ est imminent.

Une course acharnée est en cours pour lui succéder, le scrutin étant prévu dans six mois. Le candidat de droite nationaliste anti-immigration (Marine Le Pen) et celui de gauche anticapitaliste (Jean-Luc Mélenchon) rivalisent pour faire la une des journaux.

Cela ne fait qu'exacerber les tensions actuelles en France, tant sur le plan politique que dans la rue.

Le Parlement est ici paralysé, profondément divisé entre trois blocs politiques rivaux.

Il y a aussi les difficultés financières de la France. Les investisseurs font pression sur le pays pour qu'il parvienne à maîtriser sa dette publique galopante. Mais le gouvernement français craint que toute réduction des services publics ou des aides sociales n'entraîne des manifestations encore plus massives de la population.

Que faire maintenant, que va-t-il se passer ensuite ? Notre pays est-il en ruine ? On entend beaucoup ces questions en ce moment.

Les événements de samedi ont choqué et inquiété la population française. Les images de villes gazées, de pillards apparemment en toute impunité et de bâtiments publics incendiés ont suscité l'inquiétude dans tout le pays.

De nombreux passants à qui je parle expriment leur frustration de constater que, tandis qu'ils s'inquiètent pour l'avenir, leurs principaux responsables politiques semblent au contraire se concentrer avec passion sur le fait de se rejeter la faute les uns sur les autres, se reprochant mutuellement l'instabilité.

« Pendant que nous nous inquiétons pour notre sécurité, ils instrumentalisent cette situation à des fins politiques en vue de l'élection présidentielle », m'a confié Édouard, enseignant et père de trois enfants.

Macron et son Premier ministre ont imputé les violentes émeutes de samedi à des groupes d'extrême gauche radicaux et à des délinquants ; le dirigeant de la gauche radicale, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, a dénoncé l'« incompétence » du gouvernement ; Marine Le Pen, de la droite nationaliste qui aime se présenter comme ferme sur le maintien de l'ordre, a publié une vidéo assise devant le drapeau français, prononçant un discours de style présidentiel blâmant « l'administration macroniste à bout de souffle, épuisée et désorientée ».

Les autorités françaises espèrent un peu de répit pour les deux prochaines semaines. Les élèves débutent leurs vacances de février lundi.

Mais le 5 novembre, un large éventail de syndicats, ainsi que le mouvement disparate des « gilets jaunes » français qui a organisé des manifestations pendant plus d'un an en 2018 – durant le premier mandat de Macron à la présidence – ont annoncé des manifestations massives.

#5334. The challenge brewing behind the front lines in Ukraine

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

More than four years after Russia launched the full-scale invasion that has devastated Ukraine and claimed hundreds of thousands of lives, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is facing a new political challenge: whether to hold elections during wartime.

The issue emerged last week after former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, who was recently dismissed from his role, called for Zelenskyy to find a way to hold elections while fighting was ongoing.

The move was seen as the biggest challenge to Zelenskyy's leadership since the invasion began in February 2022, with Zelenskyy rebuffing calls for a wartime election.

"Elections right now are a tsunami for the state, which will split Ukraine," he said on Sunday, local time.

"That's why my strategy is to steer the country toward an ending of the war and to preserve an independent and sovereign state."

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

National elections have been suspended since the invasion began and polling shows most Ukrainians support delaying a vote until the fighting ends.

Zelenskyy won Ukraine's 2019 presidential election in a landslide and would have ordinarily served a five-year term.

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion, Ukraine introduced martial law, which suspends some civil liberties, including national elections.

Zelenskyy's presidential term expired in 2024, but he remained in office as Ukraine's constitutional and legal system provides for continuity of government during martial law. The country's parliament has also continued operating.

Security remains the biggest obstacle to holding elections.

Fighting continues along a front line stretching more than 1,200km, while Ukrainian cities, including the capital Kyiv, remain under regular bombardment from Russian drones and missiles.

An election would potentially require millions of Ukrainians to travel to polling stations, creating security risks and raising concerns about how voting could be conducted safely.

Political parties would also need to campaign while the country remained under attack, while authorities would have to find a way for hundreds of thousands of soldiers serving on the front line to vote.

As of the end of June, more than 4.4 million Ukrainians had temporary protection status in the European Union, meaning Ukraine would have to organise hundreds of polling stations across Europe.

Nearly four million Ukrainians have also been internally displaced, making voter registration more difficult and potentially diverting resources from the war effort.

Then there are those living under Russian occupation unable to vote. Ukrainian officials estimated that, as of 2024, around 4.5 million adult Ukrainians remained in Russian-occupied territory.

Russia controls about 19 per cent of the Ukrainian territory and plans to ​hold its own elections there next month, which Ukraine has said would be ⁠illegal.

Zelenskyy has previously said a wartime vote might be possible if Ukraine's allies could guarantee the security needed to hold one but no viable plan has been proposed.

The question of wartime elections in Ukraine is not new.

US President Donald Trump last year called Zelenskyy a "dictator without elections", while Russia has repeatedly used the expiry of his presidential term to paint him as an illegitimate leader.

But polls have consistently shown that a majority of Ukrainians oppose holding elections until fighting ends.

Last week, Fedorov, 35, made a shock public call for Ukraine to find a way to hold elections while at war.

"A legal, safe and realistic mechanism that will allow Ukraine to renew its full democratic process even in the conditions of a long war," he said.

The intervention comes amid a broader political crisis for Zelenskyy, who fired the young, popular Fedorov as defence minister last month.

Fedorov became a popular figure as a backer of Ukraine's drone warfare strategy and for arguing for reforms within the military.

Thousands took to the streets to demand his reinstatement. Zelenskyy has offered other roles to Fedorov, but he has so far refused.

Fedorov, a former political ally, did not explicitly state that he wanted to challenge Zelenskyy but he is now seen as a political rival to the president after his ousting.

Ukrainian politician Lesia Vasylenko said it was "unrealistic" to talk about an election while fighting continued.

"It would require a constitutional change," she told Times Radio, something that is a "difficult enough process to orchestrate at peacetime and during the martial law regime, it's virtually impossible".

For now, there is little sign that Ukraine is preparing to hold an election, but the longer the war drags on, the louder the calls will become.

— With additional reporting by Agence France-Presse

#5337. Departments water down human decision making standards as AI takes hold

Government agencies are quietly reducing human oversight of artificial intelligence (AI) and are regularly altering public guidance on internal AI uses, making it harder for outsiders to verify if it is being used safely and for valid reasons, tech experts say.

The government agency in charge of AI implementation has admitted it is not tracking changes agencies make to their AI transparency statements, the principal public documents explaining how individual government services are using AI and what ethical and safety standards are in place.

A data scientist has meanwhile tracked dozens of changes to the documents across some of the government's most powerful departments, one of which - the Department of Social Services (DSS) - The Canberra Times learned has changed its statement seven times since February 2025.

The Digital Transformation Agency (DTA) which oversees implementation and compliance with AI policy disavowed responsibility for the changes, with an executive saying it was "not a regulator," even as scientists warned it is becoming unclear who has oversight of government AI use and called for new legislation to enshrine protections and unions warned that public servants may be left carrying the risks.

A submission to the parliamentary joint select committee on AI by Dr Gabrielle Josling warned tracking government AI use under current rules was opaque and inconsistent, requiring scientists in some cases to search "procurement records, vendor publications, speeches and FOI [freedom of information] releases" to form an accurate understanding.

Changes to AI transparency statements tracked by Dr Josling and verified by this masthead varied from updates to names and simple semantic shifts as agencies rolled out more AI uses, to the removal of bans on AI use for decision-making and language guaranteeing human oversight.

One example showed the DSS scrubbing an entire paragraph committing the department to track outcomes of AI use and measure their effectiveness.

The Treasury cut a pledge not to use AI in situations where the public could be "significantly impacted" and shifted its language from "human intervention" in all AI use to "human oversight".

A provision for a human to check the accuracy of AI outputs was cut by the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, with its updated statement instead saying "human officials remain fully accountable".

The Department of Finance deleted a commitment to only deploy AI in "low-risk use cases" where it would not "directly interact with, or significantly impact the public without human intervention".

The Department of Employment and Workplace Relations flipped a statement banning AI from "service delivery", updating its statement in March to say AI could now support human decision-making and administrative action "by guiding, assessing, or making a recommendation to a human decision-maker."

The Australian Taxation Office likewise ditched limits on AI use for "administrative action".

The Australian Electoral Commission cut a total ban on AI use for public interactions, saying instead it should not be used to "provide authoritative advice or make decisions in public-facing interactions".

Spokespersons from the DSS, Treasury and the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing said human oversight remained a requirement of AI use within the departments.

The DSS spokesperson said AI was not used for decision-making and could only be deployed in approved use cases.

"The department will continue to update its public transparency statement as approved uses and governance arrangements evolve," the spokesperson said.

The DSS last updated its AI transparency statement in September.

The DTA's deputy chief executive of strategy, planning and performance Lucy Poole said changes to agencies' AI transparency statements were "not a focus of monitoring", but defended the many changes being made, describing the statements as "living documents, not static records".

The statements were "intended to give members of the public an accessible, high-level account of how Australian government agencies are currently approaching and using AI," said Ms Poole, and just one part of a broader government framework managing its adoption and responsible use.

"Agencies remain responsible for the content, accuracy and currency of their own statements. The DTA is not a regulator and does not validate or endorse individual statements," said Ms Poole.

Current government AI rules require the DTA to advise agencies about AI implementation and policy compliance, but do not empower it to assess or change how AI is being used.

Dr Josling in her submission to the joint select committee warned of a general lack of oversight of AI use by government, with current standards leaving it "unclear who, if anyone, is responsible for ensuring that the policy intent [for responsible AI use] is delivered".

"Agencies' public accounts of their AI use and governance remain largely self-attested and unverified," said Dr Josling.

The Department of Industry, Science and Resources, which contains the AI Safety Institute - launched last November and tasked with supporting safe AI deployment and governance - did not comment.

The national Office of AI - which sits within Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's department - is tasked exclusively with designing and legislating national data centre standards and copyright reform.

The DTA should provide agencies with guidance to ensure a consistent, whole-of-government approach to AI use, keep published records of past AI transparency statements, and those statements independently checked against actual department uses, Dr Josling told the committee.

Transparency standards should also be expanded to cover corporate Commonwealth entities "where AI use materially affects individuals, influences administrative decision-making, or involves sensitive information".

Intelligence agencies including the Australian Security Intelligence Organisation, the Australian Signals Directorate, the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission and the Defence Intelligence Organisation are exempt from current AI regulations.

ARC Centre of Excellence on Automated Decision-Making and Society research fellow Dr Alexandra Sinclair said Australia had fallen behind international best practice on transparent AI use, with governments in Canada, the UK and the US now publishing detailed registers of AI use cases.

"A lot of the information in the public domain about [Australian] government use of AI is high level and doesn't provide information about specific use cases," Dr Sinclair said.

"This makes it more difficult for the public or civil society to hold the government to account for potentially problematic uses of AI."

Dr Sinclair said rule changes that take effect in December requiring agencies to maintain an AI use case register should also require they be published and rules governing AI use, so far written by departments internally, developed instead by Parliament.

"The provision of AI regulation in legislation rather than soft law and policy would provide additional protections for the public," Dr Sinclair said.

The Community and Public Sector Union's (CPSU) national secretary Rebecca Fawcett said public servants should not be left to carry the risks of AI, renewing the union's calls for a pause on all complex automated decision-making inside government until stronger safeguards were in place.

"Public sector workers are best placed to identify the practical risks and unintended consequences of AI before they become serious problems for the community," said Ms Fawcett.

The CPSU has also called for a "standalone common condition on AI" in public servants' enterprise agreements to offer workplace protections, including a ban on AI use for surveillance, recruitment, performance assessment or promotion and "clear human oversight and accountability" for its use, which government negotiators in the current bargaining round have so far resisted.

Minister for the Public Service Katy Gallagher said the government continued to "listen and negotiate in good faith".

The joint select committee on AI will report to Parliament on November 30.

Dave Allen is a public service and federal politics reporter with an interest in AI, govtech, government integrity and transparency, and the changing day-to-day lives of public servants. Grazer Malic nach Tätlichkeit kurz vor der Pause ausgeschlossen. Sturm schon neun Punkte hinter Tabellenführer Rapid und unmittelbar vor den Riedern Vierter

Belmin Beganovic (re.) hat die Grazer gerade noch vor einer Niederlage bewahrt.

Graz – Sturm Graz hat die Tabellenspitze der Bundesliga aus den Augen verloren. Der Vizemeister kam am Sonntag zu Hause gegen die SV Ried über ein 2:2 nicht hinaus und hat damit nach zehn Runden schon neun Punkte Rückstand auf Leader Rapid. #5340. Jordan arrests three suspects in deadly church attack

Gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday, killing nine people and wounding 40 others.

A hearse with the coffin of a victim of a church shooting, in Karak, Jordan, Oct 25, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Alaa Al Sukhni)

Jordanian security forces have arrested three suspects in connection with an attack on a church in the US-allied country that killed nine people, state television reported on Monday (Oct 26).

The attack, in which gunmen opened fire during a funeral at a Greek Orthodox church on Friday in the village of Hamoud in Karak governorate, about 120 km southwest of the capital Amman, also wounded 40 others. The shooting lasted several minutes, witnesses said.

Jordan's Public Security Directorate said security forces located the three suspects early on Monday hiding in an abandoned house in Karak. The suspects refused to surrender and opened fire on security forces, who returned fire and arrested all three after they were wounded, the directorate said in a statement carried on state media.

No security personnel were injured, and a number of firearms and ammunition were found in the suspects' possession after their arrest.

"Terrorism has no place among us," the directorate said, adding that the suspects had met their "just fate".

The Public Security Directorate did not identify the suspects' affiliation or say whether they belonged to any militant group.

Jordanian authorities have said the attack was carried out by "extremist terrorists", but it was too early to determine whether they had links to known groups inside or outside Jordan. There has been no claim of responsibility.

Interior Minister Mazen al-Faraya said on Monday authorities were reviewing the circumstances that led young people towards extremism and would hold accountable anyone found to have participated in the attack.

King Abdullah, a US partner in the fight against Islamist militant groups, has ordered security forces to respond with an "iron fist" to the rare attack on Jordan's Christian minority.

Such violence is highly unusual in Jordan, a relatively stable state in the Middle East, though authorities say they have foiled several Islamist militant plots over the years.

#5341. Four Corners withdraws episodes by sacked reporter

The ABC's Four Corners has withdrawn two programs.

The ABC has removed two Four Corners episodes by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal.

Fazal's ABC employment was terminated after an internal investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure, but ABC management says today's decision is separate to that investigation.

The matter has been referred to the ABC Ombudsman for an independent review of the programs' compliance with editorial standards.

The ABC has withdrawn the Four Corners programs Meth Highway and Cocaine Nation by sacked reporter Mahmood Fazal due to concerns about accuracy.

"This action has been taken following concerns identified about the veracity of certain sources used in both programs," a statement from ABC management said.

Fazal's employment was terminated after an ABC investigation into his appearance on a podcast with a former underworld figure last year, ABC managing director Hugh Marks confirmed at a Senate estimates hearing in May.

The ABC's statement said the decision to remove the Four Corners programs was separate to the investigation into Fazal's appearance on the podcast.

Mahmood Fazal no longer works at the ABC. (ABC News)

It said the matter had been referred to the ABC Ombudsman for an independent review of the programs' compliance with editorial standards.

"The ABC will consider whether any further action will be required once that review is complete," it said.

In Meth Highway, released in 2024, Fazal investigated the crystal meth pipeline from Melbourne to a major source of production in South-East Asia, the program said at the time.

In 2023, Cocaine Nation covered the "shadowy underworld" of Australia's cocaine supply chain with "unprecedented access to the people involved in the trade", according to the episode's description.

Fazal's work featured de-identified sources and it is understood concerns have been raised about the real identities of those behind the masks.

In a statement posted to social media this afternoon, Fazal said he was "shocked" by the ABC's decision to remove the two Four Corners episodes.

"I believe the process ABC is following and its decisions so far set a worrying precedent for the organisation's independent [sic] and commitment to public-interest journalism," he said.

Mahmood Fazal has been sacked by the ABC following an internal investigation into an appearance on a podcast hosted by a former underworld figure, managing director Hugh Marks says.

Fazal said today's statement was the first time he had been made aware the broadcaster was investigating his work.

"The decision to remove these episodes was apparently made before the investigation was completed," he said.

"I have not been contacted by the Ombudsman, nor have I been told by them what the apparent issues are."

He said it was a "deeply worrying precedent for the ABC to remove investigative journalism from its flagship programme, apparently in response to what appear to be external criticisms".

Fazal said the Four Corners episodes were collaborative efforts involving reporters, producers, supervising producers, executive producers and broader ABC News leadership.

He said the programs had also gone through the ABC's fact-checking, editorial and legal processes before being broadcast.

"These stories are three and two years old," he said.

"If defects serious enough to justify their removal have only now been identified, the ABC should explain what they are, how those defects escaped its scrutiny for years and why the programs were removed before the reporter was given an opportunity to respond."

The withdrawal comes at a turbulent time for the broadcaster after the sudden departure of news director Justin Stevens in May.

Mr Marks confirmed he and Stevens disagreed about the direction of the organisation and announced a replacement, Reuters executive editor Simon Robinson, the following day.

Mahmood Fazal was an investigative reporter for ABC RN's Background Briefing before his Four Corners role. (ABC)

Fazal, a former member of the Mongols bikie club, is an award-winning journalist specialising in crime, violence, imprisonment and terrorism.

Before working at Four Corners, he was an investigative reporter for ABC RN's Background Briefing.

Prior to joining the ABC, he worked for VICE as a senior staff writer and host of the series Violent Times.

His reporting has appeared in The Guardian, Rolling Stone, The Sydney Morning Herald, The Monthly and The Saturday Paper.

Fazal used his contacts to line up crime stories and investigations, including with gang members.

Joel Tozer, who previously led 7.30, was appointed executive producer of Four Corners in December 2025.

As one of his first management changes, he appointed Patricia Drum to the role of editor, commissioning and standards.

The job's advertisement said the role would be charged with "leading commissioning and standards to maintain the quality and integrity of the ABC's flagship investigative journalism program".
