#5342. Pourquoi l'Internet de Starlink joue un rôle clé dans la guerre des drones qui oppose l'Ukraine à la Russie

Les satellites Starlink, exploités par la société SpaceX d'Elon Musk, offrent un accès Internet haut débit qui s'avère très précieux dans les conflits modernes.

Dans le cas de l'Ukraine, ce service est essentiel pour les communications sur le champ de bataille et pour garantir l'efficacité de sa guerre des drones contre la Russie.

Grâce à Starlink, les drones ukrainiens peuvent rester connectés à leurs opérateurs à des distances plus grandes qu'avec les réseaux radio classiques, ce qui les rend également moins vulnérables aux interférences.

Mais mardi soir, Starlink a soudainement et de manière inattendue limité la vitesse de vol à laquelle les drones peuvent se connecter à son réseau Internet.

Cela a perturbé certaines « missions » sur le champ de bataille, selon un haut responsable ukrainien, tout en entravant la capacité de Kiev à se défendre contre les attaques russes.

La limitation de vitesse à 160 km/h impliquait que tout drone volant plus vite que cela perdait la connexion, ce qui les rendait pratiquement inutilisables.

« Starlink donne à l'Ukraine la capacité de voir ce qui se profile à l'horizon et de protéger sa population », a déclaré Kurt Volker, ancien ambassadeur des États-Unis auprès de l'OTAN, à l'émission Today de BBC Radio 4. « Si cette communication est interrompue, davantage de personnes mourront, et la ralentir comme cela a été fait est une décision très cynique et insensible. »

Des sources du ministère ukrainien de la Défense ont indiqué à la BBC qu'une partie du service militaire Starshield de Starlink avait été rétablie mercredi soir, même s'il n'est pas encore clair si les restrictions concernant la vitesse à laquelle les drones peuvent voler sans perdre la connexion ont été entièrement levées.

Ces sources ont ajouté que les autorités continuaient à travailler pour faire la lumière sur « les raisons et les circonstances » de cette mesure.

Mais cette mesure a démontré une fois de plus à quel point Starlink peut influencer le conflit qui ravage le pays depuis que la Russie a lancé son invasion à grande échelle en Ukraine en février 2022.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Starlink est un réseau Internet qui utilise des satellites en orbite terrestre basse pour fournir une connexion Internet, notamment dans les zones reculées et sur les champs de bataille.

Il compte actuellement plus de 10 000 satellites actifs, ce qui en fait la plus grande constellation de satellites au monde.

Il appartient à SpaceX, l'entreprise d'Elon Musk, et constitue la principale source de revenus de la société.

Alors que Starlink est destiné à un usage civil, Starshield est son service de niveau militaire, conçu pour le Pentagone.

Starshield s'appuie sur le réseau Starlink, mais offre une sécurité renforcée, notamment grâce à un cryptage amélioré, afin que les informations confidentielles puissent être transmises sans être interceptées.

Le gouvernement américain a autorisé l'Ukraine à utiliser Starlink et Starshield pour se défendre contre la Russie. Musk a coupé l'accès de Moscou à ce service en février, ce qui a donné à Kiev un avantage dans le conflit.

En bref, Starlink utilise ses milliers de satellites pour fournir un accès Internet haut débit dans presque tous les coins de la planète, grâce à des terminaux terrestres que les utilisateurs peuvent facilement acheter et installer.

Comme le dit Musk, il suffit de suivre deux instructions : « pointer vers le ciel et se connecter ».

Cela les rend idéaux pour une utilisation sur le champ de bataille.

« C'est une connexion… qui, en gros, peut être utilisée très rapidement ; elle ne nécessite aucun équipement particulier, aucune préparation : il suffit de se rendre sur le terrain et, en général, ça fonctionne », a déclaré à la BBC un soldat prénommé Neo, membre de l'une des unités de reconnaissance par drones de l'Ukraine.

"Simplifica nuestro trabajo porque podemos traducir o transmitir en directo nuestras operaciones de reconocimiento", añadió.

Según George Barros, del Instituto para el Estudio de la Guerra (ISW), la red se ha convertido en "la columna vertebral de las comunicaciones militares en Ucrania" y es utilizada por las fuerzas navales, terrestres y aéreas de Kyiv.

En Ukraine, on utilise aussi bien Starlink (le service civil) que Starshield (le service militaire), en fonction des besoins en matière de communication.

Comme l'a expliqué M. Barros à la BBC, cela est essentiel pour une utilisation efficace d'armes telles que les drones, qui se connectent au réseau afin que les opérateurs puissent visualiser leurs cibles en temps réel, réduisant ainsi au minimum le délai entre la détection et le tir.

La Russie n'étant pas autorisée à utiliser Starlink, lorsque l'Ukraine lance des missiles à longue portée à l'intérieur du territoire russe pour attaquer des raffineries de pétrole, le réseau ne fonctionne pas.

En ce qui concerne la légitime défense de l'Ukraine, le pays dépend du réseau Starlink pour protéger son espace aérien contre les attaques russes, en particulier les drones Shahed à réaction, a ajouté M. Barros.

Les Shahed volent à des vitesses supérieures à 319 km/h, ce qui signifie que la restriction imposée par Starlink a rendu pratiquement impossibles les efforts ukrainiens pour les localiser.

Pour le soldat Neo, cela signifie que toute restriction délibérée imposée au réseau Starlink constitue « une trahison ».

En l'absence de solution de remplacement immédiate au réseau Starlink, toute limitation de vitesse ou perte de connectivité a des implications importantes pour les défenses de l'Ukraine, et les récentes restrictions ont démontré la forte dépendance de Kiev à l'égard de ce réseau.

Même si Starlink peut fournir un accès presque partout dans le monde, cela ne signifie pas pour autant qu'il soit accessible partout, et les pays doivent obtenir une licence pour l'utiliser.

La Russie fait partie des pays où il n'est pas autorisé, bien que Kiev ait déclaré par le passé que Moscou continuait à se procurer des terminaux et à les utiliser sur le territoire ukrainien occupé.

« Si SpaceX apprend qu'un utilisateur non autorisé utilise une borne Starlink, nous mènerons une enquête sur cette plainte et prendrons les mesures nécessaires pour désactiver la borne si cela se confirme », a déclaré Starlink en 2024.

Mais avec des dizaines de milliers de bornes rien qu'en Ukraine, il pourrait s'avérer pratiquement impossible de déterminer quelles bornes sont autorisées et lesquelles ne le sont pas.

Lors d'une visite à Londres mercredi, le président Volodymyr Zelensky avait déclaré qu'il espérait qu'il ne s'agissait que d'une erreur ; cependant, dans une interview accordée par la suite au Financial Times, il a affirmé : « Ce n'était pas un problème technique, c'était un choix délibéré. »

Musk a affirmé que Starshield était géré par le gouvernement américain et a laissé entendre que le Pentagone pourrait en être responsable.

« Les systèmes Starshield appartiennent au gouvernement américain et sont sous son contrôle », a-t-il écrit sur X. « Toute limitation de vitesse ou d'utilisation est décidée par les forces armées américaines et, en dernier ressort, par le président des États-Unis. »

« Starlink est un service commercial détenu et contrôlé par SpaceX. L'utilisation de Starlink est limitée aux activités civiles ou de défense et ne peut être employée à des fins militaires offensives, car cela serait inapproprié pour une entreprise commerciale », a-t-il conclu.

La BBC a tenté d'obtenir des commentaires de la Maison Blanche et du Pentagone.

Les restrictions imposées mardi soir ont coïncidé avec les attaques meurtrières menées par la Russie contre l'Ukraine, qui ont privé d'électricité 600 000 personnes et endommagé les infrastructures de communication et d'énergie utilisées par l'armée ukrainienne.

Les Ukrainiens ont affirmé n'avoir reçu aucun avertissement concernant l'arrivée des drones avant qu'ils ne frappent.

« Il est clair que cette action ne peut pas être une coïncidence et qu'elle est liée à la situation politique actuelle », a écrit Serhiy Beskrestnov, conseiller de Zelensky, sur Telegram mercredi matin.

Les relations entre les États-Unis et l'Ukraine se sont récemment détériorées, notamment depuis que les États-Unis ont annoncé un accord avec la Russie visant à importer son diesel sur le marché américain.

Zelensky a qualifié cela de « cadeau » pour le président russe Vladimir Poutine, et Donald Trump a répondu qu'il estimait qu'« il était temps que l'Ukraine ait un nouveau président ».

Dimanche, Trump a annoncé un cessez-le-feu concernant les infrastructures énergétiques, mais trois jours plus tard, l'Ukraine a repris ses attaques, accusant la Russie de ne pas respecter l'accord et les États-Unis de lui retirer un soutien crucial.

Le Kremlin a déclaré n'avoir jamais accepté de cessez-le-feu.

Zelensky a accusé les États-Unis de menacer de retenir des renseignements si l'Ukraine continuait à attaquer les installations pétrolières russes. Trump a nié ces allégations, mais il a déclaré la semaine dernière à la presse que Zelensky « ferait mieux de mettre fin » à ces attaques.

Lors de son séjour à Londres, Zelensky a reconnu se sentir trahi par les États-Unis.

L'accord conclu par Trump avec la Russie constitue la dernière tentative de son gouvernement pour faire baisser les prix du carburant aux États-Unis avant les élections de mi-mandat de novembre, après des mois passés à gérer les conséquences politiques de la guerre avec l'Iran.

Ce conflit, qui a débuté en février, a fait flamber les prix, ce qui a nui à sa popularité auprès des Américains.

#5347. Kent's wife told him to keep busy. He went on to help 1000 people

Kent Brown's wife told him he shouldn't hang around home doing nothing when he retired in 2009.

Neither of them could imagine what he would achieve in the next 17 years.

Mr Brown has since helped more than 1000 people settle in Australia through his volunteer work, including many fleeing wars and armed rebellions.

He helped file the visa papers for a nun from Erbil, Iraq, to visit her sister in Australia one last time before she died.

He has helped settle a growing number of Central Americans fleeing gang violence.

And Mr Brown - now in his 80s - is an honorary member of the Karen community from south-east Asia, thanks to his work with a handful of families.

"I don't know how I survived at work - retirement is busy," Mr Brown said. "But it's enjoyable.

"Back in 2009, my wife saw a notice inside The Canberra Times saying Migrant and Refugee Settlement Services (MARSS) are looking for volunteers.

"I took up a job teaching English to refugees.

"My first client was Afghani; I helped her with English and the kids at school.

"They asked if I'd like to do some work at MARSS in the city; they gave me an office, a computer, and help from reception."

Mr Brown won the 2025 VolunteeringACT inclusion award for his work with migrants and refugees, but he says it's rewarding enough to see people get an outcome.

"The biggest turnarounds are all refugees that have come here from very difficult circumstances," he said.

"I started helping one man from the Karen community in 2009, teaching him English.

"He lived in the mountains before the military moved in, had never gone to school, and he escaped across the river to Thailand.

"He's now a pastor here, and has children in work."

That man is Than Soe, who says Mr Brown was like a parent to him when he first arrived.

"Our children were very small when we came here; Kent helped us with their school, he helped us complete forms," Mr Soe said.

"(Later on), he helped my boys get a mechanic apprenticeship.

"Someone who didn't know me, had never seen me, came to help me; that made me think 'people here are good and beautiful'."

The pair still catch up most weeks, and Mr Brown often gets an invitation to Karen community events.

"My wife and I are travellers: I find it fascinating to talk to people from different countries, to learn about their country, their culture, their way of live.

"And I've had the opportunity to visit a lot of the places our clients come from."

Mr Brown packs his volunteering work into one day a week, around other hobbies like racing vintage cars.

"I studied mechanical engineering at university, then went into the public service," he said.

"I ended up being a regional secretary for the Department of Defence in South Australia, then worked for defence here in the ACT.

"I left in 1997 or 1998 to work for a statutory authority as a business manager.

"I've always enjoyed helping people and solving problems - the years I spent in the public service helped."

#5349. 130,000 or 230,000? The migration figures One Nation is trying to explain

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has faced questions over his party's immigration target, claiming fellow MP David Farley misspoke when he revealed their figures were "not too different" from Labor's.

The MP for Farrer told ABC's Insiders program on Sunday that One Nation's stated figure of 130,000 net overseas migration annually into Australia did not include those who enter under a Pacific labour scheme, aged-care nurses, and other in-demand skilled workers.

He conceded that those groups would add roughly 100,000 people, bringing their total to 230,000 — 5,000 fewer than the current Labor budget projections.

Party leader Pauline Hanson intervened just hours later, writing on social media that One Nation's policy is to reduce net overseas migration (NOM) to 130,000.

Speaking to Channel Seven's Sunrise program on Monday, Joyce added that Farley simply made a mistake while explaining the numbers.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

"Show me a political career where people haven't made a mistake, and I'll show you a person who's not told the truth," Joyce said.

"I'm not going to throw anybody under a bus. When people are new in parliament, they can sometimes get things incorrect, and that's what happens. God knows, I've done it enough."

The debate over Australia's migration figures has intensified in recent months, with a recent Redbridge/Accent Research poll, conducted for the Australian Financial Review, indicating that voters trust One Nation and its traditionally restrictive approach to handle migration better than Labor or the Liberal Party.

However, the disjointed nature of One Nation's ongoing public discourse on the topic has prompted claims that the party is "incoherent" and "not fit to govern" from federal minister Pat Conroy.

Since its 1997 inception, cutting immigration has been seemingly a foundational pillar of One Nation policy. During her first speech to federal parliament, Hanson alleged Australia was in danger of being "swamped by Asians", that migrants never assimilated, and that multiculturalism should be abolished.

Its website currently states One Nation would "cut immigration by over 570,000 people" through "capping visas at 130,000 per year".

In a social media post on Sunday, Hanson wrote that NOM would be cut to 130,000 — a figure the party has previously clarified to SBS News. This number would be achieved by reducing international students, temporary graduate visas, and a "much more targeted" skilled migration program, Hanson said.

Those figures are different to the ones put forward by Farley, who said One Nation is focusing on "the NOM in its true form", as separate to labour programs "that drive our economy".

"The raw number is not too different [to current projections], but the reality is, where do we need them?" he asked.

"We don't need them in the great urban metroplex — we need them out to be productive, working in agriculture, engineering, mining."

Joyce further affirmed Hanson's view that One Nation's policy remained at 130,000 people annually for NOM.

SBS News has contacted One Nation for comment.

NOM hit 306,000 in the 2024-2025 period, down from a post-pandemic peak of 538,000.

Labor is yet to unveil its plan to restrict migration, but has previously set an official cap of 185,000 places on the permanent migration program. Treasury figures project that NOM will fall to 225,000 by the 2027-28 financial year.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke was set to detail Labor's plan to ensure that forecast was met, but pulled out of a National Press Club address at the last minute over fears about the implications cuts would have for certain sectors.

"Our policy will be released when Tony Burke is in a position to do so," Conroy told ABC Radio National on Monday. "But we've been very focused on getting the right migration mix to grow the economy as well as the broader interests of Australia."

Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said the Coalition will cap NOM at or below the number of homes built in Australia the previous year. Current building rates suggest their figure would be under 180,000; however, the Coalition is yet to announce where they would restrict immigration to reach that figure.

Opposition immigration spokesperson Jonathon Duniam told ABC Radio National that the Coalition is being "fairly methodical" in assessing its figures but that he would not "put a date" on when it will reveal details.

Duniam attacked One Nation for being cavalier with its migration figures, saying it had not detailed the impact such reductions would have on industries like agriculture, which relies on working holiday visa holders for seasonal labour.

"It was the same leader of One Nation who said in an interview about a week ago as well that she did not care about the impact on business any change to the migration system would have," Duniam said.

NOM is difficult for governments to control because it is a measurement of human behaviour rather than a fixed quota.

NOM is calculated by the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) based on the movement of people, subtracting overseas departures from overseas arrivals. To be included, a person must remain in the country for any 12 out of 16 months.

Citizens, permanent residents, temporary visa holders, and asylum seekers are included, as are backpackers and working holiday makers who stay for more than a year.

In 2024-2025, 568,000 people entered Australia, according to the ABS, down 14 per cent on the previous year.

Of that cohort, 88,000 were permanent visa holders, 53,000 were New Zealand citizens, and 64,000 were returning Australians. At the same time, 263,000 people left the country.

As Hanson stated, "short-term seasonal agricultural workers who do not meet the ABS residency test are not counted in net overseas migration".

However, using Farley's figures, many of the 100,000 additional workers he says would be able to enter the country — such as workers under the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme — would be included in NOM.

PALM workers can enter under a short-term placement of up to nine months or a long-term placement of one to four years.

The visa caps One Nation plans to set would place policy restrictions on NOM, but they can't control it entirely. Australians suddenly returning home en masse from abroad would, for example, elevate the figure regardless of visa caps.

Migration experts have long cautioned that linking migration to housing shortages is a flawed argument and that, in fact, migrant workers are essential to increase housing stock.

"If we don't have workers doing the jobs we need, if we don't get the right skill set into our country, then we all are worse off," Duniam said.

"One Nation has zero regard for that, as evidenced by the multiple positions they've had on migration policy all over the last few weeks."

#5350. North Korea-South Korea tensions high as letters lodged with UN, howitzer spotted

North Korean soldiers work on their military fence at their border, as seen from an observation deck in Gimpo, South Korea, on Oct 26, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Kim Hong-Ji)

SEOUL: Tensions between North Korea and South Korea are running high this week after Pyongyang sent a letter to the UN Security Council, repeating accusations that Seoul fabricated a September landmine incident, and after a North Korean howitzer was spotted close to the border.

A Reuters witness at an observatory in South Korea overlooking the heavily armed border on Monday (Oct 26) confirmed the presence of a North Korean artillery piece positioned in clear view near the frontier.

South Korea's Yonhap news agency on Sunday identified the weapon as a self-propelled 122mm howitzer, saying its deployment near the border marked a rare public display of such artillery.

Reuters also observed three North Korean armored vehicles with their gun barrels pointed south, as well as about 20 to 30 North Korean soldiers carrying out fencing work inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ).

"It is highly unusual (for North Korea) to expose its self-propelled artillery so conspicuously,” said Lim Eul-chul, a professor at Kyungnam University in Seoul.

"By deliberately displaying it, North Korea is signalling through action, not words, that it intends to enforce its border policy through force rather than dialogue or negotiation."

It is also warning South Korea to exercise caution about escalating border friction, with the intention to prevent an accidental clash, he added.

North Korean state media KCNA reported that in the letter sent on Sunday, the country's UN representative said Seoul was using the landmine incident to depict Pyongyang's border construction as a military incursion.

North Korea warned in the letter that violations of its sovereignty could trigger self-defence measures and that South Korea would be "wholly accountable for all the ensuing consequences".

The letter is a response to a South Korean letter to the Security Council last week, which said a Sep 21 blast in the DMZ was planted by North Korean troops and constituted a violation of the Korean War Armistice Agreement.

The UN Command, which oversees the DMZ, has said a North Korean mine across the line violated the armistice. Pyongyang has denied responsibility.

A spokesperson for South Korea's Unification Ministry said on Monday that the North Korean letter appears to repeat North Korea's existing position and seeks to justify its so-called border line marking work.

The ministry had no separate comment on the placement of the howitzer. Seoul has proposed dialogue with North Korea to defuse border tensions.

North Korea's letter also repeated accusations that South Korea had opened fire on North Korean personnel, calling that a violation of the UN Charter, which bars the threat or use of force against another state's territorial integrity.

Seoul has said its military issues warning broadcasts and fires warning shots to send North Korean soldiers back across the line when they cross the military demarcation line (MDL), which bisects the DMZ.

North Korean troops have been building tactical roads and fences and laying mines near the MDL in recent years.

The Yonhap report cited photographs taken from an observatory in the South Korean border city of Gimpo that appeared to show the howitzer as well as North Korean troops conducting drills on the coast of Kaepung county, about 1.5km from the observatory.

In 2015, there was a similar incident in which South Korean troops were injured by North Korean mines. Then, Seoul resumed anti-North Korea loudspeaker broadcasts across the DMZ, triggering a military standoff. After North Korea expressed regret, the standoff ended with a high-level inter-Korean agreement.

#5351. J'ai une maladie dont les gens ont trop honte de parler

Cet article contient des descriptions détaillées des symptômes médicaux.

Monica Thomas était adolescente lorsqu'elle a commencé à ressentir des démangeaisons et des douleurs intimes, mais malgré de nombreuses consultations médicales, on a diagnostiqué chez elle une mycose vaginale.

Ses symptômes s'aggravèrent, des plaies et des ampoules la plongeant dans une douleur constante.

"J'ai été alitée pendant très longtemps parce que je ne pouvais pas marcher", dit-elle.

Monica affirme avoir subi 28 examens en six mois avant qu'on lui propose une biopsie.

Elle explique que "dans notre société, on ne parle pas vraiment" de santé gynécologique, ce qui crée un tabou autour du fait de parler des symptômes.

"Même quand on va chez le médecin, pour moi, la gêne de devoir me déshabiller… sous le regard des médecins, c’est embarrassant", dit-elle.

"Mais, de la même manière, quand on a mal, que ça démange et qu'on ressent une gêne, vivre avec ça est tout aussi pénible."

Cette femme de 34 ans, originaire du Suffolk, a finalement reçu un diagnostic de lichen scléreux.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Cette affection inflammatoire chronique touche les organes génitaux et peut provoquer l'apparition de plaques blanches accompagnées de démangeaisons, de douleurs, de fissures et de déchirures, explique le Dr Nighat Arif, médecin généraliste spécialisée dans la santé des femmes.

Elle touche les hommes et les femmes, mais est plus fréquente chez les femmes de plus de 50 ans. Il existe également un faible risque de cancer de la vulve.

"Les rapports sexuels et la miction sont très douloureux, et il y a souvent des confusions avec les maladies sexuellement transmissibles, mais ce n'est pas contagieux", explique-t-elle au podcast That Time of the Month de BBC Radio 5 Live.

Les recherches sur la prévalence du lichen scléreux vulvaire sont limitées, mais une analyse menée par l'Université de Bristol sur des personnes vivant dans les West Midlands et le Warwickshire a estimé qu'il touche environ 1 % des femmes.

Le Dr Sophie Rees, qui a participé à la réalisation de cette recherche, déclare à la BBC : "il s'agit très certainement d'une sous-estimation, car nous savons qu'il y a souvent un très long délai avant le diagnostic, et certaines personnes vivent probablement toute leur vie sans être diagnostiquées".

"Il existe malheureusement beaucoup de honte et de gêne à l'idée de demander de l'aide pour des symptômes vulvaires, ainsi qu'un manque de sensibilisation, même parmi les professionnels de la santé."

"Des recherches supplémentaires sont absolument nécessaires pour connaître la prévalence réelle", ajoute-t-elle.

Monica affirme que de multiples erreurs de diagnostic ont eu un impact "significatif" sur sa santé mentale.

"Je ne savais pas comment continuer… sans réponse, c’était une période horrible et solitaire."

On lui a prescrit des médicaments contre l'herpès. "J'étais très contrariée lors d'un rendez-vous chez un dermatologue qui s'est mis en colère contre moi parce que je disais : 'ce n'est pas ça'."

"Ensuite, elle a dit qu'elle voulait que je fasse des tests sanguins pour le VIH."

Les médecins lui ont dit qu'elle était "trop jeune" pour avoir un lichen scléreux.

"Malheureusement, cela arrive aux femmes de tous âges, même dès l'enfance. J'ai trouvé cela très difficile à accepter, mais j'ai toujours su que ce n'était pas normal."

Monica estime qu'il faudrait apporter davantage de soutien aux personnes atteintes de lichen scléreux.

"Même avec un diagnostic, on n'est pas forcément traité comme il le faudrait ; je n'ai même pas droit à un bilan de santé", dit-elle.

"Je gère ça toute seule avec ma crème à base de stéroïdes et j'espère que je fais tout correctement."

Selon le site web du NHS, la cause du lichen scléreux est inconnue. Il pourrait être dû à une réaction du système immunitaire qui attaque et endommage la peau par erreur.

Elle n'est pas contagieuse et ne résulte ni d'une infection ni d'une mauvaise hygiène personnelle. Les frottements ou les lésions cutanées peuvent déclencher ou aggraver l'affection.

Clare Baumhauer, 53 ans, originaire du Kent, a ressenti ses premiers symptômes à l'âge de cinq ans.

"J'avais des démangeaisons et des douleurs, et on me grondait sans cesse ; je n'étais évidemment pas consciente de ce qui se passait."

Ses symptômes se sont aggravés à l'âge adulte, avec des larmes, des ampoules et des plaies.

"Mais comme on ne voit pas d'autres vulves, je n'avais aucune idée que la mienne n'était pas normale. J'avais aussi subi huit frottis cervico-vaginaux pendant cette période, et personne ne m'avait jamais rien dit."

En 2016, Clare a eu une déchirure qui n'a pas guéri.

"J'avais 43 ans cette année-là, et après 38 ans de maladie, je n'en pouvais plus."

Un médecin généraliste a annoncé à Clare qu'elle avait l'herpès et qu'elle devait se rendre dans une clinique de santé sexuelle. Elle dit avoir été "choquée" car elle était mariée depuis 25 ans.

Elle a finalement été orientée vers un spécialiste pour une biopsie et on lui a diagnostiqué un lichen scléreux et un cancer de la vulve.

"Je n'avais jamais entendu parler du lichen scléreux et j'avais un cancer dont je n'avais jamais entendu parler, dans un endroit dont je n'avais jamais entendu parler."

"C’était la première fois que j’entendais le mot vulve, aucun professionnel de la santé ne l’avait mentionné, alors c’était beaucoup à assimiler à ce moment-là."

Clare était en rémission d'un cancer de la vulve depuis sept ans, lorsqu'un examen de contrôle régulier a révélé une récidive et qu'elle a subi une intervention chirurgicale il y a trois ans.

En juin, un autre examen a révélé des cellules précancéreuses et elle a subi une sixième intervention chirurgicale.

Clare pense que si on lui avait diagnostiqué un lichen scléreux plus tôt, son cancer aurait peut-être pu être diagnostiqué avant d'atteindre le stade trois.

"J'ai dû subir deux séances de radiothérapie, ce qui m'a provoqué une ménopause précoce et immédiate, un lymphœdème et des lésions nerveuses."

Monica encourage les femmes qui constatent des changements corporels à tenir un journal.

"Il est vraiment important que nous apprenions à mieux connaître notre corps, à savoir ce qui est normal pour nous aussi au niveau de nos parties intimes, car en réalité, nos vulves changent."

"Si l’on vous ignore, demandez plusieurs avis, insistez car vous n’êtes pas obligé de vivre sans réponses."

Elle a recommandé le guide sur le lichen scléreux, qui contient un schéma et un modèle pour vous aider à parler aux médecins.

#5353. Популярный блогер вспомнил ужаснувший его сюжет из «Секса с Анфисой Чеховой»

Популярный российский блогер Василий Бейнарович, известный как Фауст, вспомнил сюжет из программы «Секс с Анфисой Чеховой», который сильно напугал его в юном возрасте. Историей он поделился в шоу «Правило 34», выпуск вышел на YouTube.

«Девушка рассказывала [в передаче], что ее заразили СПИД, и она теперь намеренно ходит по клубам, знакомится с мужчинами и заражает их. Я тогда сидел и думал: "Боже, какой ужас, какой кошмар"», — раскрыл Бейнарович.

Блогер также предположил, что этот сюжет мог повлиять на то, что во взрослом возрасте он стал крайне серьезно относиться к контрацепции и не допускать случайных связей.

Ранее Анфиса Чехова рассказала, что ей предложили перезапустить шоу про секс. По словам телеведущей, она отказалась, поскольку не видит смысла возрождать передачу.

Программа «Секс с Анфисой Чеховой» выходила на канале ТНТ с 2005 по 2009 год. В эфире обсуждали различные темы, связанные с интимными отношениями.

#5354. ASX rebounds to end on a high; CSL names new chair

Updated October 26, 2026 — 4:51pm,first published October 26, 2026 — 5:20am

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

The Australian sharemarket has rebounded after an early fall to close in the green, with materials and energy stocks posting gains thanks to a rise in oil prices over the weekend.

The S&P/ASX 200 gained 14.7 points or 0.17 per cent, to 8809 on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.33¢.

The gains were largely thanks to advancing energy and materials stocks off the back of a rise in oil prices. Earlier in the day, Brent crude advanced above $US116 a barrel while West Texas Intermediate rose above $US102 before retreating slightly in the afternoon.

The gains were linked to fears the US would restart its war with Iran, with President Donald Trump telling Fox News it was “getting to be decision time” on whether he would make a deal with Tehran or “finish it off”. Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said if rationality existed, the US would not attempt an attack.

Woodside Energy rose 1 per cent and Santos added 1.3 per cent. Among the refiners, Ampol advanced 0.3 per cent and Viva Energy surged 3.2 per cent. Meanwhile, miners BHP and Fortescue added 1.3 per cent and 2.4 per cent respectively.

Gold miners also reported gains, with Northern Star gaining 2.1 per cent and Evolution rising 1.6 per cent as the gold price steadied at about $US4000 ($5690) per ounce.

Technology stocks fell early, following their Wall Street peers, but rebounded as the day progressed. WiseTech grew 1.7 per cent, Xero rose 1.4 per cent and TechnologyOne added 1.7 per cent. Embattled AI company NextDC slumped 2.5 per cent as it announced its chairman, Douglas Flynn, would stand for re-election at its annual meeting with investors next month but retire once a replacement is in place, and chief executive Craig Scroggie will forfeit millions in bonuses.

Pharmaceutical giant CSL has named its interim chief executive, Gordon Naylor, as its next chair, replacing Brian McNamee, who will end his decades-long association with the Australian pharmaceutical giant.

Naylor will take over as chair on March 31. He will hand over chief executive duties to Deborah Waterhouse in February.

McNamee, as CEO, helped steer the company’s transformation from a government agency into one of Australia’s largest listed companies, but it has struggled with a string of downgrades over the past year which sent its shares sharply lower. CSL shares ended the day down 1.6 per cent.

On Wall Street on Friday, the S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent as the index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain.

Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher.

The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology, and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive.

“Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.

The latest round of corporate earnings is being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon.

Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent.

American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite reporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade.

JPMorganChase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent.

While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent.

European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit.

Treasury yields in the US edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late on Thursday.

Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the US. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation.

Wall Street expects the US central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily towards another rate hike in December.

Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.

#5355. The communication gap in the AI workplace

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Australian companies are redesigning jobs, tasks and teams around artificial intelligence faster than many are explaining to employees what those changes will mean for their work.

Nearly half of Australian IT decision-makers and business leaders surveyed for HP’s 2026 Work Relationship Index say AI is already changing tasks, workflows, teams or roles. More than half say its adoption has created new roles or teams.

But only 19 per cent of Australian knowledge workers say there has been discussion about AI’s potential impact on roles or headcount, while 40 per cent say their organisation clearly communicates how AI and new technologies may affect their role.

Brad Pulford, HP vice president and managing director for Australia and New Zealand, says uncertainty can grow when the technology moves faster than the conversation around it.

“AI is moving faster inside organisations than people’s understanding of it,” Pulford says. “When people see change but don’t understand it, uncertainty fills the gap. Leaders need to close it deliberately: explain what’s changing, who it affects and why, and check that the message is really landing.”

Gartner has found a similar gap between AI adoption and workforce readiness. Its Global Talent Monitor survey of 574 Australian employees, conducted in the first quarter of 2026, found only half reported receiving clear guidance, training or support for AI use. Fewer said their organisation had communicated how their roles would evolve.

At the same time, 38 per cent of Australian employees were expected to use AI in their role. Of those, 85 per cent had access to enterprise AI tools, while 86 per cent were also using personal AI tools to improve efficiency or complete more complex tasks.

Businesses have spent heavily on AI tools and are beginning to redesign work around them.

HP found 57 per cent of Australian IT decision-makers and 53 per cent of business leaders said AI adoption had created new roles or teams. Pulford says relatively few leaders reported that AI was replacing jobs.

Employees are nevertheless thinking about what the technology could mean for their careers. Six in 10 Australian knowledge workers surveyed by HP said they were prioritising transferable skills over climbing a traditional career ladder.

“Communication and employee experience need to be considered part of AI implementation because employees ultimately determine whether the technology delivers value,” Pulford says. “You can deploy very sophisticated technology, but if people don’t understand it, trust it or know how to use it effectively, the implementation will fall short.”

HP’s research found trust in leadership was the biggest driver of how people felt about work. Pulford says employers need to explain where new roles are emerging and give workers a path to acquire the skills required for them.

“At its best, AI can help take friction out of repetitive tasks and create more space for creativity, problem-solving, customer engagement and human connection,” he says. “But employees will only see that opportunity if organisations give them the skills and confidence to participate in it.”

Confidence with AI is not developing evenly across the workforce.

HP’s findings link skills with confidence. Across every generation, most Australian knowledge workers surveyed said access to upskilling made them less anxious about AI’s impact on their role and employer investment in their development made them feel more secure.

Pulford says training needs to connect AI with the work employees do every day.

“Confidence comes from giving people the opportunity to use AI in ways that are relevant to their day-to-day work,” he says. “That means moving beyond broad awareness or one-off training and helping employees understand where AI can genuinely make their day easier, where it can save time, and where human judgment still matters.”

Employees also need hardware capable of running the tools businesses expect them to use.

Only about a third of Australian knowledge workers surveyed by HP said they had been given an upgraded computer to run AI, compared with about half of business leaders and IT decision-makers.

Pulford says organisations should audit the technology their employees already have.

“Technology should make change easier to navigate, not add another layer of complexity,” he says. “Closing that gap with capable devices, reliable tools and proactive IT support is one of the fastest ways to make change feel manageable.”

AI-ready workplace technology can combine local AI processing with cloud services, security and collaboration tools. HP’s Intel Powered EliteBook X G2i, for example, provides on-device AI capability alongside enterprise security and AI-enabled collaboration features in a device designed for different working settings.

Pulford says the broader requirement is for technology to adapt to the work employees are doing rather than forcing them to continually adjust to new systems.

“Employees don’t want more technology for technology’s sake. They want tools that give them the confidence to do their best work as their roles evolve,” he says.

Technology alone, however, cannot tell an employee whether their job will change, what skills they will need or which decisions will remain theirs.

As companies redesign work around AI, those questions will become harder to leave unanswered. Giving employees AI tools is one thing. Giving them a clear understanding of what the technology means for their jobs, skills and responsibilities is another.

As AI reshapes how Australians work, having the right technology underpin that shift matters more than ever. The Intel® powered HP EliteBook X G2i is built for this new era of work, combining on device AI capability, enterprise grade security and seamless collaboration tools in a lightweight, adaptable design, so professionals can work confidently across hybrid environments. #5357. Mega gallery: why Canberra is leading the search for the next Cathy Freeman

When it comes to junior athletics, Canberra is ahead of the curve, and it could help produce the ACT's next Olympic gold medallist.

It's been a momentous year for track and field with the nationwide unification of the sport's biggest organisations, Australian Athletics and Little Athletics, which was announced last December.

The historic move was designed to boost participation and give kids a clearer pathway to progress from Little Athletics into high-performance competition, keeping them in the sport longer.

The change has been a huge success since its implementation, but the ACT has benefited even more than other states and territories because it actually made the shift years earlier for its 4000 athletes.

"Capital Athletics is the leader in the national space because we merged back in 2023, and nationally they've only had it like that for the last six months," Capital Athletics chief executive Adam Horner told The Canberra Times.

"We've seen the benefits of it a long time ago, and it's now starting to pay dividends with bigger competitions being held and kids staying within their clubs.

"Kids used to have to eventually move from a Little Athletics club to a senior athletics club, but now they have more continuity, consistency, and there's no disruption to their training or competition environment.

"The quality of performances and the engagement of the community is absolutely booming in Canberra, and we're getting a lot of great kids coming through, enjoying the sport."

Long-distance sprinter Cameron Myers, 20, has made a habit of setting records in recent years as the breakout star from the Canberra region, and his success is inspiring a new generation of youngsters to hit the track.

Out at Ginninderra Athletics Club's Saturday meet at Charnwood Oval, The Canberra Times got to see how track and field sports are thriving, with hundreds of kids aged 3 and up running, hurdling, throwing, and jumping with giant grins on their faces.

Lars Sagar broke his own personal best in under-12s high jump that many times, he finished the day with a new benchmark of 147 centimetres which, if not for his spiky hair, is about the exact same height as he is.

One official raced to congratulate every competitor in an under-8s race when every personal best was shattered in the blink of an eye.

Ginninderra is one of the largest and oldest athletics clubs in the ACT region, but it's a similar scene around the capital, with every weekend an opportunity to unearth the next Cathy Freeman.

"We're punching above our weight in our performances nationally," Horner said.

"We have a great young sprinter Kwame Antwi-Tuffour from Murrumbateman, and Ginninderra's Elijah Wilson was in the Under-20 World Championships in discus."

The greatest challenges for athletics are also faced by other sports in Canberra - facilities accessibility and condition limitations, and tackling the cost-of-living pressures which can hurt participation levels.

On the latter point Capital Athletics has had a lot of recent requests for fee exemptions or payment plans from parents, but it is trying to keep their sport as low-cost as possible to retain kids so clubs like Ginninderra can continue to grow.

"We're actually very proud because we were able to drop some of our costs this financial year," Horner said.

"We had about 45 per cent of our membership fees reduced, and we had about 10 per cent maintained. We feel like that's making the sport more accessible to athletes."

#5358. For some in Australia, hope is fading and anger is rising

Sulaiman "Sully" Zandinan is a Yazidi immigrant who has settled in Toowoomba. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

Sulaiman Zandinan does not pause to think about the question.

"Proud. Amazing. Freedom. Supportive. Happiness. Perfection," he said.

The words flow easily and enthusiastically.

"I'm so proud and lucky that I'm here," he said. "I live in this amazing country.

Sulaiman Zandinan is also a qualified soccer referee. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

Sully, as he is known, is 23 years old. He came to Australia as a 15-year-old refugee, settling in the regional city of Toowoomba, on Queensland's Darling Downs.

He is not among the many in Australia feeling disenchanted with life, with politics or fearing for the future.

Sully is not among the 6.22 out of 10 Australians who told a recent poll their life satisfaction had fallen, or the three in five Australians who think life was better 50 years ago.

Sully and many like him, who have endured dreadful hardship and suffering, are grateful that Australia has embraced them and love it.

Sulaiman Zandinan teaches English at Harristown State High School in Toowoomba. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

But many in Australia are not feeling the same way.

They are worried about the future and feel their daily struggles are not heard by people making decisions that impact their lives.

Our best stories start with listening to yours. Tell us what Australia should know.

The ABC is launching a new project, ABC Your Say, to give people from across the country the chance to voice the issues, challenges and opportunities that are shaping their communities.

We want you, the audience, to be part of the national conversation and tell us what matters most to you. For eight weeks, from July 19 to September 12, we will be iniviting people across the country to have "Your Say".

You can send your written submissions to Your Say — ABC News here.

Australians are restive. Support for One Nation is shifting the pendulum as people, disenchanted with governments and mainstream political parties, look to alternatives.

Crushed by cost-of-living pressures, nowhere to rent and priced out of the real estate market, for some, hope is fading, and anger is rising.

An Australian National University (ANU) poll in March this year found that life satisfaction was at its lowest level since the poll first started in 2019. And more Australians (54 per cent) were, when they answered the poll questions, dissatisfied with the direction of the country than those who were satisfied (46 per cent).

But according to the study, this wasn't the case for migrants born in non-English speaking countries, like Sully.

The ANU poll found that despite facing greater economic vulnerability, this group reported more positive orientations toward Australia on almost every attitudinal measure.

Sully adores his community of Toowoomba, 150 kilometres west of Brisbane. It is Australia's second largest inland city, where the second most spoken language, after English, is Kurdish Kurmanji, the traditional Yazidi dialect.

A Yazidi, from northern Iraq, Sully's family was captured and imprisoned for two years by the Islamic State group in 2014. He was just 12. They escaped in 2016 and lived in a refugee camp for two years before coming to Australia and settling in Toowoomba.

With no English, he worked hard at Harristown State High School. Embracing his lifetime love of soccer, he is now a qualified referee in the men's Queensland National Premier League. And he is back working at his old school, where students hail from more than 40 countries, and 29 per cent learn English as an Additional Language or Dialect (EAL/D).

Sulaiman Zandinan is proud of the work he does with his students, both in the classroom and on the pitch. (ABC News: Grace Nakamura)

Another finding of the ANU poll is that, contrary to some narratives, young Australians are not disengaged from democracy or intolerant of opposing views. The poll found that those aged 18 to 24 are the most satisfied with democracy and more likely to support the rights of those with extreme views to speak in public.

Jeffy Thomas is a 20-year-old nursing student at the University of Southern Queensland. Far from being disengaged, she is heading off soon to Queensland's Youth Parliament program.

Jeffy Thomas grew up in Kuwait and England. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

"I've seen really ambitious young people around me who have really strong opinions, and I'm really hopeful for the future because if there are people like them getting involved in the community, I'm pretty sure we're going to have better days, better laws and things that we really haven't looked into that will be achieved," she said.

Asked her say on what needs fixing, Ms Thomas said mental health was an area that needed attention and was often overlooked, especially for children.

"More funding would be great, especially in regional communities … it is harder to access services like that for anyone of any age," she said.

Jeffy Thomas is in her second year studying nursing at the University of Southern Queensland. (ABC News: Aisling Brennan)

ABC Your Say is inviting people from across the country to be part of the conversation.

Wendy and Brian Newman are a retired couple, in their 70s. They live in a home they built in the tiny western Queensland town of Surat, on the Great Inland Way, 450km west of Brisbane.

Wendy is annoyed by the way those in power talk about those in the bush.

Wendy Newman says she is sick of political parties talking down to regional Australians. (ABC News: Bella Munro)

"When they're talking about anything to do with rural or regional Australia, [they] tend to talk about the people as if they're country bumpkins who know nothing, you know, that are backward, that are slow, that you don't pay attention to them because they don't really know what they're talking about," she said.

Mrs Newman has a background in teaching, worked in the autism space and spent 10 years as a local councillor on the Maranoa Council.

Wendy Newman lives in a house she built with her husband, Brian, in Surat. (ABC News: Bella Munro)

"They're [country people are] not dumb. They're not stupid. And yes, they do know what they're talking about when they're talking about things like managing our environment, but they're not listened to. And they are quite intentionally denigrated by many of the political parties when it suits them," Mrs Newman said.

"My advice to people is never give up … be patient, be kind to others, be respectful, be responsible for what you do. Life is hard. You have to work hard for it. Keep fighting for your dreams and goals."

#5359. The hidden underbelly of Australia's weight-loss drug boom

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

This article contains references to eating disorders.

For Kansasin Darwan, living in Bajool in central Queensland, the weight-loss injection was supposed to be a solution. Instead, she says, it left her barely able to function.

The 48-year-old says she had gained weight during perimenopause and believed her Australian GP was unlikely to prescribe a weight-management medicine because she did not meet the relevant clinical criteria.

In Australia, GLP-1 weight loss drugs are generally prescribed for chronic weight management in adults with a body mass index (BMI) of 30 or higher, or a BMI of 27 to under 30 with at least one weight-related health condition.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

So, while on holiday in her home country of Thailand, Darwan went to a beauty clinic in outer Bangkok and bought an injectable medicine branded as Mounjaro.

Beauty clinics in Thailand are generally supervised by doctors. However, the screening process for GLP-1 use can be less extensive than the assessment typically conducted by GPs in Australia. For example, some customers at beauty clinics may be prescribed GLP-1 drugs even if they do not have diabetes or are within a healthy weight range.

Darwan brought the drugs back to Australia and began using them to lose weight.

"I couldn't concentrate while driving. I wasn't feeling like myself. I couldn't sleep. Even my children noticed that I was different," she tells SBS Thai.

Eighteen out of every 1,000 Australians, or almost 2 per cent of the population, are now taking GLP-1s regularly, according to a study by scientists at the University of New South Wales (UNSW) published in November 2025.

Darwan's experience offers a glimpse into a fast-growing market for weight-loss injections, where some Australians are seeking access overseas, while others are obtaining medicines through social-media sellers and informal supply channels.

An investigation by SBS Thai found weight-loss medicines being offered without a doctor's prescription in Australian community groups, reports of products entering the country through informal channels, and unapproved peptides being marketed as weight-loss products.

But access to these medicines is not uniformly occurring outside the established medical system. Many Australians obtain weight-loss drugs through registered health professionals and pharmacies.

For consumers navigating this market, the distinction between an approved prescription medicine, an experimental drug and an unapproved product can be difficult to see — with experts and authorities warning that using medicines outside approved pathways can carry serious risks.

For some consumers, access does not require a trip overseas.

SBS Thai found GLP-1 injectable medicines openly advertised in Australian Thai community Facebook groups, with some sellers offering the products without requiring a prescription.

We contacted one Melbourne-based seller, posing as a potential customer interested in buying "Mounjaro". The seller offered a 5mg vial for $750, saying it had been sourced from a beauty clinic in Udon Thani, a provincial city in north-east Thailand.

We contacted the clinic identified by the seller, which confirmed that it supplied products to the Melbourne-based seller.

SBS Thai has not independently established the circumstances of every shipment or whether every product sold through the channel was imported in accordance with Australian requirements.

The price for the 5mg multi-dose pre-filled injection pen also appeared significantly higher than the price we found for the same branded medicine at Australian pharmacies, where it was listed between $375 and $415 depending on the pharmacy and required a prescription.

The seller's claim of easy access raises significant regulatory and health concerns.

In response to an SBS Thai query, a Therapeutic Goods Administration (TGA) spokesperson said: "It is not legal to import GLP-1 medicines or peptide products into Australia for commercial purposes without appropriate authorisation and declaration."

The spokesperson said GLP-1 receptor agonists, including semaglutide and tirzepatide, are prescription-only medicines in Australia and should be used under the supervision of a qualified health professional.

The regulator has also warned about unregistered products being sold as GLP-1 medicines, particularly those obtained online or from overseas.

In March, TGA testing found several imported products labelled as containing GLP-1 or GLP-1 analogues contained none of those ingredients. The regulator advised consumers to obtain prescription medicines from registered Australian pharmacies rather than social media or other digital platforms.

The regulator has also increased its focus on unapproved peptide products.

Earlier this month, with assistance from NSW Police, the TGA seized more than $120,000 worth of unapproved peptide and anabolic steroid products from two NSW properties. The TGA said the products had allegedly been imported, relabelled and promoted for sale through social media and a website.

One of the products seized was labelled "retatrutide" — a name that also appeared in SBS Thai's investigation.

We found retatrutide offered at $300 for a 10mg vial at a Thai grocery store in Geelong, Victoria. The seller claimed the injectable product could help with weight loss and work similarly to other GLP-1 medicines.

Retatrutide is different from approved GLP-1 medicines such as Ozempic and Wegovy. While those medicines contain semaglutide, retatrutide is an experimental drug that acts on three hormone pathways involved in appetite and metabolism. It is not approved for sale as a medicine in Australia.

SBS Thai did not independently test the product or establish what was inside the vial. The TGA says unapproved peptide products have not been evaluated for safety, quality or effectiveness.

There is also a separate health warning involving products labelled retatrutide.

In June, Victoria's Department of Health said it had been notified of six cases of acute liver injury since January among people who had used products labelled as retatrutide. The department said investigations were continuing.

The informal market is emerging alongside a rapid increase in legitimate use of GLP-1 medicines.

Researchers at UNSW found that total sales of GLP-1 medicines rose from about 58,000 in May 2020 to 500,000 in April 2025. They also noted a significant disruption in sales from late 2022 to early 2024, when a drug shortage caused sales to drop by almost 80 per cent.

The researchers found that private, non-subsidised access had grown sharply, accounting for 43.8 per cent of estimated use by April 2025, with prices up to $600 per month.

The study did not include Wegovy and Saxenda, which are marketed specifically for weight loss. The researchers said their figures should therefore be regarded as a minimum estimate of overall GLP-1 use.

That expanding market is also being discussed heavily on social media.

Like Darwan, Ople Petchdee, who lives in Croydon South in Melbourne's east, also bought a GLP-1 injectable from a beauty clinic just outside the Thai capital, Bangkok.

Petchdee, who has called Australia home for the past 15 years, says she became interested in the medicines after seeing friends post about their experiences.

"Everyone posted on their Facebook, on their social media, that these medications helped them lose weight. So, my friends suggested I use them, too," she tells SBS Thai.

For Trevor Steward, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Melbourne, the concern is not only how people obtain GLP-1 medicines but also how the drugs are presented and understood online.

Steward is currently running a clinical trial examining how GLP-1 drugs affect the neurobiological function of people with binge eating disorder.

"It's about someone's mental and physical wellbeing. And that's something that needs to be considered holistically with a doctor involved," Steward tells SBS Thai.

He says there are also unanswered questions about what happens when treatment stops for people with eating disorders.

"If the weight comes back, we can maybe stipulate that the food noise will come back. And how will that person cope with that, thinking that they have achieved a certain sense of recovery and then falling back into that old pattern of behaviour before."

Steward says social media often strips away that nuance, framing GLP-1 medicines as a shortcut to achieving a particular body shape or weight, rather than treating them as serious medications to be considered in the context of a person's overall mental and physical health.

For Darwan, who had gone looking for a way to lose weight, reality was harder.

"My mood was depressing. I suffered from energy loss."

#5360. Saudi Arabia says intercepted Houthi missile targeting Riyadh as airport flights resume

Authorities sent text messages to residents warning them of a "hostile aerial threat" targeting the city.

Large plume of black smoke rises from the fuel storage depot at King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia on Sep 19, 2026. (File Photo: Reuters/Stringer)

RIYADH: The Saudi-led military coalition said Monday (Oct 26) it intercepted a ballistic missile fired by Yemen's Houthis, after the Iran-backed group claimed a new attack on the international airport in Riyadh.The operation came a day after explosions rattled the Saudi capital and authorities sent text messages to residents warning them of a "hostile aerial threat" targeting the city.The Houthis have carried out waves of strikes on the King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, including an attack this month that killed 13 people and wounded more than 300, the deadliest in the kingdom in more than a decade.Coalition spokesman Turki Al-Malki said on Monday that air defences "intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile" fired by the Houthis toward Riyadh, and destroyed two ballistic missile launchers in Yemen's capital Sanaa."We continue the process of dismantling the ballistic missile network of the terrorist Houthi militia," Al-Malki wrote on X.Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Monday the group "successfully targeted" the airport with a ballistic missile, and struck oil pumping stations with drones."The Yemeni Armed Forces carried out two qualitative military operations targeting the Saudi enemy troop concentrations and weapons depots" in the Aden and Lahj governorates in Yemen, which caused "dozens of casualties", Saree added.

On Sunday, the Houthis said they had launched an attack on the airport in Riyadh, after the kingdom announced that flights had resumed.The airport closure was a major blow for Saudi Arabia, forcing the postponement of the kingdom's flagship investment conference until 2027 and disrupting travel plans for thousands of passengers.The Dakar Rally also joined a growing list of events that were cancelled, postponed or relocated amid the fallout from the war.Saree had earlier warned that Riyadh airport was still "unsafe" and a "military target", and urged airlines and travellers to avoid it."The Saudi regime shall bear the consequences of any operations at the airport," the spokesman said.Saudi Arabia and the government it backs in Yemen have come under sustained attack in recent weeks from the Houthis as a years-long truce broke down in the summer, shifting the focus of the wider US-Iran war that erupted in February.

As operations resumed at Riyadh airport, Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis met Saudi de facto ruler Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.During the meeting, Mitsotakis "responded favourably to the kingdom's request to keep the Patriot system in Saudi Arabia, given the current challenging circumstances", his office said.Greece has deployed a battery to operate the US-made Patriot air defence system in Yanbu, a major oil export hub on the Red Sea coast.On Sunday, the Saudi-led military coalition said it intercepted at least 10 ballistic missiles."The bombardment has been very heavy since this morning - may God keep us safe. Everything is shaking because of the explosions," one resident in Saudi Arabia's Khamis Mushait told AFP on Sunday on condition of anonymity.The kingdom's civil defence agency later said two people were injured in the south by falling debris, also reporting damage to several buildings and vehicles.Images released by the SPA showed a building with part of its upper facade destroyed, exposing metal rods. Another image captured large windows shattered, with shards of glass strewn across the pavement and part of the road.

#5361. Qu'est-ce que le PHP et pourquoi a-t-il déclenché une vague mondiale de mesures de cybersécurité ?

Pendant plus d'une décennie, de graves failles sont passées inaperçues dans la technologie qui sous-tend une grande partie d'Internet.

Il a fallu recourir à l'intelligence artificielle (IA) pour les mettre au jour, ce qui a déclenché une alerte mondiale en matière de cybersécurité.

Ces vulnérabilités se trouvent dans un langage de programmation appelé PHP, utilisé à l'échelle internationale depuis les années 2000 pour créer des sites web.

Les gouvernements et les agences de cybersécurité du monde entier s'efforcent de limiter les répercussions de cette découverte faite mercredi, et ont exhorté les opérateurs de sites web à installer un nouveau correctif d'urgence ou à envisager de mettre leurs plateformes hors ligne.

La société de cybersécurité Wiz – l'une des entreprises dont les chercheurs ont mis au jour ces failles – a qualifié ces failles de « plus graves » jamais détectées par l'IA.

OpenAI, dont la technologie a permis de détecter ces failles, a qualifié cette découverte de « l'un des problèmes de sécurité les plus graves de ces dernières années ».

La plupart des gens n'ont peut-être jamais entendu parler de PHP – abréviation de « PHP : Hypertext Preprocessor » –, mais ils y sont très certainement confrontés au quotidien.

PHP est à la base d'un grand nombre de plateformes, notamment les boutiques en ligne, Wikipédia et WordPress – le système de gestion de contenu qui sous-tend de nombreux sites web tels que les blogs.

Lorsque vous consultez un site web comme Wikipédia, c'est le code PHP qui rassemble les informations dont vous avez besoin et les présente sous une forme lisible sur le web, a expliqué Paul Spain, directeur général de Gorilla Cyber Security, à la BBC.

Mais en raison d'une faille susceptible de permettre à des pirates de prendre le contrôle des serveurs web concernés sans authentification et de voler des données sensibles, toutes les applications développées en PHP se sont retrouvées exposées.

L'IA pourrait faciliter et accélérer ce type d'attaques, a déclaré M. Spain, estimant que cette faille pourrait toucher « des millions et des millions » de sites web.

Ce serait « catastrophique » si des pirates informatiques ou des États utilisaient cette faille à des fins malveillantes et s'emparaient de données privées sur des sites web, a déclaré Jill Slay, chercheuse en cybersécurité à l'université d'Adélaïde.

Cette alerte a perturbé les services à l'échelle mondiale, des plateformes de jeux aux portails gouvernementaux en passant par les forums en ligne.

C'est notamment le cas de Wikimedia — l'organisation à l'origine de l'encyclopédie en ligne Wikipédia — qui a mis hors ligne plusieurs de ses systèmes à titre de mesure de précaution.

Des sites et des pages ont été mis hors ligne par le gouvernement finlandais, le conseil municipal d'Édimbourg et la BBC, tandis que l'agence néerlandaise de cybersécurité a également retiré son site web.

Un certain nombre d'organismes publics écossais, notamment des conseils municipaux et des conseils de santé, ont également mis leurs sites Internet hors ligne.

Certains experts avertissent que cette vulnérabilité pourrait exposer à un risque accru les sites Internet mal entretenus, en particulier ceux appartenant à de petites structures disposant de ressources limitées en matière de sécurité.

D'autres tentatives d'exploitation de ces failles sont à prévoir dans les semaines à venir, puisque les détails techniques sont désormais rendus publics, a déclaré Salil Kanhere, chercheur en cybersécurité à l'UNSW de Sydney.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Les développeurs de la plateforme PHP ont publié mercredi des correctifs visant à corriger les failles de sécurité qui se cachaient dans leur logiciel depuis des années.

« Tous les utilisateurs de PHP sont vivement encouragés à effectuer la mise à jour sans délai », a déclaré la société.

Les autorités et les organismes de sécurité du monde entier se sont fait l'écho de ces avertissements, exhortant les exploitants de sites web à sécuriser leurs plateformes.

L'Agence nationale de sécurité américaine (NSA) a demandé à toutes les organisations utilisant PHP de mettre leurs systèmes hors ligne si elles n'étaient pas en mesure d'appliquer immédiatement les correctifs, ajoutant que cette faille pouvait offrir un « accès direct » permettant d'exploiter la base de données d'un système.

« Ces risques sont suffisamment graves pour nécessiter l'application immédiate de correctifs dans l'ensemble des ministères et agences du gouvernement américain », a déclaré l'agence.

Le Centre national de cybersécurité du Royaume-Uni a émis des recommandations similaires et a conseillé aux organisations de vérifier la présence éventuelle de « portes dérobées installées par un pirate ».

Ses homologues de l'Union européenne, de Singapour et d'Australie ont également publié des alertes similaires.

La Première ministre japonaise, Sanae Takaichi, a exhorté la population à vérifier si leurs sites web accessibles au public fonctionnaient sous PHP.

« Nous demandons instamment à tout le monde de prendre des mesures dès ce soir », a écrit Mme Takaichi sur X.

« S'il est difficile d'appliquer rapidement le correctif, la suspension temporaire des sites web et d'autres mesures similaires peuvent être considérées comme un moyen efficace de réduire les risques », a-t-elle déclaré.

Les entreprises technologiques s'empressent également de sécuriser leurs systèmes.

Le géant du commerce électronique Amazon a déclaré avoir été la cible de multiples tentatives quelques jours avant la divulgation publique de la faille PHP. On ignore comment les attaquants potentiels ont eu connaissance de cette vulnérabilité.

Ces failles ont été découvertes par des chercheurs des sociétés de sécurité Calif et Wiz.

Ces chercheurs ont utilisé des outils d'intelligence artificielle avancés, capables d'analyser le code et de détecter les failles bien plus rapidement que ne le peuvent les humains ou les anciens systèmes.

« Les logiciels modernes sont incroyablement complexes, et certaines failles peuvent passer inaperçues pendant des années », a déclaré M. Kanhere.

« Les bogues sous-jacents n'étaient pas nouveaux ; ce qui a changé, c'est notre capacité à les détecter », a ajouté M. Kanhere.

Des détails concernant cette découverte ont fuité sur Internet cette semaine, contraignant les développeurs de la plateforme PHP à annoncer en urgence l'existence de cette faille de sécurité et son ampleur considérable.

Cet incident « met en évidence la capacité de l'IA à détecter des failles de sécurité », mais aussi la manière dont elle peut « aider les pirates à développer rapidement des outils offensifs et des exploits », a déclaré OpenAI dans un article de blog.

Le créateur de ChatGPT a indiqué avoir publié un programme permettant de vérifier si la plateforme PHP est sécurisée.

« Bon nombre de ces failles proviennent de la manière dont les logiciels ont été conçus par le passé, c'est-à-dire en privilégiant la fonctionnalité au détriment de la sécurité », a déclaré Ryan Ko, du Cyber Research Centre de l'université du Queensland.

Les propriétaires de sites web sont invités à sécuriser leurs sites à l'aide de la dernière version de PHP.

Ce correctif PHP constitue une petite mise à jour de routine pour la plupart des équipes techniques, a déclaré M. Spain.

L'Agence nationale de sécurité américaine (NSA) a appelé à une « vigilance accrue » au cours des prochaines semaines et à suivre de près les mises à jour proposées par les éditeurs de logiciels.

« Il est primordial de faire preuve de vigilance lors de l'application des correctifs liés à ces systèmes », a-t-elle déclaré.

La responsabilité incombe principalement aux exploitants de sites web, mais les utilisateurs doivent rester attentifs à tout conseil de sécurité émis par les services concernés, comme les demandes de changement de mot de passe, a déclaré M. Kanhere.

Il a également averti le public de se méfier de tout message de hameçonnage exploitant la médiatisation de cet incident.

#5363. Gina Rinehart takes fight for helipad at Hancock’s Perth HQ to tribunal

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Gina Rinehart’s company Hancock Prospecting has taken its fight to build a helipad atop its West Perth headquarters to the State Administrative Tribunal after it was knocked back by the local council.

The City of Perth grounded plans for the helipad at the Ord Street building in December, despite two councillors backing the idea of a helicopter landing in the city precinct, and the lord mayor describing Rinehart as an “amazing Australian”.

Opposition to the helipad stemmed from concerns over noise, whether it was conducive with the area’s existing planning scheme, and whether allowing the CBD’s first private-use helipad would set an undesirable precedent.

The area, in West Perth, is an office and residential precinct, with the City of Perth flagging nearby sites could accommodate more residents in the future.

But Ord Street Holdings counsel Grant Donaldson, KC, in his opening statement in SAT on Monday, argued the helipad would only be used in “daylight hours” between midday and 7pm up to 12 times a year for “occasional corporate transport”.

“That’s 144 minutes per annum, that equates to the sound of an electric kettle boiling for six minutes, once every fortnight, between the hours of noon and 7pm,” he said.

“This case boils down to what negative impact is this use going to have on the objects of the current or new scheme?”

The mining giant has previously likened Perth to Tokyo and New York as a “global city”, saying “rooftop helipads are commonplace across the world’s leading cities, and our proposal would elevate Perth’s status”.

But City of Perth barrister Tim Houweling said the fundamental issue in the case was noise.

Neighbouring buildings have also objected to the helipad.

The Child and Adolescent Health Service made a submission to the City of Perth stating that sudden, intermittent helicopter noise could interrupt testing of children with conditions including autism, sensory issues, ADHD or anxiety.

The submission also raised concerns that its roof is old and made of asbestos, and helicopter downwash could disrupt the asbestos dust that has settled.

After the council initially refused the helipad application, Hancock Prospecting lodged a revised development plan outlining a new flight path, in a bid to get the request over the line.

Previous plans had the helicopter approaching from the east or west of the eye-popping five-storey headquarters, in a route that would have seen it come down over the inner-city suburb of Subiaco or a mix of residential and office buildings in West Perth.

Instead, the new flight path has the eight-seat Bell 429 helicopter approaching the building from the south-west, tracking Thomas Street on the outer fringe of Perth’s CBD botanic garden Kings Park, before turning and descending once it reaches Ord Street.

A Hancock Prospecting spokesperson said the company’s original application was “developed with expert input and independent technical analysis which confirmed the helipad and flight path can operate safely and appropriately”.

“However, as part of our extensive good faith efforts to reach agreement with the City of Perth, we have proposed an amended flight path and further reduced the proposed operating timeframes,” they said.

SAT judge Henry Jackson is presiding over the appeal, and will make a ruling on the helipad at the conclusion of the two-day trial which will hear from acoustic and planning experts.
