#5364. ASX rebounds to end on a high; CSL names new chair

Updated October 26, 2026 — 4:51pm,first published October 26, 2026 — 5:20am

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

The Australian sharemarket has rebounded after an early fall to close in the green, with materials and energy stocks posting gains thanks to a rise in oil prices over the weekend.

The S&P/ASX 200 gained 14.7 points or 0.17 per cent, to 8809 on Monday. The Australian dollar was trading at US70.33¢.

The gains were largely thanks to advancing energy and materials stocks off the back of a rise in oil prices. Earlier in the day, Brent crude advanced above $US116 a barrel while West Texas Intermediate rose above $US102 before retreating slightly in the afternoon.

The gains were linked to fears the US would restart its war with Iran, with President Donald Trump telling Fox News it was “getting to be decision time” on whether he would make a deal with Tehran or “finish it off”. Meanwhile, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said if rationality existed, the US would not attempt an attack.

Woodside Energy rose 1 per cent and Santos added 1.3 per cent. Among the refiners, Ampol advanced 0.3 per cent and Viva Energy surged 3.2 per cent. Meanwhile, miners BHP and Fortescue added 1.3 per cent and 2.4 per cent respectively.

Gold miners also reported gains, with Northern Star gaining 2.1 per cent and Evolution rising 1.6 per cent as the gold price steadied at about $US4000 ($5690) per ounce.

Technology stocks fell early, following their Wall Street peers, but rebounded as the day progressed. WiseTech grew 1.7 per cent, Xero rose 1.4 per cent and TechnologyOne added 1.7 per cent. Embattled AI company NextDC slumped 2.5 per cent as it announced its chairman, Douglas Flynn, would stand for re-election at its annual meeting with investors next month but retire once a replacement is in place, and chief executive Craig Scroggie will forfeit millions in bonuses.

Pharmaceutical giant CSL has named its interim chief executive, Gordon Naylor, as its next chair, replacing Brian McNamee, who will end his decades-long association with the Australian pharmaceutical giant.

Naylor will take over as chair on March 31. He will hand over chief executive duties to Deborah Waterhouse in February.

McNamee, as CEO, helped steer the company’s transformation from a government agency into one of Australia’s largest listed companies, but it has struggled with a string of downgrades over the past year which sent its shares sharply lower. CSL shares ended the day down 1.6 per cent.

On Wall Street on Friday, the S&P 500 fell 0.5 per cent as the index posted its second-straight weekly loss. The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.2 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite slipped 0.2 per cent after giving up a modest gain.

Several AI-related companies rallied, helping ease some of the impact from the broader market slide. Micron Technology rose 2.5 per cent, Intel gained 1.7 per cent, Microsoft added 0.7 per cent, and Advanced Micro Devices closed 1.7 per cent higher.

The tech sector’s influence is also capable of quickly switching over to a heavy weight. Stocks that have benefited from the frenzy over AI have been swinging over rising worries about their path ahead. Investors are worried about whether their high prices are justified. Many of those companies have been borrowing to fund investments in AI technology, and high interest rates are making those loans more expensive.

“Investors appear increasingly focused on the economics of AI, particularly the substantial upfront costs required to build AI infrastructure and the uncertainty around the timing of returns on those investments,” said Angelo Kourkafas, senior global strategist at Edward Jones, in a research note.

The latest round of corporate earnings is being closely watched to help get a better sense of whether those investments are paying off, or might pay off. Several influential AI-related companies report their latest financial results next week, including Google’s parent, Alphabet, along with Microsoft and Amazon.

Industrial companies had some of the biggest losses. Caterpillar fell 2.4 per cent.

American Express slumped 3.7 per cent, one of several financial stocks that lost ground, despite reporting profits for its most recent quarter that beat analysts’ forecasts. The company did announce its first major job cuts in roughly a decade.

JPMorganChase fell 1.5 per cent, Citigroup dropped 1.5 per cent and Capital One Financial slid 1 per cent.

While higher oil prices weighed down much of the market, they helped boost energy companies. Chevron rose 2.9 per cent and ConocoPhillips gained 3.6 per cent.

European markets closed mostly lower. France’s main index fell 0.4 per cent, though yields on French government bonds eased a bit.

Treasury yields in the US edged higher following sharp drops on Thursday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury edged up to 4.99 per cent from 4.96 per cent late on Thursday.

Yields have been rising globally, partly over worries about governments taking on too much debt. Inflation also remains a concern and is stubbornly well above 3 per cent in the US. That prompted the Federal Reserve to raise its benchmark interest rate at its last meeting in an effort to cool inflation.

Wall Street expects the US central bank to hold rates steady at its meeting next week, but is leaning heavily towards another rate hike in December.

Wall Street will also get several big economic updates next week, including the Fed’s preferred measure of inflation. The personal consumption expenditures index is expected to show that inflation rose at a 3.7 per cent rate in September, sharply above the Fed’s 2 per cent target.

#5366. Страна ЕС оценила перспективы отношений с Россией

Тибор Гашпар. Фото: Пресс-служба Госдумы РФ / РИА Новости

Словакия заинтересована в прагматичных отношениях с Россией, заявил заместитель председателя Национального совета (парламента) страны Тибор Гашпар в беседе с «Известиями».

Он отметил, что особое значение будут иметь энергетика, поставки природного газа и продолжение поставок нефти, так как энергетическая стабильность напрямую влияет на словацкую экономику и граждан. По его словам, вполне обоснованно ожидать стремления к достижению конкретных результатов в энергетической сфере.

Гашпар также подчеркнул, что в интересах обеих стран развивать сотрудничество в области культуры, науки, туризма и гуманитарных вопросов.

Ранее портал Advance писал, что в Евросоюзе появляются сигналы, что «политическое табу» на диалог с Россией будет отменено. На это указывает возобновление прямого экономического сотрудничества РФ и Словакии.

#5367. Mercedes CLA 200 4matic: Auch die Verbrenner-Version kann überzeugen

Der elektrische CLA setzt neue Effizienzmaßstäbe. Doch die Plattform erlaubt auch Verbrenner-Derivate. So was sehen wir uns doch gleich einmal an!

Interessant und begründet im Gesamtpaket: Wo bei der E-Version der Basisantrieb hinten erfolgt, geschieht das beim Verbrenner vorne.

Der Mercedes CLA ist auf der sportlichen Seite zu Hause, ein bisschen jedenfalls. Nicht zu hundert Prozent. Dass er nicht übermotorisiert ist, kann man als sympathisch empfinden. Angetrieben wird der CLA 200 vom neuen 1,5-Liter-Mildhybrid-Benziner mit dem 4Matic-Allradantrieb. Als Systemleistung sind 184 PS angegeben. Kombiniert werden ein 1,5-Liter-Turbobenziner mit 163 PS mit einem Elektromotor, der den Rest beisteuert. Mercedes gibt für den 4Matic einen kombinierten Normverbrauch von rund 5,2 Litern je 100 Kilometer an. In unserem Test kamen wir auf einen Wert knapp über sechs Liter, am Ende standen 6,3 Liter pro hundert Kilometer am Bordcomputer, das ist für ein sportlich ausgelegtes und halbwegs ausgewachsenes Fahrzeug ein vernünftiger Wert. Der Allradantrieb macht vor allem bei Nässe, auf verschneiten Straßen und beim Beschleunigen auf rutschigem Untergrund den Unterschied.

#5370. Rybakina finds Ningbo spark again ahead of WTA Finals title defence

Oct 26 : A year after winning the Ningbo Open transformed Elena Rybakina's season, the world number one returned to the Chinese city and retained her title on Sunday, as her game clicked into gear before another tilt at the WTA Finals.

Her 2025 success proved the springboard for a stellar run as she secured the last spot in the eight-player WTA Finals field the following week, before winning the season finale and carrying that momentum into the current campaign.

The 27-year-old Kazakh went on to capture the Australian Open title in January before claiming her third Grand Slam crown at the US Open last month.

Rybakina's 6-2 6-2 win over Leylah Fernandez in the Ningbo final on Sunday came after she had suffered defeat in her first match as world number one in Beijing and an injury-enforced absence from Wuhan.

#5371. Joseph Kabila lance le FRN : quels objectifs face au pouvoir de Tshisekedi ?

Crédit photo, (Photo de Jospin Mwisha / AFP via Getty Images)

Le lancement d'une nouvelle coalition politico-militaire remplaçant l'alliance AFC-M23 qui combat les forces gouvernementales congolaises dans l'Est du pays a surpris beaucoup d'observateurs de la scène politique congolaise.

Dénommé Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN), cette nouvelle alliance est dirigée par l'ancien président Joseph Kabila, condamné à mort par contumace par un tribunal militaire en fin septembre 2025.

En prenant la tête de cette rébellion qui contrôle l'Est de la RDC, les manœuvres de Kabila et de ses alliés sont disséquées par des analystes politiques qui estiment que la création du FRN ''rabat les cartes sur le plan militaire, politique et diplomatique en RDC''.

Crédit photo, (Photo by Jospin Mwisha / AFP via Getty Images)

C'est au cours d'une conférence de presse tenue dans la résidence même de l'ancien président, Joseph Kabila à Goma, cette ville de l'Est de la RDC contrôlée par le mouvement rebelle M23, que la création du FRN, Front pour la refondation de la nation a été annoncée.

Autour de la table, les principaux leaders de ce nouveau mouvement politico-militaire qui remplace désormais l'AFC-M23 qui combat depuis plusieurs années les forces gouvernementales dans cette partie de la RDC.

"Est créé un mouvement politico-militaire Front pour la refondation de la nation (FRN)", et "devient président : Joseph Kabila", a déclaré Claude Ibalanky, conseiller du FRN, lors de la conférence de presse commune tenue dans la résidence de l'ancien président.

Placé désormais à la tête de ce mouvement rebelle, Joseph Kabila, ancien président de la République aura comme adjoints les chefs rebelles Corneille Nangaa, Bertrand Bisimwa, Freddy Kaniki et Sultani Makenga.

La naissance de ce mouvement politico-militaire, qui rassemble les forces de Joseph Kabila et de l'AFC-M23, intervient dans un contexte politique incertain en RDC.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

Depuis plusieurs mois, la majorité présidentielle défend un projet de révision constitutionnelle qui alimente les spéculations sur une éventuelle candidature de Félix Tshisekedi à un troisième mandat. Âgé de 63 ans, le président congolais achève en principe son second et dernier mandat de cinq ans en 2028.

Pour l'opposition, qui a organisé plusieurs manifestations contre ce projet, cette révision constitutionnelle constitue une « manœuvre politique » destinée à permettre au chef de l'État de se maintenir au pouvoir, alors que la Constitution congolaise limite la présidence à deux mandats.

Sur le plan militaire, l'AFC-M23 s'est emparée de vastes territoires dans l'est de la RDC à la faveur d'une offensive menée l'année dernière.

Les autorités congolaises accusent depuis plusieurs mois l'ancien président Joseph Kabila de soutenir les groupes rebelles qui contrôlent une partie de l'est du pays, voire d'en être le véritable chef.

Joseph Kabila est apparu à Goma en 2025 et plusieurs de ses anciens alliés l'ont depuis rejoint dans cette partie du territoire congolais contrôlée par la rébellion du M23.

Crédit photo, (Photo de Jospin Mwisha / AFP via Getty Images)

Joseph Kabila a accédé au pouvoir en RDC en 2001, à la suite de l'assassinat de son père, Laurent-Désiré Kabila. Il a dirigé le pays jusqu'en janvier 2019, date à laquelle il a cédé le pouvoir à Félix Tshisekedi, alors son allié politique.

Le 30 septembre 2025, un tribunal militaire de haut rang l'a condamné à mort par contumace après l'avoir reconnu coupable de « complot, trahison, viol, crimes de guerre et crimes contre l'humanité ».

Il a également été condamné à verser plus de 30 milliards de dollars de dommages et intérêts à l'État congolais ainsi qu'aux provinces du Nord-Kivu et du Sud-Kivu.

Dans son jugement, la haute cour militaire de Kinshasa a estimé que l'ancien président, absent durant son procès et non représenté par un avocat, avait été « en intelligence avec le Rwanda ».

Selon le tribunal, Joseph Kabila est le véritable chef du groupe rebelle AFC-M23.

Son entourage a qualifié le procès de « comédie », sans que cela n'empêche les magistrats militaires d'ordonner son arrestation immédiate.

Crédit photo, (Photo de Daniel Buuma/Getty Images)

Selon Makangu Silas Mimile, expert en géopolitique, l'alliance FRN constituée par plusieurs éléments pourrait donner à la crise sécuritaire que la RDC connait depuis plusieurs années, une autre dimension.

''La première dimension, c'est la dimension politique qui serait une sorte de légitimation à la contestation du pouvoir de Kinshasa'' déclare Dr Silas Makangu.

''Cette rébellion risque d'avoir désormais une légitimation à cause du statut de celui qui est à la tête de cette alliance, en l'occurrence le Président Joseph Kabila'' et ''pourrait donner à la contestation du régime en place, une dimension nationale au regard de ce que Kabila a été et ce qu'il est au plan politique'' a-t-il précisé.

Au niveau militaire dit-il, ''il y a un risque qu'il y ait un rapprochement entre les réseaux dormants de Joseph Kabila au sein de l'armée, avec l'AFC-M23'' estime l'analyste.

''Rappelez-vous qu'il a été chef d'Etat major pendant quelques années, il a été président de la République pendant 18 ans. Il existe certainement un réseau Kabila, c'est-à-dire des gens qui ont été promus, qui ont été formés, qui ont été nommés durant son régime et qui pourraient malheureusement lui être loyale. Et ces réseaux dormants pourraient être une pépinière pour l'AFC-M23'' pense Silas Makangu Mimile.

Pour sa part, Christian Moleka, analyste politique et coordonnateur national de la Dynamique des politologues de la RDC (Dypol) estime que l'alliance créée (FRN) ''vient conforter les discours tenus par le président (Tshisekedi) depuis pratiquement deux ans, qui déclarait que Kabila était le vrai leader de l'AFC-M23''.

''Maintenant que les masques sont tombés, ça conforte le narratif du président à savoir c'est toujours l'homme qui était aux manettes et maintenant il assume de prendre le combat'' dit-il.

Crédit photo, (Photo de Daniel Buuma/Getty Images)

Dans les objectifs officiellement déclarés, le FRN parle de vouloir ''refonder la nation, de restaurer le fonctionnement de la République et mettre fin à la tyrannie''.

Interrogé sur ces déclarations, Dr Silas Makangu invite à lire entre les lignes pour comprendre les objectifs réels de ce mouvement politico-militaire.

''On peut aussi lire entre les lignes, qu'ils voudraient étendre la base politique de l'opposition au-delà du territoire contrôlé jusque-là par l'AFC-M23, c'est-à-dire qu'il est possible, fort probable je dirais, qu'ils recourent à la conquête de nouveaux territoires, de nouvelles villes, voire de nouvelles provinces''.

L'analyste politique soutient qu'un des ''objectifs non avoués que le président Kabila qui a mal digéré son exclusion et sa condamnation à mort, voudrait chercher à réapparaître sur la scène politique et jouer un rôle prépondérant voire tenter de revenir à la magistrature suprême''.

En prenant la tête de cette rébellion, l'ancien président Kabila veut peser sur la vie politique et militaire en RDC.

Alors que plusieurs provinces à l'Est du pays sont désormais placées sous le contrôle du FRN, faut-il redouter une reprise généralisée des combats?

Pour Christian Ndombo Moleka, une reprise des combats n'est pas à écarter mais une offensive militaire vers Kinshasa est ''peu probable à ce stade du rapport des forces sur le terrain.

''On s'attend à une reprise des combats dans le sud Kivu, vers Uvira et éventuellement une extension vers le Katanga, c'est le scénario le plus probable'' pense l'analyste congolais.

''Ce serait une opération qui essayerait de couper le coffre-fort du régime, le Katanga. S'ils parvenaient à couper le coffre-fort Katangais, ce serait un fort levier de pression vis-à-vis du pouvoir de Kinshasa''.

Quant à une éventuelle offensive militaire sur Kinshasa, ''il y a quand même lieu de se poser la question sur la capacité militaire des mouvements rebelles et la faisabilité d'une telle opération'' relativise Christian Ndombo Moleka.

''Pour arriver à Kinshasa, il faudrait un véritable soutien diplomatique des Etats de la région. Est-ce que les chefs d'Etat de la région sont pour ou contre le fait que Kabila soit à la tête d'un mouvement rebelle ? Est-ce qu'il a les capacités militaires, est-ce qu'il a suffisamment de personnel, de moyens logistiques, et la stratégie pour parvenir à cette fin, le temps nous le dira''.

Selon les deux analystes, le fait que Kabila soit mis en avant dans ce mouvement donne de l'eau au moulin à Kagamé qui déclare que la crise est essentiellement congolaise et que le Rwanda n'a été indexé que maladroitement et de bâtir un narratif vers les sanctions américaines.

Toutefois, l'AFC-M23 dépend logistiquement du soutien de Kigali.

''Les choses ne vont fondamentalement pas changer, c'est le branding qui a évolué, mais l'influence rwandaise sur le M23 ne va pas changer avec le FRN'' explique Christian Ndombo Moleka.

Crédit photo, (Photo de MAHMUD HAMS/AFP via Getty Images)

Les deux analystes congolais estiment qu'un repositionnement des forces politiques est en cours, tant dans le cadre du dialogue politique lancé par le président que des différents processus de paix actuellement engagés.

Ils s'interrogent toutefois sur l'attitude qu'adoptera le FRN, sans se prononcer de manière définitive.

« Le FRN va-t-il s'inscrire dans la continuité de ce que le M23 a signé à Doha, notamment le cessez-le-feu, ou va-t-il inaugurer une nouvelle dynamique remettant en cause l'ensemble des processus engagés, au risque de rebattre totalement les cartes et de réinstaurer un rapport de force ? »

Autant de questions qui, à ce stade, restent sans réponse dans le contexte politique actuel de la RDC.

#5373. Enosh has a $600,000 deadline. The clock is ticking

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Share your feedback and help us improve this feature. Read more about how we use AI at SBS here.

Should you invest in shares, or property? Is university still worth it, or should you start your own business? With the path to financial security becoming less clear, Insight asks how aspirational people are getting ahead, and whether Australia is a good country to build wealth. Watch Insight episode Gettin' Rich on SBS On Demand.

Enosh Tampoe, 23, and his family migrated from Sri Lanka 16 years ago and have been living in the same rental property since then.

The Sydney mortgage and finance adviser says that as an immigrant family "starting from scratch", he felt financially behind his friends at times growing up.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

"There were situations where I did feel like [I was] potentially behind — just because at the end of the day, there is that intergenerational wealth ...You'll notice obviously, they have their own houses; they have nice cars ..." he told Insight.

"Having that support from parents — whether it's in the form of getting money or continuing to live at home rent-free and all that stuff — definitely helps."

Feeling he couldn't rely on the "whole natural pathway of doing well in school, getting through uni and [getting] a big boy job" to build wealth, he took a hard approach to saving at an early age and bought a Sydney apartment two years ago.

Now, he's giving himself 10 years to save a $600,000 deposit for a $3 million Sydney home where his whole family can live.

"My end goal is … that great Australian dream: owning my own home, building my family and raising them in a nice neighbourhood," he said.

To reach his goal faster, he lives with his parents and rents out his apartment — taking advantage of the tax benefits of negative gearing to build equity.

Negative gearing refers to a situation where the ongoing costs of an investment exceed the rental income received, and the overall loss can then be claimed as a tax deduction.

But as of 1 July 2027, the federal government will restrict the tax benefits of negative gearing to new residential builds.

Enosh says this new law has reduced his borrowing capacity by "around 20 per cent", putting his plans to buy a second investment property this year on hold.

"If I were to purchase a second investment property, I'm not getting that benefit towards my salary or wage, that tax benefit."

Leticia Coco also became a homeowner in her early 20s — when her mother died from cancer, and she and her brother inherited the family home.

The siblings sold the house, and after setting up an emergency account, travelling and receiving laser eye surgery with the money, the occupational therapist eventually bought an apartment.

"It meant a lot, that inheritance," she said.

"(Without it, I'd be) saving or feeling like purchasing property was out of reach.

"I do feel wealthy in some ways, but yeah, you can't put a price on having your mum around."

Now a mother herself and living on the NSW North Coast, Letitia is hoping her inheritance will financially support her far into the future.

"I'm trying to use my inheritance or my head start … to help me get to maybe semi-retirement by the time I'm about 45 or 50."

Although house prices are cooling in parts of the country, overall property prices remain stubbornly high in comparison to income.

Economist Chris Richardson says the reason property continues to rise in value is that there is not enough supply to keep up with demand; and the undersupply of housing in Australia is a result of a decades-long culture of overregulation.

"In housing our policy is, 'No, you can't build that.' In economic reform, it's, 'No, you can't do that — there'd be some losers'," he said.

"We have chosen as a nation to spend decades pouring cement over our ability to change. It's part of the reason why our living standards have stagnated and struggled."

While there are many sentimental and emotional reasons people strive to buy a home, property remains a significant driver of everyday Australians' wealth.

Richardson, who worked with the International Monetary Fund and the Australian Treasury, says Australians have $12 trillion tied up in housing.

"In Australia, we have a system that means you get a terrible return if you're putting your money in a bank and earning interest, but you get a rather better return in housing and in super."

Because of this, he said it's not surprising that two-thirds of household wealth is in property — with much of the rest in superannuation.

He says that although we "all love hearing about ‘get rich quick', the safe and smart way is ‘get rich slow and sure'".

"Get the best possible income that you can. From that, save as much as you can. Get that money, stack it away, get the best return on it."

But building wealth and owning property is not the goal for everyone, including journalist and content creator Tara Meakins.

The 37-year-old is renting in Sydney and has no plans to buy a home — preferring to lean into the flexibility of freelancing, which allows her to work when and where she wants.

"This year I've been to Bali, Singapore, Hong Kong; I've never had to ask anyone for a day of annual leave," she said.

"It's just been such a joy to lead this life ... I live every day in the here and now; I can't imagine anything worse than being locked into one location."

For Tara, wealth is much less about money and more about experience and making memories.

She says she might buy one day, "much further down the track", when she decides where in the world she wants to live.

As budget reforms and rising interest rates reduce the borrowing capacity of prospective buyers, property prices in parts of Australia have fallen.

This was particularly helpful for photographer Alex Clisdell, who lives at home and is using property to generate equity.

The 26-year-old bought his first investment property in early July at a significant discount — $150,000 less than the original asking price.

"That money, which would've been spent on the down payment, now becomes capital that I can use for renovations," he said.

"Gonna use those renovations to generate equity and get the snowball rolling."

Investing in shares was one of the ways Alex saved a deposit. During the COVID-19 pandemic, he taught himself about shares and exchange-traded funds (ETFs) via social media videos and invested his JobKeeper payments.

"You give a 20-year-old $1,500 a week or a fortnight and (they're) buying European holidays, cars, this and that.

"I just decided to put it all in the share market."

The other way he saved was through building his photography and media company, which originally started as a side hustle but now employs eight people.

"I got to the last year of my [architecture] master's, and I was making more doing the photography part-time than my mates were earning as architects working full-time."

Alex, who describes himself as "not a big spender", continues to reinvest his money back into his business or shares and is already planning for retirement.

"What I'm kind of working towards next is accumulating that asset base and that wealth base," he said.

He says he plans to exit the workforce when he accumulates $10 million.

Financial adviser Glen Hare specialises in working with clients aged 20-45 and says younger Australians are increasingly turning to investing to build wealth because they feel buying property isn't achievable.

But Hare cautions young investors against the "false hope" that investing in shares automatically leads to owning property.

"Saving whatever's leftover at the end of the month gives you no clarity as to when you'll get there," he said.

"Whereas if you know you need $100,000 deposit … and you can save $2,000 per month, within four years, you'll have a deposit."

Alex, who has generated wealth from investing in shares, believes that money and investing in property buy freedom.

He says the "biggest wealth in life is freedom" and the choice to "do what you want, when you want, when you want, with whomever you want".

"Every time I buy another share or add more equity to that investment property, I feel like I'm almost buying a piece of my future back."

#5374. Gina Rinehart takes fight for helipad at Hancock’s Perth HQ to tribunal

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Gina Rinehart’s company Hancock Prospecting has taken its fight to build a helipad atop its West Perth headquarters to the State Administrative Tribunal after it was knocked back by the local council.

The City of Perth grounded plans for the helipad at the Ord Street building in December, despite two councillors backing the idea of a helicopter landing in the city precinct, and the lord mayor describing Rinehart as an “amazing Australian”.

Opposition to the helipad stemmed from concerns over noise, whether it was conducive with the area’s existing planning scheme, and whether allowing the CBD’s first private-use helipad would set an undesirable precedent.

The area, in West Perth, is an office and residential precinct, with the City of Perth flagging nearby sites could accommodate more residents in the future.

But Ord Street Holdings counsel Grant Donaldson, KC, in his opening statement in SAT on Monday, argued the helipad would only be used in “daylight hours” between midday and 7pm up to 12 times a year for “occasional corporate transport”.

“That’s 144 minutes per annum, that equates to the sound of an electric kettle boiling for six minutes, once every fortnight, between the hours of noon and 7pm,” he said.

“This case boils down to what negative impact is this use going to have on the objects of the current or new scheme?”

The mining giant has previously likened Perth to Tokyo and New York as a “global city”, saying “rooftop helipads are commonplace across the world’s leading cities, and our proposal would elevate Perth’s status”.

But City of Perth barrister Tim Houweling said the fundamental issue in the case was noise.

Neighbouring buildings have also objected to the helipad.

The Child and Adolescent Health Service made a submission to the City of Perth stating that sudden, intermittent helicopter noise could interrupt testing of children with conditions including autism, sensory issues, ADHD or anxiety.

The submission also raised concerns that its roof is old and made of asbestos, and helicopter downwash could disrupt the asbestos dust that has settled.

After the council initially refused the helipad application, Hancock Prospecting lodged a revised development plan outlining a new flight path, in a bid to get the request over the line.

Previous plans had the helicopter approaching from the east or west of the eye-popping five-storey headquarters, in a route that would have seen it come down over the inner-city suburb of Subiaco or a mix of residential and office buildings in West Perth.

Instead, the new flight path has the eight-seat Bell 429 helicopter approaching the building from the south-west, tracking Thomas Street on the outer fringe of Perth’s CBD botanic garden Kings Park, before turning and descending once it reaches Ord Street.

A Hancock Prospecting spokesperson said the company’s original application was “developed with expert input and independent technical analysis which confirmed the helipad and flight path can operate safely and appropriately”.

“However, as part of our extensive good faith efforts to reach agreement with the City of Perth, we have proposed an amended flight path and further reduced the proposed operating timeframes,” they said.

SAT judge Henry Jackson is presiding over the appeal, and will make a ruling on the helipad at the conclusion of the two-day trial which will hear from acoustic and planning experts.

#5375. This department paid KPMG $115k while former partner sat on risk committee

Education staff handed KPMG $115,000 after the firm's integrity scandal erupted, raising questions about the department's audit and risk committee.

One of the committee members is a former KPMG partner, who led its federal government account for 15 years.

Education staff signed two contract variations with KPMG in May: $26,000 on May 5 for "project assurance services" and $89,000 on May 18 for a CCTV in childcare evaluation.

These contracts and others meant Education spent more with KPMG ($2.23 million) than any other consultancy in 2025-26, according to its annual report published on Wednesday, October 21.

Federal agencies have faced scrutiny for their dealings with the firm since March, when allegations emerged that staff in its audit division misused client information to win new work.

KPMG leaders denied the allegations throughout April, saying they had not been substantiated through investigations.

Then on May 14 - days before Education signed the second contract variation - KPMG staff admitted that a senior partner improperly accessed and displayed a client's board documents.

The government banned agencies from starting new contracts with KPMG in June because of uncertainty about its controls on staff ethics and integrity, and that ban was extended in October.

Questions have now been raised about the department's response to the KPMG scandal, and the role of its audit and risk committee.

The committee met five times in 2025-26 to discuss financial and performance reporting, internal controls and systems of risk in areas such as fraud and corruption, cyber security and privacy.

Former KPMG partner Cath Ingram joined the committee in 2022, after leading the firm's federal government account for 15 years.

Ms Ingram has advised Attorney-General's, Canberra Airport and the Australian National University Foundation in committee and board roles since moving on from KPMG.

She attended all Education audit and risk committee meetings in 2025-26, but it is unclear whether there were any discussions regarding the department's external contracts at these meetings.

The Canberra Times does not suggest that Ms Ingram had any influence on decisions by Department of Education staff in relation to contracts with KPMG, or any other contracts.

A Department of Education spokesperson said it assessed value for money for all procurement activities in accordance with the Commonwealth procurement rules.

"The audit and risk committee is not involved in procurement decisions," the spokesperson said.

"The KPMG consultancy expenditure reported in 2025-26 relates to contracts awarded between October 2023 and December 2025.

"These contracts were established through open tender processes in which multiple suppliers were invited to respond.

"The audit and risk committee provides advice on the appropriateness of financial and performance reporting, systems of risk and systems of internal control.

"All audit and risk committee members are required to declare conflicts of interest annually and as they arise.

"Ms Ingram declared her previous roles at KPMG when she commenced as a member on the department's audit and risk committee."

When pressed on the audit and risk committee's role, the spokesperson said the committee had been updated on the department's actions in relation to KPMG contracts.

"The department follows whole of government guidance issued by the Department of Finance in relation to procurement," they said.

"Upon receipt of the procurement policy note the department sought assurances from KPMG in relation to active contracts.

"The audit and risk committee is not involved in the selection, procurement, or contract management of vendors; this work is undertaken by department delegates."

Liberal senator Richard Colbeck, who has advocated for more careful scrutiny of consulting spend, said the bar for transparency had become much higher since both the PwC tax leaks scandal and allegations involving KPMG.

"The department should proactively publish as much information as possible about the procurement process," Senator Colbeck said.

"That includes demonstrating that proper procurement rules were followed, that value-for-money assessments were undertaken, that any conflicts of interest were declared and managed appropriately, and that contract decisions were made independently of any advisory or committee roles.

"Where public money is being spent, the evidence should be available to support the decisions that were made.

"The lesson from recent consulting controversies is that transparency is not an optional extra; it is essential to maintaining public trust."

Regarding Ms Ingram's role on the audit and risk committee, Senator Colbeck said public confidence depended not only on actual integrity, but on the appearance of integrity.

"It is impossible to exclude away all conflicts of interest," he said.

"The most important thing is to ensure that there is a robust conflict of interest management system in place and that it is followed and reported upon.

"Transparency is the best safeguard against any doubt."

Greens senator Barbara Pocock, who has advocated for more transparency and integrity in government contracting, said the government had enacted a temporary freeze on KPMG contracts for good reason.

"KPMG has broken the community's confidence through its misuse of confidential information and its mistreatment of whistleblowers - it has proven it can't be trusted," Senator Pocock said.

"No department or agency should be contracting with KPMG, including variations and extensions on existing contracts, until they have been properly investigated and regulated.

"If we want to see the consulting and audit sectors cleaned up the government must subject these massive partnerships to the same rules of tax, transparency and whistleblowing as other large entities through corporations law, separate the functions of consultancy from audit and regulate them properly, and ban unethical contractors like KPMG from government work."

Education Minister Jason Clare has been contacted for comment.

#5379. ABC rejects claims of antisemitic bias ahead of fronting royal commission

The ABC and SBS will on Thursday appear before the royal commission. (AAP: Danny Casey)

The ABC has rejected "claims that its journalism has contributed to antisemitism or social division".

ABC and SBS will face questioning over complaints of bias and antisemitism when they appear at the royal commission on Thursday.

The public broadcasters' editorial policies and complaints procedures will be under scrutiny.

The ABC has rejected "claims that its journalism has contributed to antisemitism or social division" ahead of appearances by ABC and SBS executives at the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion on Thursday.

The public broadcasters are expected to be probed on allegations of bias in their reporting of events related to the Middle East.

Ahead of proceedings, the ABC issued a statement on Wednesday night that said its "reporting has been evidence-based, fair, impartial and consistent with its Charter obligations".

In its statement ahead of the hearing, the SBS said it represented "Jewish Australian stories and perspectives in a way that is respectful, accurate and inclusive".

The ABC's editorial director Gavin Fang and ombudsman Fiona Cameron will front the commission on Thursday morning.

They will be followed by SBS's director of Audio and Language Content David Thanh Man Tue Hua, director of News and Current Affairs Amanda Wicks and ombudsman Amy Stockwell.

Gavin Fang will represent the ABC at the commission on Thursday. (ABC News: Tobias Hunt)

The commission's current hearing block, being held in Sydney, is focusing on antisemitism and hate speech in the online environment and in traditional media and broadcasting.

In opening remarks last week, counsel assisting Richard Lancaster SC noted the ABC and SBS "occupy a particularly important, trusted position in the Australian media landscape".

Mr Lancaster said the organisations' "statutes, charters and policies commit them to high standards of accuracy, impartiality and balance".

He said the broadcasters would be asked about their policies and management of "allegations of antisemitism and the effectiveness of those measures".

"This will involve asking if there is any demonstrable antisemitic bias in the reporting of journalists or in the editorial policy in those media organisations."

Fiona Cameron will attend as the ABC ombudsman. (Supplied)

Mr Lancaster told the commission that some of the submissions it received were "highly critical" of the coverage of the Middle East conflict by the ABC and SBS.

Submissions to the commission through its website have not yet been published, but a number of commission witnesses have been critical of the ABC in their testimony.

Amanda Wicks will be among three representatives from the SBS at the royal commission. (ABC News)

Speaking of her lived experience of antisemitism, Léa Levy, who emigrated to Australia from France in 2015, told the commission that during the Gaza war the ABC "never talked about Israelis' pain".

Former editor-in-chief of the Age newspaper Michael Gawenda claimed the ABC and other outlets "minimised antisemitism".

"They ran pieces by people who claimed that it was a concocted notion, this notion of antisemitism, done by a powerful lobby that was trying to cover up and silence criticism of Israel."

In its statement released on Wednesday evening, the ABC issued a strongly worded rebuttal of such claims.

"The ABC has devoted extensive coverage to the rise of antisemitism in Australia and included all relevant perspectives," the statement read.

"The ABC reporting has consistently centred on the experiences of Jewish Australians while providing context regarding broader social and political issues."

The ABC's coverage of the Middle East triggered a surge in complaints after October 7, 2023. (ABC News: Keana Naughton)

Ahead of appearing at the hearing, the SBS released its 39-page submission to the royal commission.

The ABC has not made its submission publicly available.

Australia's commercial networks have not been asked to appear at the commission, set up in the wake of last December's terrorist attack during a celebration of the Jewish holiday Hanukkah at Bondi Beach, in which 15 people were killed.

The ABC put questions to the royal commission on why only the ABC and SBS were being asked to appear.

In a statement, the commission said it had called on the ABC and SBS to give evidence "following concerns raised by members of Australia's Jewish community … about reporting sentiment and bias".

Commissioner Virginia Bell said in her remarks last week at the opening of block three that it was not the job of the commission "to resolve individual complaints".

The former High Court judge said the commission's focus was rather "on the adequacy of the broadcasters' complaint-handling mechanisms, including with respect to allegations of bias in the reporting of events in the Middle East relating to the state of Israel".

Virginia Bell said it was not the job of the commission "to resolve individual complaints". (ABC News: Liam Patrick)

The ABC's coverage of the Middle East has seen a surge in the number of complaints lodged with the corporation's ombudsman.

These reached a peak in the months following the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel and subsequent Gaza war.

In the 2023-24 year, the ABC reported receiving a five-year high of more than 7,000 complaints relating to content and editorial standards.

The broadcaster said almost half of these, 49 per cent, were attributable to the Israel-Gaza war.

In the year 2024-25, 4,192 content complaints were handled by the ABC ombudsman's office, 26 per cent of which were related to Middle East coverage.

The ABC said to date the ombudsman had recorded breaches for five instances of ABC coverage concerning the Middle East.

The broadcaster said no complaints of bias had been upheld by the ombudsman in relation to ABC News coverage of the Middle East.

The ABC and SBS are also expected to be questioned at the commission on why they have decided not to adopt the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance's (IHRA) working definition of antisemitism.

The IHRA definition, stating that "antisemitism is a certain perception of Jews, which may be expressed as hatred towards Jews", has been adopted by both the commission and the Australian government, but is a subject of controversy.

Detractors argue that it is used to stifle free speech and legitimate criticism.

The ABC and SBS have said they rely instead on their existing editorial guidelines on hate speech.

In its statement, the ABC said while IHRA's core definition was broadly consistent with the ABC's approach, "the IHRA's examples are contested and there has been criticism that in some cases they risk conflating legitimate political criticism of Israel with antisemitism".

Jillian Segal has been called to the commission to speak to concerns about coverage from the ABC and SBS. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

SBS's statement did not directly address the dispute over use of the IHRA definition, but said the broadcaster was guided by its charter to serve diverse audience and contribute to social cohesion.

"SBS's commitment to factual, balanced and impartial journalism is supported by strong editorial standards, independent complaints processes, and ongoing engagement with communities across Australia," the statement said.

The Australian government's Special Envoy to Combat Antisemitism, Jillian Segal, is a strong supporter of the IHRA definition of antisemitism and has consistently urged public institutions to adopt it.

The commission has called Ms Segal to speak to concerns about ABC and SBS coverage.

She is due to testify before the broadcasters when proceedings get underway at 10am AEST on Thursday.

While the commission's focus will be on allegations of antisemitism, the broadcaster has also been accused of being overly sensitive to complaints from Jewish Australians.

In a damning judgement issued last September in the Antoinette Lattouf case, Judge Darryl Rangiah found the broadcaster had "let down the Australian public badly when it abjectly surrendered the right of its employee Ms Lattouf to appease a lobby group".

Justice Darryl found Ms Lattouf was unlawfully terminated when she was taken off-air in response to what he described as "an orchestrated campaign by pro-Israel lobbyists".

According to the ABC, in the six months to December 2025, 51 per cent of complaints claimed the ABC's Israel-Gaza coverage was broadly pro-Palestinian and 47 per cent claimed it was broadly pro-Israel.

The broadcaster said, "this indicates that perceptions of bias are arising from strongly held views across the community rather than systematic editorial favouritism".

#5380. Le Rwanda accueillera la première course de Formule 1 en Afrique depuis 1993

Le Rwanda a signé un contrat de 10 ans avec la Formule 1 pour accueillir des courses dans le pays africain, à partir du début des années 2030.

L'événement, baptisé Grand Prix d'Afrique, se déroulera sur un nouveau circuit construit spécialement à cet effet à Bugesera, à 40 kilomètres au sud de la capitale Kigali et à proximité du nouvel aéroport international de la ville. Ce sera la première course de Formule 1 en Afrique depuis 1993.

Un communiqué de la F1 indique que ce projet est le fruit d'« années de collaboration visant à garantir que les bases solides, avec le meilleur partenaire, soient en place pour offrir un Grand Prix réussi, durable et de classe mondiale pour les générations à venir ».

Le circuit, conçu par l'ancien pilote de F1 Alex Wurz, a été « conçu pour s'intégrer harmonieusement au paysage naturel, en utilisant les dénivelés de la région pour créer une expérience de course unique et stimulante tout en offrant des opportunités de visionnage exceptionnelles aux fans », ajoute le communiqué.

La F1 espère que cette course offrira à ce sport l'opportunité d'accroître sa notoriété en Afrique, un marché relativement inexploré comparé à l'Europe, l'Asie et les Amériques.

Il n'a pas encore été déterminé à quel moment de l'année cette course pourrait s'intégrer au mieux au calendrier.

Cette course risque d'être controversée, le Rwanda ayant déjà été accusé de blanchiment d'argent par le sport.

Il est probable que les organisateurs souhaitent éviter de programmer la course pendant la principale saison des pluies, de mars à mai. Une saison des pluies plus courte et moins perturbatrice se déroule d'octobre à novembre.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

La F1 s'est engagée à limiter la saison à 24 courses maximum.

Le président rwandais Paul Kagame a déclaré : « Pendant plus de trois décennies, le championnat du monde de sport automobile le plus prestigieux s'est déroulé sans ce continent, et cela change avec cet accord. »

« Le Rwanda est fier d’accueillir le Grand Prix d’Afrique de Formule 1 et de partager ce moment avec plus de 100 millions de fans à travers l’Afrique, dont beaucoup de jeunes qui méritent de voir ce sport chez eux et de s’y projeter : en tant qu’ingénieurs, techniciens, entrepreneurs et, un jour, pilotes. »

« Le circuit de Bugesera, à proximité du nouvel aéroport international, apportera des emplois, des compétences, du tourisme et de nouvelles entreprises à notre pays et à notre région pour les décennies à venir, car notre objectif n'a jamais été un simple week-end de course, mais un bénéfice durable pour notre population. »

Le président de la F1, Stefano Domenicali, a déclaré que ce nouveau contrat était « un moment historique pour la F1 », ce qui signifierait que ce sport serait présent « sur tous les continents habités ».

Domenicali a ajouté : « L'Afrique a toujours fait partie de l'avenir de la Formule 1, et dès le début, nous étions déterminés à y revenir de la bonne manière, avec le bon partenaire, un engagement à long terme et une vision claire pour créer un impact significatif. »

Cette course risque de susciter l'opposition de groupes de défense des droits de l'homme qui accuseront le Rwanda de « sportswashing », comme cela a été le cas avec son parrainage des clubs de football de Premier League Arsenal et Aston Villa.

La République démocratique du Congo, voisine du Rwanda en Afrique centrale et orientale, a porté plainte contre le pays devant la Cour internationale de Justice (CIJ), l'accusant d'avoir violé de multiples traités internationaux portant sur la prévention du génocide, la discrimination raciale, les droits des femmes et la torture.

Un porte-parole de la F1 a déclaré : « Nous avons l'opportunité d'inspirer et de transmettre la passion de la F1 à 100 millions de personnes à travers l'Afrique, et le sport peut être une force positive pour le bien. »

Mais Felix Jakens, responsable des campagnes d'Amnesty International Royaume-Uni, a déclaré : « Le Rwanda investit dans les plus grands événements sportifs mondiaux pour redorer son image et détourner l'attention de son bilan catastrophique en matière de droits de l'homme. »

« La Formule 1 affirme que le sport peut être une force positive pour le bien. Cela sonne creux si la F1 se désintéresse de ses partenaires. »

« La Formule 1 ne doit pas rester les bras croisés. Elle devrait user de son influence auprès des autorités rwandaises pour impulser le changement, plutôt que de prêter son image à une opération de relations publiques. »

La construction du circuit sera supervisée par trois entreprises, Tilke, architecte de circuits de F1 de longue date, et DAR travaillant aux côtés de WurzDesign, créateur du circuit.

Il est conçu pour être rapide et fluide, avec un dénivelé important, en utilisant les contours naturels du paysage vallonné du Rwanda.

Le premier Grand Prix en Afrique a eu lieu lors de la dernière manche du Championnat du monde au Maroc en 1958.

L'Afrique du Sud a accueilli une course pendant l'ère de l'apartheid - de 1960 à 1966 à East London, aujourd'hui connue sous le nom de KuGompo City, avant que la course ne soit déplacée à Kyalami, près de Johannesburg, de 1976 à 1985.

Kyalami a fait son retour pour deux courses en 1992 et 1993, alors que l'apartheid touchait à sa fin.

Le pays a mené des discussions avec la F1 ces dernières années en vue d'un retour sur différents circuits, notamment à Kyalami et au Cap, mais aucun accord n'a pu être conclu.

#5383. SBS WorldWatch is changing. Here's what viewers need to know

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

SBS WorldWatch will soon become a digital-only service, ending its run as a broadcast television channel.

The multilingual news service, which provides news bulletins from international broadcasters, will move entirely to SBS On Demand.

SBS says the shift will allow it to increase the number of bulletins available in most languages.

From 18 September, the channel, which provides international news in 38 languages from 49 broadcasters worldwide, will cease broadcasting and all SBS WorldWatch programming will continue on SBS On Demand.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

As the channel closes, SBS WorldWatch will expand its existing digital service over the coming weeks to include two or more daily bulletins in most languages.

This is more content than could be accommodated on a single linear channel, SBS says, allowing audiences to watch bulletins as soon as they become available rather than waiting for a scheduled broadcast.

SBS On Demand also features two 24-hour FAST channels for English-language news — Euronews and France 24.

SBS Director of News and Current Affairs, Mandi Wicks, said SBS WorldWatch played an important role in connecting Australians with news and perspectives from around the world, in their preferred language.

"Moving to SBS On Demand gives us the opportunity to build on that service, with more international news bulletins and greater flexibility for audiences to decide when and how they watch," she said.

"We recognise this will be a change for some audiences who are accustomed to watching SBS WorldWatch on linear television. We're committed to supporting them through the transition, while continuing to evolve our services for the future."

SBS is providing multilingual information and guidance through SBS Audio language programs and on SBS WorldWatch channel 35 ahead of the change.

Further information is available here, with additional support available via the SBS Help Centre.

The SBS WorldWatch — News In-Language hub can be found on the SBS On Demand homepage, where audiences can also search for content in their preferred language.

Additional bulletins will be added over the coming weeks.

The full SBS On Demand offering features more than 15,000 hours of local and international programming across more than 60 languages, spanning news and current affairs, documentaries, drama, world movies, entertainment, food, children’s content and sport.

This includes dedicated language collections, as well as selected English-language programs with subtitles in Arabic, Simplified Chinese, Traditional Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese.

SBS On Demand is a free streaming service for all Australians, accessible via the app on Smart TVs, mobiles, and tablets, or on the SBS website. The app is free to download from the Apple App Store for iOS here and Google Play for Android here.

#5384. 'Clipped and called a liar': Gallagher lays bare cost of 'roastings' as top bureaucrats flee APS

Finance and Public Service Minister Katy Gallagher says the use of Senate estimates clips on social media has gone too far, warning that hard-working bureaucrats are being driven out of their careers by political attacks.

In an interview with The Canberra Times about the heightened safety risks experienced by politicians as political debate became more polarised, Senator Gallagher said she knew public servants who had quit because they had been ridiculed online.

"I've worked with a couple of very senior public servants who have retired or left because they will not come to Senate estimates," she said.

"They won't come because they've been called a liar, and that matters to them. Their professional career is being apolitical public servants, and so to be just roasted and then clipped and called a liar ... That is an issue that we should think about a bit more."

The minister and ACT Labor senator did not go as far as backing the Secretaries Board's call for a ban on the editing of videos clipped from estimates to post on social media for party political purposes, which Coalition frontbencher James Paterson has blasted as "an affront to democracy".

But, she said, while the public was entitled to "accountability and transparency" from the bureaucracy, the portrayal of estimates hearings "should be truthful".

"I don't think they should be clipped in a way that makes it tell a different story," she said.

Senator Gallagher shared her concerns while reflecting that the heat of political discourse online was spilling into real life, after the vehicle attack on independent Indi MP Helen Haines outside her electorate office shocked the nation.

The minister, whose evidence to estimates is regularly clipped by political rivals, said she had been accosted in public over how she was portrayed - such as when Nationals senator Matt Canavan posted his grilling her over a $30 billion federal budget overspend in February.

"I got absolutely inundated," Senator Gallagher said.

"This guy just comes up to me, I'm just at the supermarket, and starts abusing me and going, 'Where's our $30 billion? Where have you embezzled all this money?' In a really menacing way."

She acknowledged that being in government meant that "you're on the receiving [of criticism] and you're not giving it like the opposition".

But, she argued, lines of questioning at estimates were increasingly tailored towards "generating footage [to] make sure that you can whip up enough outrage with something and then move on."

"I believe in accountability and being accountable to the Parliament and trying to give as much information as we can, but we also have to protect ourselves and our institutions and the public servants that appear with us as well."

If public servants were expected to be "frank and honest," Senator Gallagher said, it was not helpful to "clip videos that make them look like fools, so that they get piled on."

"There's human consequences to this," she said.

After ACT independent senator David Pocock's social media post about Australia collecting more tax from beer than offshore gas exports went viral in February, she said, "the pile on that those public servants got was unbelievable."

"They have no right of reply," she said, citing a hearing where a public servant was "called a liar" and accused of having doctored a submission, which they later proved was untrue - but the damage was done.

"There's no consequence for senators and their behaviour. They can just throw this stuff out there and then move on as they do to the next video, and then meanwhile the public servant's left shattered, with their career ended."

Senator Pocock agreed that politicians "need to take care in what and how we ask our questions, show respect to public servants and disagree civilly."

"Senate Estimates hearings are publicly broadcast for good reason and are an essential part of a strong, open democracy," he said.

"Care does need to be taken in how clips from senate estimates are cut and shared on social media. It's definitely something my team and I are mindful of when using clips from estimates."

Senator Pocock's office does not believe his beer tax post, or any others, made a harmful contribution to the political debate.

Senator Canavan, who became Nationals leader weeks after his post about the $30 billion overspend, was scathing of Senator Gallagher's comments.

"I am sorry? Katy was described as a 'mean girl' by one of her own senators," he said, referring to the reported comments of the late Kimberley Kitching.

"Is she seriously throwing mud about other Senators doing their job and holding the government to account? We need more accountability, not less, otherwise people will become more frustrated than they are."

Voters had "legitimate frustrations" with the government and the bureaucracy that needed to be "responded to through the normal Parliamentary process," Senator Canavan said.

"Seeking to subvert or reduce Parliamentary accountability will not help our social harmony."

He stood by his social media clip about Senator Gallagher, which related to a $50 billion overspend on government programs.

"She could not account for $30 billion of that figure. She is the Finance Minister. Such a failure deserves to be exposed and Senate Estimates is precisely about doing that."

Acting opposition finance and public service spokesperson and Liberal Party deputy leader Jane Hume said politicians' and public servants' salaries "are paid for by taxpayers".

"It is entirely reasonable for taxpayers to see how their money is being spent and to hold those who spend it to account," Senator Hume said.

"Australians have every right to see their government being held to account. If any Minister doesn't like the questions being shared, perhaps they should start by answering them."

Greens deputy leader and democracy spokeswoman Steph Hodgins-May said Senate estimates existed "so the public can understand how political decisions are affecting the departments that serve all of us."

"It's about the transparent expenditure of public money, and we deserve to know how well that's working," Senator Hodgins-May said.

"Every senator at the table is asking questions on behalf of the Australian people. It's not about blaming public servants - it's about getting clear, honest answers, even when they can be hard to get, and holding ministers accountable for the decisions they make."

#5385. More flexible jobs, higher tax relief among measures to help older workers stay employed

The raising of the retirement and re-employment ages will be brought forward to 2029 as assurance that seniors can keep working if they wish to, said tripartite partners.

Participants attend NTUC's e2i Career Pulse Workshop at Orchard Hotel on Oct 26, 2026. (Photo: CNA/Ili Mansor)

SINGAPORE: More support for flexible jobs and higher tax relief for working seniors were among several tripartite measures announced on Monday (Oct 26) to encourage older workers to keep working if they want to, and employers to hire or retain them.

The statutory retirement and re-employment ages will rise from 64 and 69 currently to 65 and 70 from 2029 – a year ahead of the previous timeline of 2030.

It will mean that employers cannot dismiss employees on the grounds of age before they turn 65, and must offer re-employment to eligible employees until they are 70.

“This sends a clear signal that seniors who wish to continue working longer would have the opportunity to do so,” Minister of State for Manpower Dinesh Vasu Dash said at the launch of the tripartite report.

CNA Games Guess Word Crack the word, one row at a time Buzzword Create words using the given letters Mini Sudoku Tiny puzzle, mighty brain teaser Mini Crossword Small grid, big challenge Word Search Spot as many words as you can Show More Show Less The Ministry of Manpower (MOM), National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) said in a press release that the change gives senior workers greater assurance that they can continue working if they wish to.Other measures include extending wage support for employers who re-employ seniors, raising support for lower-wage senior workers and increasing financial assistance for those who are not re-employed.These recommendations by the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment have been fully accepted by the government, with details on implementation to follow in the first half of 2027.Mr Dinesh said: “Senior employment should not simply mean doing the same job for more years. It should mean having meaningful options across a longer career span, and leveraging senior workers for business success.”NTUC deputy secretary-general Desmond Tan said that senior workers should have “genuine options” in how they continue contributing, from full-time jobs to flexible arrangements.Senior workers also need assurance that they will not have to navigate career transitions alone, as well as fair access to training and opportunities, he said.SNEF vice-president Tan Hwee Bin said investing in older employees is becoming a “business necessity” amid a tight labour market and slowing workforce growth.“We need a mindset shift in how we build our workforce, recognising that full-time and part-time employees can play complementary roles,” she said.“By redesigning jobs and offering more flexible arrangements, employers can retain valuable experience and build more resilient multi-generational teams.”

The Ministry of Manpower (MOM), National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) and Singapore National Employers Federation (SNEF) said in a press release that the change gives senior workers greater assurance that they can continue working if they wish to.

Other measures include extending wage support for employers who re-employ seniors, raising support for lower-wage senior workers and increasing financial assistance for those who are not re-employed.

These recommendations by the Tripartite Workgroup on Senior Employment have been fully accepted by the government, with details on implementation to follow in the first half of 2027.

Mr Dinesh said: “Senior employment should not simply mean doing the same job for more years. It should mean having meaningful options across a longer career span, and leveraging senior workers for business success.”

NTUC deputy secretary-general Desmond Tan said that senior workers should have “genuine options” in how they continue contributing, from full-time jobs to flexible arrangements.

Senior workers also need assurance that they will not have to navigate career transitions alone, as well as fair access to training and opportunities, he said.

SNEF vice-president Tan Hwee Bin said investing in older employees is becoming a “business necessity” amid a tight labour market and slowing workforce growth.

“We need a mindset shift in how we build our workforce, recognising that full-time and part-time employees can play complementary roles,” she said.

“By redesigning jobs and offering more flexible arrangements, employers can retain valuable experience and build more resilient multi-generational teams.”

Singapore’s labour force is ageing in tandem with the general population. Workers aged 50 and above made up about 40 per cent of the labour force in 2025, up from around 34 per cent in 2015.

“Population ageing is expected to further increase the share of seniors in the labour force. By 2030, one in four Singaporeans will be aged 65 and above,” the workgroup said in its report.

It noted that labour force participation drops sharply among residents in their late 50s and older.

According to government surveys, caregiving responsibilities are the top reason workers in their 50s are not working or looking for work, while flexible work arrangements are the top initiative that could keep them in the workforce.

A new Flexi-Load Programme will help employers create and scale up jobs with flexible workloads, such as part-time or fractional work, for older workers.

It will replace the existing Part-time Re-employment Grant, which ends after 2027. The grant gives employers S$2,500 for each resident senior worker offered part-time re-employment, other flexible work arrangements and structured career planning, capped at S$125,000 for each company.

The grant covers workers aged 60 and above, and funds employers based on changes to their human resource policies. Since 2020, it has supported about 68,500 seniors and about 7,800 employers.

The new Flexi-Load Programme will cover workers aged 50 and above, and require employers to “demonstrate the outcome of creating additional flexi-load roles”, said the workgroup.

This will be accompanied by a new programme office for career longevity, led by the Skills and Workforce Development Agency. It aims to help workers plan their career and skills transitions more proactively, and support employers to adopt structured career planning and implement flexible workload arrangements.

It will draw on flexible workload models developed through the Alliance for Action on Empowering Multi-Stage Careers for Mature Workers, including job redesign and matching workers with project-based opportunities.

These efforts form part of a wider ecosystem that includes stronger human capital capabilities, SkillsFuture support and career conversion programmes, Tripartite Jobs Council support for workers impacted by artificial intelligence-related changes, and the Workplace Fairness Act against age discrimination, said the workgroup.

The SkillsFuture Jobseeker Support scheme will also be reviewed for senior workers navigating job transitions.

Singapore’s approach to retirement has achieved consistently high re-employment outcomes, the workgroup said, with more than nine in 10 eligible employees who wish to continue working offered re-employment.

Employers who cannot offer re-employment must give affected workers a one-off Employment Assistance Payment while they look for other work.

The government will raise the recommended amount for this payment to reflect wage growth in recent years. It is currently three-and-a-half months’ salary, with a minimum of S$6,250 and a maximum of S$14,750.

The government will also enhance the Earned Income Relief for workers employed past the retirement and re-employment ages. Workers aged 55 and above can already claim up to S$8,000 in relief depending on their age.

A new Re-employment Credit will be introduced from 2028 to defray employers’ business costs associated with retaining senior workers.

It will replace the Senior Employment Credit, which provides up to 7 per cent in wage offsets for employers who hire Singaporeans aged 60 and older and who earn less than S$4,000 a month.

The wage ceiling for the new credit scheme will be higher to account for wage growth.

The tripartite workgroup also recommended improving wage support for lower-wage senior workers in particular. This will be done by enhancing the Workfare Income Supplement, which is paid to lower-wage workers in cash and Central Provident Fund payments.

The Progressive Wage Credit Scheme will also be updated. It co-funds employers’ wage increases required under the Progressive Wage Model and local qualifying salary requirements, as well as voluntary pay rises for lower-wage workers.

During a panel discussion, the workgroup co-chairs were asked how a balance will be struck between two segments of jobseekers – fresh graduates and seniors.

Mr Dinesh said these two groups should not be seen as competing for the same jobs, pointing out that the bulk of senior workers are lower-wage workers.

Junior hires have a runway to competence before they add value to an organisation, and getting senior workers to guide and mentor them could be a complementary effort in succession planning, he said.

MOM is looking at what can be done to strengthen such mentorships, he added.

#5388. ABC News bringing more regional stories to audiences using AI with journalist oversight

ABC Gippsland journalist Jack Colantuono reads the radio news in Sale before creating a local news briefing. (ABC News)

ABC News is piloting an AI-assisted workflow that converts original journalism gathered by reporters for local radio bulletins into a digital briefing, expanding access to regional stories that might otherwise not feature online.

Using an ABC-developed AI tool, journalists can quickly reformat existing verified stories, freeing up time to do more original reporting.

All stories are fact-checked, edited and approved before publication.

ABC Radio is a vital daily news source. Each weekday, regionally presented and produced news bulletins air on more than 40 stations across Australia with important local news and information.

But many of those stories do not make it online, so if you miss the bulletin, you might not hear about them.

ABC News is piloting an AI-assisted project to help bridge that gap and bring this important local journalism to a wider audience using existing resources.

The pilot will enhance our local news offering on the ABC News website and app by converting existing regional radio stories into digital briefings to make them available to the online audience across the day.

While the AI tool helps reformat the copy, the original stories are written by ABC journalists. The reformatted versions are always fact-checked, edited and approved by our journalists before publication. The AI tool does not generate any stories.

The digital local briefings are a new product that get more local stories to more people. Using this AI production tool assists journalists to do that without replacing any existing processes, tasks or jobs.

Manually converting existing radio stories to digital articles is time-consuming. Internal trials using an ABC-developed AI tool called ABC Assist to help with this task have showed it can reduce the time it takes by up to half, while still meeting editorial standards. This creates a more sustainable workflow for our reporters without impacting quality and accuracy.

Journalists are freed up to do more original reporting and news gathering for audiences rather than just repurposing content. While the AI tool helps reformat the stories, the original stories are written by ABC journalists and the reformatted versions are always fact-checked, edited and approved by our journalists before publication. The AI tool does not generate any new stories.

Any content produced with AI assistance must comply with the ABC's editorial guidance on AI and AI Principles, including being clearly disclosed to the audience.

ABC Assist was designed by ABC staff for ABC staff, considering our Editorial Policies, Guidance and the ABC's AI Principles. It was developed to help journalists with production research and transcription tasks and was trained on decades of Australian content from the ABC archive.

The briefings start with the ABC journalism that you know and trust, gathered by our journalists across Australia to create radio news bulletins for their local communities.

The workflow for the local news briefing process undertaken by ABC journalists. (ABC News)

ABC Assist then helps the journalist reformat the verified ABC journalism that has already been broadcast, making minor style changes, reducing word count, and suggesting short headline options for a digital audience.

The journalist then fact-checks and edits the reformatted version of the stories before sending them to be approved for publication by an editorial leader with local knowledge and a digital subeditor.

This pilot project was developed in a consultation with teams across ABC News. Since October 2025, regional Victorian newsrooms have worked with technical specialists to develop the workflow, assess the accuracy of the AI results and plan the audience-facing concept.

The local briefings process has side-by-side verification to enable journalists to fact-check any changes. (ABC News)

Local staff, including reporters, content producers, local editors and regional editors, participated in end-to-end internal production trials, with close attention paid to content quality.

Feedback from the local teams was taken into account, including specific treatment for legally sensitive stories and side-by-side version comparison to ensure accurate fact-checking.

Local news is disappearing in many parts of Australia as traditional media outlets have been cut back or shut down. It is estimated that since 2019 more than 200 local newspapers in regional Australia have significantly cut their services or closed, leaving some communities without any dedicated local news source.

This pilot means a listener who missed the morning radio bulletin can read the same local stories on the ABC News website or app. It gives those stories a life beyond the airwaves, making sure important local news is available to a wider audience.

If you have any feedback about this pilot, please contact us via this form.
