#5389. "Mon mari m'a rejetée parce que j'ai donné naissance à des jumeaux"

Aujourd'hui, nous nous intéressons au témoignage de Catherine Mugure, qui raconte les difficultés qu'elle a rencontrées dans sa vie de couple.

L'histoire de Catherine commence alors qu'elle est à l'université, après sa rencontre avec celui qui deviendra son compagnon. Elle tombe enceinte, ce qui l'oblige à interrompre ses études.

Comme ses parents étaient très stricts, une attitude assez courante chez des parents qui souhaitent le meilleur pour leur fille, Catherine n'a d'autre choix que d'aller vivre avec son compagnon. Tous deux décident alors de commencer une vie de couple.

Pour Catherine, son compagnon était son meilleur ami, quelqu'un avec qui elle partageait tout. Elle était convaincue qu'il était l'homme avec qui elle voulait passer sa vie.

Cependant, il y avait une chose que son compagnon détestait particulièrement.

« Il disait qu'il ne voudrait jamais être avec une vierge. À cette époque, j'en étais une, mais à cause de ses propos, je ne lui ai jamais avoué », raconte Catherine.

La jeune femme n'a jamais compris pourquoi son compagnon rejetait l'idée d'être avec une vierge, mais elle ne voulait pas compromettre leur relation.

Le jour de son anniversaire, Catherine décide finalement de lui offrir sa virginité.

« Cet événement m'a fait perdre ma fierté et je suis aussi tombée enceinte. »

« Même si nous nous sommes violemment disputés après que mon mari a découvert que j'étais vierge, je considère cette année comme une année de malchance. Nous n'avions pas d'autre choix que de vivre ensemble puisque nous attendions un enfant », explique-t-elle.

Lorsque le moment de l'accouchement arrive, Catherine met au monde son enfant sans complication. Toutefois, son mari n'est pas présent et commence à adopter un comportement étrange.

« Il buvait beaucoup et rentrait à la maison très tard. Chaque fois que nous évoquions le sujet, il disait que je l'avais trompé », se souvient-elle.

Les disputes s'intensifient alors et, pour la première fois, Catherine décide de s'enfuir de chez elle. Son bébé a alors environ six mois.

Elle était devenue mère à l'âge de 21 ans. Lors de leurs disputes, son mari lui répétait que si elle décidait de partir, elle ne devait jamais essayer d'emmener leur enfant avec elle, sous peine de mourir.

La vie continuait normalement, sans que son mari ne sache que Catherine préparait secrètement sa fuite.

Elle lui demande l'autorisation de rendre visite à ses parents. Il accepte, mais lui pose d'abord une question : allait-elle lui laisser l'enfant ? Catherine répond :

« Si tu veux que je te le laisse, je te le laisserai. Mais je veux aller parler à mon père pour qu'il m'aide à retourner à l'université. »

C'était la raison qu'elle invoquait pour rentrer chez ses parents, mais au fond d'elle-même, elle savait qu'elle s'apprêtait à fuir. Son mari l'accompagne même jusqu'au départ et l'autorise à emporter leur enfant.

À son arrivée chez ses parents, sa mère est surprise de la voir entrer avec un sac rempli de vêtements.

Lorsqu'on lui demande pourquoi elle est venue, Catherine répond que l'eau a été coupée chez elle et qu'elle est venue faire sa lessive.

« Le lendemain matin, je suis allée me laver et me préparer avant de partir. J'avais laissé une lettre, aussi bien chez mes parents que chez mon mari, sans qu'il le sache. J'ai ensuite laissé l'eau couler dans la salle de bain pour que les gens pensent que j'étais toujours en train de laver mon linge. »

« Je suis partie en laissant mon enfant endormi sur le lit. »

« Quand ils ont lu ma lettre et ont commencé à me chercher, j'avais déjà éteint mon téléphone. Ils m'ont cherchée jusque dans les morgues, parce que dans ma lettre j'avais écrit que si je continuais à vivre avec mon enfant, soit je le tuerais, soit je me suiciderais », raconte Catherine.

Lorsque je lui demande si elle pensait réellement ce qu'elle avait écrit, elle répond :

« Quand on est en dépression ou sous une immense pression psychologique, il n'y a rien qu'on ne soit capable de faire. »

« J'ai gardé mon téléphone éteint pendant trois mois », poursuit-elle en pleurant.

Durant cette période, elle trouve refuge chez une amie qui l'héberge quelque temps. Peu à peu, elle en vient même à oublier qu'elle avait un enfant.

Alors qu'elle sombre de plus en plus dans la détresse psychologique, Catherine commence néanmoins à reconstruire sa vie et à réfléchir à la manière de repartir de zéro, seule.

Après ces trois mois, Catherine rallume finalement son téléphone.

« Ma mère a été la première à m'appeler. Elle s'est mise à pleurer en me disant qu'au moins, j'aurais dû lui expliquer ce qui se passait. »

Cet appel marque la reprise des contacts avec sa famille, mais aussi le début d'une séparation de deux ans avec son mari.

Même si Catherine poursuit sa vie de son côté, le destin les réunit un jour de manière inattendue dans un magasin en ville où elle vendait des téléphones.

« J'interpellais les clients pour leur vendre des téléphones : "Bonjour chéri, bonjour bébé, venez acheter un téléphone !". Soudain, j'ai aperçu celui qui était mon mari et j'ai été très surprise. Je ne m'y attendais pas, et je pense que lui non plus. »

Ce jour-là, il lui demande de lui vendre un téléphone. À partir de là, il commence à lui rendre visite chaque jour. Ils prennent l'habitude de boire un café ensemble avant de rentrer chacun chez soi.

Mais peu de temps après, Catherine découvre qu'elle est enceinte de leur deuxième enfant.

« Il a été facile de se remettre ensemble parce qu'il prenait soin de tous nos besoins. »

Le couple décide alors de récupérer leur premier enfant, qui vivait chez sa grand-mère, et de reprendre la vie commune.

Mais contre toute attente, même après avoir obtenu cette seconde chance de vivre à nouveau comme une famille, les problèmes demeurent les mêmes.

Après quelque temps, les disputes reprennent. Cette fois encore, la réconciliation ne dure pas longtemps et le couple finit par se séparer une deuxième fois.

Bien que leur relation ait été marquée par de nombreuses difficultés, l'ex-mari de Catherine n'a jamais cessé de subvenir aux besoins de ses enfants.

Cette situation lui permettait de rendre visite à la famille quand il le souhaitait.

C'est ainsi que Catherine se retrouve enceinte d'un troisième enfant du même homme.

« Après tout ce que j'avais vécu avec mon premier et mon deuxième enfant, j'avais décidé que je n'aurais plus jamais d'autre enfant avec lui.

Après avoir fait un test, j'ai confirmé que j'étais de nouveau enceinte, pour la troisième fois. »

À cette époque, Catherine souffrait déjà de problèmes de santé. Elle était atteinte de diabète et d'hypertension. Malgré cela, elle avait pris la décision d'interrompre cette grossesse.

Mais lorsqu'elle se rend à l'hôpital, les médecins lui annoncent une nouvelle qu'elle n'aurait jamais imaginée.

« Cette grossesse ne peut pas être interrompue. Si vous essayez, vous risquez de mourir. Vous attendez des jumeaux et vous souffrez également de fibrose », lui explique le médecin.

C'est à partir de ce moment que tout bascule.

Même si les médecins lui conseillent de mener sa grossesse à terme et de prendre soin d'elle-même, son ex-mari réagit très mal lorsqu'il apprend qu'elle attend des jumeaux.

« Dans ma famille, il n'y a pas de jumeaux. Dans la vôtre non plus. Donc ces enfants ne sont pas les miens. »

Cette réaction marque le début d'une nouvelle période de souffrance pour Catherine.

Alors qu'elle approchait du sixième mois de grossesse, elle commence à perdre les eaux : les bébés arrivaient prématurément. Elle est transportée d'urgence à l'hôpital, où elle subit une césarienne. Ses deux précédents accouchements s'étaient également déroulés par césarienne.

Les jumeaux naissent, mais le drame survient rapidement : au lendemain de l'accouchement, l'un des bébés meurt.

« On m'a demandé d'aller à la nurserie voir mes enfants. Quand je suis arrivée, j'ai vu que l'un d'eux était allongé sur une table. Il était déjà décédé. L'autre, lui, allait bien. »

Son mari les abandonne alors à l'hôpital.

« Mon mari m'a rejetée parce que j'avais donné naissance à des jumeaux, et il n'est jamais revenu jusqu'à aujourd'hui », raconte Catherine.

Après sa sortie de l'hôpital, Catherine a dû faire face à l'une des périodes les plus difficiles de sa vie.

« J'ai failli perdre la raison. J'ai même été près de tuer mes trois enfants. Mais Dieu m'a donné la force de continuer », confie-t-elle.

Concernant le jumeau qui a survécu, les médecins lui avaient annoncé qu'il ne vivrait probablement pas longtemps, car il souffrait d'une maladie cardiaque. Pourtant, contre toute attente, l'enfant a aujourd'hui trois ans.

Catherine adresse un message aux autres mères qui traversent des épreuves similaires :

« Votre force réside dans votre état d'esprit », affirme-t-elle.

Aujourd'hui, Catherine a réussi à aller de l'avant. Malgré les épreuves qu'elle a traversées, elle poursuit sa vie et consacre son énergie à l'éducation de ses enfants.

#5390. «Реал» победил «Барселону» в матче Ла Лиги

Мадридский «Реал» одержал победу над «Барселоной» в матче десятого тура Ла Лиги. Об этом сообщает корреспондент «Ленты.ру».

Встреча прошла в Барселоне и завершилась со счетом 2:1 в пользу гостей. Первый мяч на 41-й минуте встречи забил нападающий Реала Килиан Мбаппе. На 61-й минуте счет сравнял полузащитник Рафинья Диас. На 87-й минуте сделал дубль Мбаппе.

Таким образом, после 10 матчей «Барселона» остается лидером чемпионата Испании, имея в активе 27 очков. «Реал» располагается на третьем месте, набрав 24 очка.

Ранее тренер Дмитрий Аленичев заявил, что даже с Жозе Моуринью, Хосепом Гвардиолой или Юргеном Клоппом у руля «Реал» вряд ли сможет обыграть нынешнюю «Барселону». Он посчитал, что сделать это будет нереально.

#5391. AFLW ladder with one round to play; ‘Difficult decision’: Dons sack inaugural coach

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Essendon will replace inaugural AFLW coach Natalie Wood next season after informing her that her contract would not be renewed for 2027 after the team’s 1-10 record this season.

Wood was informed on Tuesday about the decision, but players were only told after Sunday’s five-point loss to Hawthorn.

Wood is still planning to coach the final round game next Sunday against fellow strugglers Collingwood.

The Dons will be the third AFLW club seeking a coach, joining St Kilda and expansion club Tasmania Devils.

“The club is not offering me a contract as of next year,” Wood said post game on Sunday.

“It’s been a topic of conversation and a lot of questions with our poor performances this year

“It’s a disappointing end, as clearly I would have liked, like the last couple of years, to have better performances on the field.”

The Dons have struggled with injuries and form this season, but Wood was heartened by the club locking in several future leaders to new contracts but they will look for a new coach.

“We have fallen short of what we wanted on field. We believe a change is the right step,” Essendon chief executive Tim Roberts said.

“Natalie has handled this with real integrity, and her commitment to coaching out the season says a lot about her and how much she cares about the players.

“We thank Natalie for everything she has given the club over five seasons, and we wish her all the best for the next step in her football journey.”

Wood was the first female coach to reach 50 games while leading the team for five seasons since they entered the competition.

“[I] just continued on with the week as normal,” Wood said.

“We had two amazing players in Alex Morcom and Maddi Gay having their 50th and 75th game today, so really important celebrations, and we also had Amelia Radford announce her retirement.

“I would prefer no one ever knows, and I’d just disappear off into the sunset without any discussion or interview, but I was particularly aware this week of not wanting to get in the way of those three players.

“We really wanted to beat Hawthorn today. I thought we put up a really good fight, it was an ugly game of footy, tricky conditions. But always forefront of my mind is playing group first – so I thought it was best to hold off until today.

“Aysha (Ward, AFLW general manager) is heavily pregnant and is going on leave in two or three weeks, so I think the club is keen on getting a start in searching for their new coach.”

Wood said it was hard leading the AFLW side while Essendon as a club has faced so many leadership changes in recent seasons.

“Am I disappointed it’s fallen out this way? It depends how narrow of a view I have of it. Sometimes,” Wood said.

“I remember in my job interview, we were discussing about the wants of the role. [At the time], no female coach had lasted longer than two years, and I was not wanting to step into a senior coaching role without being well prepared and supported to have a career that’s longer than two years,” Wood said.

“To be the first female coach to coach 50 games, I’m really proud of that. To build a team from ground-up, as one of the last expansion teams and the season coming forward, it was a mad rush.

“At the same time, the club’s had a lot of instability. There’s been four CEOs, three presidents, three men’s senior captains and three senior coaches, so to build a culture within a program while the instability of the club – and it’s in a good spot now – it’s been hard at times while there’s been so much change in structure and leadership.

“When I look back to the start of the season and we had so many players sign long-term contracts, players who are really important to the program going forward - we’ve built a culture and place where players really want to be. I’ve done something right.”

The Hawks scored a vital win in their quest to make the top eight, winning by five points in rain-soaked conditions at the club’s new base in Dingley.

The Bombers were brave but couldn’t find the last goal they needed to get the win.

Two-time reigning AFLW premiers North Melbourne have fought past a stern challenge from Adelaide to win by nine points and return to the top of the ladder.

The Crows conceded the first two goals in scrappy, wet conditions at North Hobart Oval but kept North goalless in the second term, then kicked two majors to lead by three at halftime.

Adelaide were up by a point at the final change but couldn’t hold on as North overran the Crows late to win 5.8 (38) to 4.5 (29).

Kangaroos stars Jasmine Garner and Ash Riddell had 32 disposals apiece, while Erika O’Shea had 26 and 16 intercepts.

Crows Ebony Marinoff (30 disposals) and Chloe Bown (22) were busy and Christina Leuzzi kicked two goals.

Essendon will replace inaugural AFLW coach Natalie Wood next season after informing her that her contract would not be renewed for 2027 after the team’s 1-10 record this season.

Wood was informed on Tuesday about the decision, but players were only told after Sunday’s five-point loss to Hawthorn.

Wood is still planning to coach the final round game next Sunday against fellow strugglers Collingwood.

The Dons will be the third AFLW club seeking a coach, joining St Kilda and expansion club Tasmania Devils.

Five-goal Sydney star Chloe Molloy has exploded against West Coast to deliver a 22-point victory that seals a finals berth and keeps the Swans in touch with the top four.

Molloy’s terrific bag of five, including three final-term majors, proved the difference at Henson Park as Colin O’Riordan’s Sydney prevailed 12.6 (78) to 8.8 (56).

“Colin challenged us at the start of the week to seize the moment,” Molloy told Fox Footy.

“Sometimes you can shy away from the bigger moments and an opportunity to lock in the finals.

Gold Coast coach Rhyce Shaw was surprised and frustrated at the circumstances around Dekota Baron’s removal from their narrow AFLW win over Richmond.

But Shaw was also adamant that player welfare must come first.

Baron, a Rising Star nominee this season, was floored by a nasty collision with Tigers opponent Montana McKinnon in the first quarter of Saturday’s match on the Gold Coast.

Baron’s head cannoned into McKinnon’s hip. After initially being cleared by doctors to keep playing, the ARC (AFL review centre) intervened and ruled that she needed a head injury assessment.

Melbourne are closing on a AFLW top-four berth after grinding their way to a massive win over the Western Bulldogs on Saturday night.

In wet conditions which hit Victoria hard this weekend – there were fears the game might be delayed because of lightning – the Demons beat the Bulldogs 5.7 (37) to 2.8 (20) at Whitten Oval.

Melbourne are third ahead of next weekend’s trip to Adelaide, while Gold Coast’s narrow win earlier on Saturday meant the Bulldogs dropped to fifth.

The Bulldogs now have another big game on Friday night in Geelong against the Cats, who are on a 10-game winning streak. Star Bulldog Isabelle Pritchard also finished Saturday’s game on the bench with a knee injury.

The Bulldogs did not kick a goal from 15 minutes into the first term until seven minutes into the last.

Geelong have secured an AFLW qualifying final at “our house” with a 30-point win that also put a massive hole in Fremantle’s top-eight hopes.

There could be major injury ramifications out of Saturday’s physical clash at GMHBA Stadium, which the Cats won 9.10 (64) to 5.4 (34).

A heavy collision early in the last quarter put Geelong’s Rachel Kearns out of the game, while Fremantle player Noa McNaughton needed help from two trainers when she also went off in the final term with an ankle injury.

Geelong forward Chantal Mason suffered an ugly cut to her face in a marking contest. Fremantle’s Aoife Healy, Aisling McCarthy and Kiara Bowers, plus Cats player Aishling Moloney all needed injury treatment during the game.

Brisbane had successive wins for the first time in their tough season, mauling home side St Kilda by 52 points at RSEA Park on Saturday.

The Lions’ 11.9 (75) to 3.5 (23) win ended a tough few days for the Saints under interim coach Matt Brewer.

He dropped Jesse Tawhiao-Wardlaw and Maya Louvel-Finn for not meeting team standards.

Tyanna Smith’s second goal reduced the margin to 13 points at halftime and the Saints looked a chance. But they only managed two behinds in the second half as the Lions took control.

#5393. Let's bin the silly arguments over bins

Bins, like fences, are great sources of discord.

I still can't forgive my neighbours who objected to me putting my recycling in "their" yellow top bin. I got into the habit of placing the odd can and bottle into "their" bin when it was out on the kerb early on Mondays. If "their" bin wasn't full, I reasoned, why put two bins out?

But one evening, the two women who live behind me knocked on my door and told me that they had spotted me doing so. And it just wasn't on. Not on.

I pointed out that it wasn't actually their bin but the council's. All the same, my reasonableness cut no ice. It buttered no parsnips.

Since then, lots of people have told me their bin horror stories - or so they perceive these matters of utter triviality to be.

The management committee of an apartment block in which a friend lives has just put in cameras to spot people putting items in the wrong recycling bin. The penalty has not yet been disclosed but presumably the transgressor will be forced to sit in the stocks and get pelted with rotten tomatoes, organic of course.

Some councils say that "dog poo and other pet waste can be bagged and disposed of in the red general waste bin". But there are instances of people objecting when they spot a dog owner putting the waste into "their" bin.

And don't get anyone going on those lads who go round yellow top bins at night to get the cans which earn 10 cents in the excellent recycling centres in NSW.

To my mind, if people want to work really hard to earn ten cents, more power to their elbows. Such enterprise should be encouraged. They are strivers who deserve to get ahead.

My local one in the Woolies car parks gets 34,000 cans a day. On a Saturday morning, streams of enterprising people queue to push the cans and bottles in.

Every time I see them, I admire their energy. It also makes me reflect on how 10 cents is significant money for some people.

But putting your waste in "their" bin is the big issue of our times. The Nine news organisation actually did a poll on it and found that "Australia divided over whether it's OK to put stuff in other people's bins on bin night".

Divided is the right word: 49 per cent said it was OK and 51 per cent said no way.

There is etiquette on this big issue apparently. "The polite thing to do is ask first. If a neighbours bin isn't full and you aren't about to fill it with smelly, inappropriate items, then it is most likely that they wont mind, but you should never assume," according to the Australian Seniors organisation, quoting the director of the Australian School of Etiquette (there is such a thing).

But some people just don't know this etiquette.

In June, the Nine network reported that "what started as a petty dispute over rubbish bins with her neighbours escalated into all-out war, with the mum-of-three flying into a rage". Escalation is the right word: "Danielle's pretty handy with a chainsaw. Even when she's dressed in heels."

Nine's A Current Affair also covered "neighbours at war over wheelie bin placement".

There are wars on this planet but I don't feel that "wheelie bin placement" is one of the more serious ones.

#5394. China's Communist Party elite hold key talks on governance

The fifth plenum comes ahead of a major party congress next year, where Chinese President Xi Jinping is almost certain to secure a historic fourth term and oversee a leadership reshuffle.

A Chinese flag flutters atop the Great Hall of the People during sunset in Beijing, China on Sep 30, 2026. (Photo: Reuters/Florence Lo/Pool)

BEIJING: China's President Xi Jinping opened a key meeting of Communist Party elites in Beijing on Monday (Oct 26), state media said, which observers will be closely watching for clues as to the country's direction and future leadership.

Roughly 300 members of the ruling Communist Party's Central Committee in attendance at the meeting, called the fifth plenum, will be looking to tighten discipline within their ranks, according to state media.

That includes measures to reduce corruption and make cadres more effective and loyal.

Xi opened the session on Monday, presenting a draft decision by the Central Committee that "sets out strategic plans for strengthening full and rigorous Party self-governance", state news agency Xinhua reported.

Few details from the closed-door gathering, held under tight security, will be made known until it concludes on Thursday, but the timing of the meeting is crucial.

The fifth plenum comes ahead of a major party congress next year, where 73-year-old Xi is almost certain to secure a historic fourth term and oversee a leadership reshuffle.

Previous plenums have represented key moments for Xi to cement his authority.

The Chinese leader has waged a 14-year campaign against corruption that has purged thousands of officials, including dozens of the Central Committee.

Yet he remains frustrated with cadres he deems are not implementing his orders.

State media published an article ahead of the plenum, based on a speech Xi gave in January in which he railed against "two-faced" officials who appear to comply with central directives but "inwardly resist", pursue "individualism" and are "politically opportunistic".

Analysts told AFP that Xi is trying to maximise efficiency and loyalty among cadres by imposing more supervision and rules.

But as a result of his expansive purges, this year's plenum is expected to have the lowest turnout since former leader Mao Zedong's death in 1976.

Eight of the Central Committee's seats lie vacant, with another 15 members under investigation and at risk of being replaced.

Xi's anti-corruption drive has also targeted the military, toppling five of the seven members of the Central Military Commission (CMC), the party's top armed forces body.

Of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022, only two have not been purged or disappeared, according to the Asia Society Policy Institute.

The plenum could see new members appointed to the CMC; the party could wait until next year's congress to replenish it; or Xi might even restructure party control over its vast military.

The talks also come at an unsteady time for the world's second-largest economy, which has struggled to address persistently sluggish domestic spending and a protracted crisis in the crucial property sector.

Turbulent political and economic ties with the United States are also weighing on China's leaders.

Authorities are expected to release a summary of the outcomes after the meeting concludes on Thursday.

#5395. Rush to vaccinate little penguins against H5N1 as another seal is diagnosed

SBS acknowledges the Traditional Custodians of Country and their connections and continuous care for the skies, lands and waterways throughout Australia.

Bird flu has likely spread to a second seal, one day after the first mammal in Australia was confirmed to have contracted the virus.

Five suspected H5 bird flu cases were recorded in South Australia on Monday, including a long-nosed fur seal at The Pages Conservation Park, the state's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said in a statement on Monday morning.

The Pages — which covers two small islands between Kangaroo Island and the mainland — is a haven for the endangered Australian sea lion.

The fur seal has been tested for bird flu, with results expected in the coming days.

The first positive case of the virus in a mammal was confirmed on Sunday in a long-nosed fur seal at Beachport, 300km south of Adelaide, which authorities believed was contracted from wild birds.

Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.

Before the new case was announced, Environment Minister Murray Watt said the spread from birds to mammals was inevitable and the government was examining whether further vaccination programs were needed.

"We are likely to see mass mortalities of birds and mammals, and I know that is a very distressing thing for Australians to hear. But we also need to be realistic," he told ABC TV on Monday.

"This is what we've seen happen overseas. Australia is very fortunate that we've been the last continent on Earth to have this strain of bird flu happen. But we are likely to see those kind of events as we have overseas."

Agriculture Minister Julie Collins said the federal government was investigating whether bird flu vaccines were available for use in mammals.

"There are trials underway in North America, in California and Hawaii, and this is using a vaccine that's been developed for cattle," she told ABC radio.

"There certainly is nothing commercially available, but we do continue to look at that research."

Bird flu vaccinations have been rolled out to at-risk species, including the little penguins on Victoria's Phillip Island.

Many were corralled into pens to receive the first of two vaccinations on Sunday night.

With case numbers on the rise, authorities have stepped in to do what they can to defend the 5,000-strong colony.

The penguins' nightly ritual of returning to the same burrow, along the same path, made them ideal candidates for vaccination, Phillip Island Nature Parks reserve manager Ben Thomas said.

As a world-first in scale, the process has taken some experimentation and fine-tuning.

"We've had our teams out late into the night for a week now and learning a lot along the process," Thomas said.

"We started on some of the quieter penguin pathways to fine-tune the whole process and get it working as quickly as we can, so we can process as many penguins as we can each night.

"We've now moved to the western end of the penguin parade, where the larger numbers are, and it's working really well."

A further 600 penguins were vaccinated over the weekend, taking the total number that have received a first dose at Phillip Island and St Kilda to about 1,000.

#5398. Les sept pays africains où les salaires sont les plus élevés

Un récent rapport de LiveGDP a mis en évidence d'importantes disparités de salaires entre les pays africains. Djibouti se distingue par le salaire mensuel moyen le plus élevé, net d'impôts et autres cotisations obligatoires.

Selon ce rapport, les salaires varient en fonction de divers facteurs, notamment le niveau de développement économique, la productivité du travail, la vigueur de secteurs clés tels que le pétrole, les mines, le tourisme et les services financiers, ainsi que la demande sur le marché du travail. Parmi les autres facteurs influençant les revenus des travailleurs figurent les taux d'imposition, l'inflation, le taux de change et le contexte de l'emploi dans chaque pays.

Le Kenya se classe 10e sur 54 pays africains en termes de salaire mensuel moyen net. Les données montrent qu'un travailleur kenyan gagne en moyenne 199 778 FCFA par mois après déductions, ce qui place le pays au 132e rang mondial.

"Le Kenya affiche un salaire mensuel moyen de 344 dollars après déductions, le plaçant au 10e rang en Afrique", indique le rapport. En Afrique de l'Est, le Kenya a devancé ses voisins, la Tanzanie, l'Ouganda et le Rwanda, mais est resté derrière Djibouti, qui arrive en tête non seulement de l'Afrique de l'Est, mais aussi de tout le continent, avec un salaire moyen de 2 836 dollars (1 647 007 FCFA) par mois.

Cependant, LiveGDP souligne que les salaires, à eux seuls, ne permettent pas de mesurer directement la qualité de vie ni le pouvoir d'achat, car le coût du logement, de l'alimentation, des transports, de la santé, de l'éducation et l'inflation varient d'un pays à l'autre.

Vous trouverez ci-dessous la liste des sept pays africains où les salaires sont les plus élevés.

Djibouti affiche le revenu disponible mensuel moyen le plus élevé d'Afrique, s'élevant à environ 367 311 shillings kenyans (2 836 dollars américains, environ 1,63 million de francs CFA).

Situé à l'entrée de la mer Rouge et du golfe d'Aden, à proximité de l'une des routes maritimes les plus fréquentées au monde, le pays est devenu une plaque tournante majeure pour le transport de marchandises et les services portuaires.

Sa position stratégique sur les routes commerciales de la mer Rouge et la présence de bases militaires internationales ont contribué à sa croissance économique.

L'Afrique du Sud arrive en deuxième position avec un salaire moyen de 1 270 dollars américains (environ 737 552 FCFA). Comptant parmi les plus grandes économies du continent, le pays a développé des secteurs minier, financier, manufacturier et des services.

Les Seychelles suivent avec un salaire moyen de 790 dollars américains (environ 458 792 F CFA). Son économie repose principalement sur le tourisme, la pêche et les services financiers, et sa faible population contribue à un revenu par habitant élevé.

Maurice fait partie des pays où les salaires sont les plus élevés d'Afrique en raison de son économie diversifiée qui comprend le tourisme, les services financiers, la technologie et les industries textiles. Le pays est également connu pour son bon environnement des affaires.

Le Gabon bénéficie de vastes ressources pétrolières et autres ressources naturelles. Malgré sa faible population, les revenus du secteur pétrolier en ont fait l'un des pays aux salaires les plus élevés du continent.

Le Botswana s'est forgé une réputation de stabilité politique et de bonne gestion des revenus tirés de l'exploitation minière des diamants. Le secteur minier constitue un pilier essentiel qui contribue à maintenir des niveaux de salaires élevés par rapport à de nombreux pays africains.

Des informations vérifiées à portée de main

La Namibie complète le top sept des pays aux salaires les plus élevés. Son économie repose sur l'exploitation minière, la pêche et le tourisme, et les niveaux de salaires y sont soutenus par une population peu nombreuse et un secteur formel dynamique.

Selon les chiffres, le Kenya se classe 10e en Afrique, avec un salaire mensuel moyen de 344 dollars américains (environ 199 778 FCFA) après déductions. Il devance ainsi de nombreux pays d'Afrique de l'Est, dont la Tanzanie, l'Ouganda et le Rwanda.

Le Soudan du Sud a enregistré la moyenne la plus basse, à 70 $ ou 40 652 FCFA, suivi du Burundi à 75 $ ou 43 556 FCFA, de la Sierra Leone à 80 $ ou 46 460 FCFA, de la Gambie à 85 $ ou 49 363 FCFA, et du Malawi et du Soudan à 90 $ ou 52 267 FCFA.

Cependant, LiveGDP souligne que les données salariales ne permettent pas, à elles seules, de mesurer directement le niveau de vie. Le coût du logement, de l'alimentation, des transports, de la santé, de l'éducation, ainsi que l'inflation et les taux de change varient d'un pays à l'autre.

Par conséquent, ce classement indique le revenu disponible des travailleurs après déductions, mais ne constitue pas une mesure complète du pouvoir d'achat ni de la qualité de vie dans chaque pays.

#5399. ABC presenter Trevor Chappell to hang up mic after 26 years

Trevor Chappell has long been a familiar voice for shift workers and insomniacs. (ABC)

After 26 years of keeping Australia's night owls company on ABC radio across Australia, Overnights presenter Trevor Chappell has decided to call it a day.

The 65-year-old will host his last Overnights show on Thursday, July 30.

While the rest of the country has slept, Trevor has been a familiar voice for shift workers and insomniacs since 2000.

Having worked in mining, trained as a teacher and even dabbled in acting school (he quit when he realised he could never remember the lines), Trevor's love affair with radio started with a pamphlet he found on the coffee table of his Melbourne share house. It took him to the Western Australian Academy of Performing Arts to study broadcasting.

It was there that one of his lecturers gave him some advice that he has carried with him ever since: "Never underestimate the relationship you have with your listeners because they know you far better than you know them".

The much-loved presenter has developed a personal connection with many of his listeners. (ABC)

It didn't take too long for Trevor to get snapped up as a producer and roving reporter, before he was offered the Overnights gig.

He recalls that terrifying first night on air in 2000 when he was surrounded by pieces of paper with extensive notes and tightly written scripts. But when his first talkback caller rang in — Pamela from Queensland — all the nerves disappeared.

"She was so kind and welcoming that it made it so easy," Trevor says.

"She would regularly call. It was always wonderful when I talked to her."

Like so many of his listeners since, Trevor developed a personal connection with Pamela and visited her during a trip to Queensland. Sadly, when she went into a nursing home, it became too difficult for her to call.

The relationship with Overnights listeners is an intimate one. Trevor says they have been companions to him as much as he has been a companion to them.

"I got to know people over a period of time, It's not friendship, it's companionship. You get to know people," he says.

"You get to know their history, what makes them laugh. You can muck around a bit and not be too serious.

"By having that relationship, it encourages more people to call in as well."

Trevor has had many regular callers over the decades. (ABC )

There's Simon, who calls in and always says "box of birds".

There's Don, who used to call in every year to request the same song for his wedding anniversary.

There's the regular caller who makes notes of all the things Trevor got wrong since they last spoke.

And then there are the people Trevor has lost. Like June from Portland and the show's royal correspondent, Barry.

Barry is the show's former "royal correspondent" (ABC News)

These have been, Trevor says, among the many times he has cried on air — moments that have struck him out of nowhere.

He still gets choked up remembering the listener who called in to reminisce about taking her child for their first day of school.

"A woman said it affected her most when she went shopping and she had no-one's hand to hold and it still makes me feel funny," Trevor says.

There was the widow who had just nursed her husband through his final days, watching him slowly slip away with Alzheimer's. When she told Trevor she was up in the night because she felt so lonely, he had to play a song to pull himself together.

Trevor has broadcast from the Royal Melbourne Show. (ABC)

Like when Trevor asked listeners what colour the werewolf's hair was in the Warren Zevon song, Werewolves of London.

As people kept calling in to say that the werewolf's hair was "perfect", Trevor was adamant they were wrong.

"I had misheard the lyric for my whole life. I thought the lyric was 'his hair was purple'," he says.

"I went to a song and looked it up. I had to come back and apologise."

Trevor still laughs at the incredibly creative insult he received from one listener, who texted in to say he sounded like "a eunuch in a wind tunnel".

Working through the night has suited Trevor, who describes himself as shy. (ABC Melbourne: Kristian Silva)

Another time, Trevor received a text and asked Overnights gardening expert, Sabrina Hahn, "Can you give me some advice on using kar-le?"

"[Sabrina] laughed and laughed and then she said, 'I think you meant kale'. So that became a running gag for ages."

These memories speak to the deep connection Trevor has with listeners. There's a closeness that develops during the night because, as Trevor says, "We are different to day people".

People reveal things about themselves that they wouldn't in daylight hours.

"It's the best job. You talk to really interesting people and you have the time to talk to people. Daytime radio does not give you the time," he says.

"I can talk to a listener for three or four minutes."

Trevor achieved his aim of creating a positive show. Mindful that many Overnights listeners live with anxiety, Trevor has never wanted the show's topics to be triggering or distressing.

"I don't think I'd change anything … I feel proud of what we have done and I will feel sad to leave it.

For Trevor, working the graveyard shift has been a lifestyle, not just a job, and one that has suited him just fine.

It was quiet in the night, and Trevor describes himself as shy. But his time has come to hang up the microphone.

Red Symons and Trevor were passing ships in the nights for many years at ABC Southbank when the former Skyhooks guitarist presented 774 ABC Melbourne Breakfast.

Red Symons and Trevor often crossed paths as one shift ended and another began. (ABC Archives)

"Trevor and I were two lonely, old guys who bumped into each other in the night," Red says.

"He was always pleased to see me because it meant that he was nearly finished. I was pleased to see him because I was about to start.

"What we had in common was that we both had the company of the callers."

Long-time colleague Michael Pavlich started working with Trevor in the 1990s, when they were both producers with 774. And Michael was Trevor's studio producer for a large portion of his Overnights stint.

The pair produced one of Trevor's favourite Overnight shows when Trevor did live crosses into the studio from the side of the road in the Pilliga Forest in northern New South Wales. The site had been nominated by Overnights listeners as one of the scariest places in Australia.

Chappell (right) with long-time producers Michael Pavlich and Helen Richardson in 2020. (ABC Melbourne: Kristian Silva)

Michael says he could never have imagined in the 1990s that the pair would still be colleagues all these years later.

"Through his dedication and his commitment to the time slot, Trevor has built a national audience that established ABC Overnights as a significant presence on the media landscape," Michael says.

"The spontaneous nature of the program and the uncontrollable laughter that often resulted always provided a wonderful antidote to the unsociable working hours we shared.

"He is a gifted communicator who takes pride in his honesty, and someone who always treats listeners and colleagues with an even temperament and great respect. He has never thrown an underarm in his life."

(Trevor is no relation to the cricketer of the same name, who is best remembered for bowling the infamous underarm delivery on the final ball of a one-day international against New Zealand in Melbourne in 1981, under instructions from his captain and older brother, Greg Chappell.)

Overnights day producer John Standish says it has been a pleasure producing Trevor in recent years, after Trevor returned to Overnights from a stint on Afternoons.

For Trevor's part, he says he simply could not have lasted so long without the support of his wife Cathy and his producers.

Even so, this much-loved presenter and member of the ABC team is not sure how he will say goodbye.

"I'm trying not to think about it. It will be really sad. I'm going to have to try really hard to hold back the tears."

#5400. Tassie, Vic gold output clears Kaiser Reef debt as cash hits $40M

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month.

Dual-asset gold producer Kaiser Reef has wiped a key debt from its books after a solid September quarter, a move expected to unchain about $600,000 a month in operating cash flow.

The company banked 6263 ounces of gold during the period, boosting its cash and bullion balance to a healthy $40 million and allowing it to fully repay the senior secured gold loan used to acquire its flagship Henty gold mine in Tasmania.

Production from the company’s two Australian assets continued to build momentum during the period, with total gold output rising to 6263 ounces from 6000 ounces in the prior quarter. The cornerstone Henty mine churned out 5692 ounces of gold and a further 5259 ounces of silver, while its Maldon project in Victoria chipped in another 572 ounces of gold. Impressively, the Maldon operation has now lifted its output for three consecutive quarters, jumping 65 per cent since March.

Total production generated an underlying cash flow of $5.6 million for the quarter, which more than covered $2.8 million in debt and deferred payments, allowing Kaiser to increase its net cash and bullion position by a hefty $2.8 million.

The strong financial position enabled the company to make a final delivery of 104 ounces of gold in October, wiping the slate clean on the 1872-ounce Auramet gold loan. With that facility retired, Kaiser’s only remaining gold delivery obligation is a deferred payment to Catalyst Metals as part of the Henty acquisition, requiring 50 ounces per month through to October 2030. However, the company says repaying the principal acquisition loan from the mine’s own cash flow is an important milestone.

Kaiser Reef managing director Brad Valiukas said: “Kaiser delivered 6263oz of gold across Henty and Maldon during the quarter, while increasing cash and bullion to A$40 million, paying down debt and advancing Maldon. We have completely repaid the Auramet gold loan, on schedule, with the final delivery made in October. The gold loan helped us acquire Henty, and repaying it from Henty’s own cash flow is an important milestone for Kaiser.”

The impressive quarterly report further underscores a remarkable full-year turnaround for Kaiser, which swung from a $20.24 million statutory loss in FY2025 to a $16.8 million after-tax profit in FY2026, backed by an impressive $44.7 million cash inflow from operations.

The Henty mine, nestled in Tasmania’s richly endowed Mount Read Volcanics belt alongside the legendary Rosebery and Mount Lyell operations, remains the company’s gold-producing workhorse. A recent resource and reserve update effectively offset mining depletion, maintaining the mine’s ore reserve at 198,000 ounces of gold and its overall resource at 429,000 ounces. In a shrewd move to sweat its assets, the company is also working with fellow ASX-lister Flynn Gold to process its ore through Henty’s 300,000-tonne-per-annum processing plant. As part of the expansion plan, Kaiser has applied to increase its tailings capacity by two million tonnes.

While Henty provides the cash flow, Kaiser’s Maldon operation in Victoria’s fabled Golden Triangle offers a significant high-grade growth opportunity. The project, with a strong track record of producing 1.75 million ounces at a staggering 28 grams per tonne (g/t) gold, is anchored by the fully permitted 200,000-tonne-per-annum Porcupine Flats processing facility. Its Union Hill deposit hosts an inferred resource of 187,000 ounces grading a solid 4.44g/t gold, with site stockpiles adding a further 11,700 ounces.

All up, the company’s global resource stands at 5.53 million tonnes grading 3.46g/t gold for 615,000 ounces. With FY27 total production targeted at around 32,000 ounces and no hedging in place, the gold producer appears well positioned to capture more upside should the bullion price remain steady.

Another major milestone for the quarter was the start of underground development at the Union Hill mine. The new development will provide access for underground diamond drilling to test the northern extensions of existing workings at Maldon’s Eaglehawk, Linscott’s, Ladies and Sailors Reefs targets.

The underground push adds another dimension to a busy surface exploration campaign aimed at building a pipeline of fresh drill targets. Recent infill soil sampling has outlined strong, continuous gold and arsenic anomalies across multiple structures, with some promising trends extending over 1.5 kilometres of strike. This work has been bolstered by a helicopter-borne magnetic and radiometric survey, providing a clearer picture of the structural architecture, with a surface diamond drilling campaign also ongoing.

With the Henty operation humming along and paying the bills, Kaiser appears to be in an enviable position of being largely debt-free and sitting on a sizeable cash pile as it methodically advances exploration across one of Victoria’s most celebrated high-grade goldfields. With no hedging in place and a production target of 32,000 ounces for FY27, the company looks to be fully exposed to any upside in the gold price. As drill rods turn on both surface and underground hotspots at Maldon, punters will likely be watching closely for the results to start flowing.
